topics.title: Types of solutions and percentage, ppm concentration

learn.hook: The saline drip in an AIIMS ward and the sea breeze over Marina Beach are both solutions. Chemistry just asks: what dissolved in what, and how much?
points: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components. The component in larger amount is usually the solvent; the others are solutes. A binary solution has exactly two components.

By physical state of solute and solvent there are nine types: gas in gas (O₂ in N₂), liquid in gas (chloroform vapour mixed with N₂), solid in gas (camphor in N₂); gas in liquid (O₂ in water), liquid in liquid (ethanol in water), solid in liquid (glucose in water); gas in solid (H₂ in palladium), liquid in solid (amalgam of mercury with sodium), solid in solid (copper dissolved in gold).
Mass percentage (w/w) = (mass of component ÷ total mass of solution) × 100. Volume percentage (V/V) = (volume of component ÷ total volume of solution) × 100.
Mass by volume percentage (w/V) = mass of solute in grams dissolved in 100 mL of solution; common in medicine and pharmacy (normal saline is 0.9% w/V NaCl).
Parts per million (ppm) = (amount of component ÷ total amount of solution) × 10⁶; used for trace amounts such as fluoride in drinking water or pollutants in air.

example.q: 0.0025 g of fluoride ions are present in 500 g of a water sample. Find the concentration in ppm and the mass percentage.

learn.reallife: Packaged drinking water labels in India list dissolved solids and fluoride in ppm (mg per litre), and the BIS standard sets limits on them. Hospital IV bottles of normal saline are labelled 0.9% w/V sodium chloride.

quiz.q: A solution contains 5 g of glucose in 45 g of water. What is the mass percentage of glucose?
quiz.explain: Mass % = mass of solute ÷ mass of solution × 100 = 5 ÷ 50 × 100 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the mass of solvent (45 g) instead of the mass of solution (50 g)

quiz.q: Which of the following is a solid solution in which the solute is a liquid?
quiz.explain: In an amalgam the solvent (sodium) is a solid and the solute (mercury) is a liquid.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which component is the solute and which is the solvent

quiz.q: 10 mL of ethanol is mixed with water to make 50 mL of solution. What is the volume percentage (V/V) of ethanol?
quiz.explain: V/V % = volume of ethanol ÷ volume of solution × 100 = 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the volume of water (40 mL) instead of the total solution volume

quiz.q: A water sample of mass 2 kg contains 0.006 g of lead ions. What is the concentration of lead in ppm?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert 2 kg into 2000 g before dividing

quiz.q: Normal saline is labelled '0.9% w/V NaCl'. How many grams of NaCl are present in 500 mL of it?
quiz.explain: 0.9% w/V means 0.9 g per 100 mL, so 500 mL contains 0.9 × 5 = 4.5 g.
quiz.mistake: Treats 0.9% as the amount in the whole bottle, ignoring the 'per 100 mL' meaning

quiz.q: Which concentration term is most convenient for expressing the amount of a pollutant gas present in trace amount in air?
quiz.explain: When a solute is present in trace quantities, percentages become tiny and awkward, so parts per million is used.
quiz.mistake: Thinks percentages work equally well for very small amounts

quiz.q: In a binary solution of 2 g of iodine in 100 g of carbon tetrachloride, which statement is correct?
options: CCl₄ is the solute because it is a liquid
Both are solvents because the mixture is homogeneous
A binary solution must contain water
Iodine is the solute and CCl₄ is the solvent
quiz.explain: The component present in the larger amount (CCl₄) is the solvent; iodine is the solute. A binary solution simply has two components.
quiz.mistake: Believes the solvent must always be water or must be decided by state alone

quiz.q: A 250 g solution contains 20% by mass of sugar. How much water is in it?
quiz.explain: Sugar = 20% of 250 g = 50 g, so water = 250 − 50 = 200 g.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mass of sugar instead of the mass of water

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'What exactly makes something a solution, and how do I say how concentrated it is when the amount is tiny?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Homogeneous mixture of solute in solvent, and ppm for tiny traces. I can read my water bottle label now!
teach.nudge: You told me about the mixture, but how would you express a trace amount like fluoride in water?

topics.title: Mole fraction, molarity and molality

learn.hook: A pharma lab in Hyderabad prepares the same solution in summer and winter. Why do chemists there prefer molality over molarity for precise work?
points: Mole fraction of component i: xᵢ = nᵢ ÷ (total moles). In a binary solution x₁ + x₂ = 1; it has no units.
Molarity (M) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres (mol L⁻¹). It changes with temperature because volume expands or contracts.
Molality (m) = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent in kg (mol kg⁻¹). It does not depend on temperature because mass does not change.
Mass percentage, ppm, mole fraction and molality are temperature independent; molarity is temperature dependent.
To go from molarity to molality you need the density: mass of solution = density × volume; mass of solvent = mass of solution − mass of solute.

example.q: A solution has 1.0 mol NaCl (58.5 g) in 1.000 L of solution. Its density is 1.0585 g mL⁻¹. Find its molality.
steps: Mass of solution = 1000 mL × 1.0585 g mL⁻¹ = 1058.5 g

learn.reallife: Doctors at AIIMS read blood glucose in mmol per litre (a molarity unit), while chemists making precise measurements over changing temperatures prefer temperature-independent units such as molality and mole fraction.

games.title: Term ↔ definition
pairs: Moles of a component ÷ total moles
Moles of solute per litre of solution
Moles of solute per kg of solvent
Mass of component per 100 g of solution

quiz.q: 46 g of ethanol (C₂H₅OH, M = 46 g mol⁻¹) is mixed with 90 g of water (M = 18 g mol⁻¹). What is the mole fraction of ethanol?
quiz.explain: Ethanol = 1 mol, water = 5 mol. x(ethanol) = 1 ÷ (1 + 5) = 0.167.
quiz.mistake: Divides moles of ethanol by moles of water only (1/5 = 0.2)

quiz.q: 4 g of NaOH (M = 40 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. What is its molarity (in mol L⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert 250 mL into litres or stops at the number of moles

quiz.q: 18 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water. What is the molality (in mol kg⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Moles of glucose = 0.1; mass of solvent = 0.500 kg; m = 0.1 ÷ 0.5 = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Uses grams of water instead of kilograms, or reports moles as molality

quiz.q: Why does the molarity of a solution change when it is warmed, while its molality does not?
options: Volume of solution changes with temperature but mass of solvent does not
Moles of solute increase on heating
Mass of solvent increases on heating
Molality is defined using volume of solvent
quiz.explain: Molarity has volume in its denominator, and liquids expand on heating. Molality uses mass, which stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heating changes the amount of solute

quiz.q: A 10% (w/w) aqueous solution of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is given. What is its molality (in mol kg⁻¹, to two decimals)?
quiz.explain: 100 g of solution has 10 g glucose in 90 g water: m = (10/180) ÷ 0.090 = 0.62 mol kg⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Takes the solvent mass as 100 g instead of 90 g (gives 0.56)
steps: Take 100 g solution: 10 g glucose + 90 g water

quiz.q: In a binary solution the mole fraction of the solute is 0.15. What is the mole fraction of the solvent?
quiz.explain: In a binary solution x₁ + x₂ = 1, so x(solvent) = 1 − 0.15 = 0.85.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that mole fractions of all components add up to 1

quiz.q: A solution contains 58.5 g NaCl (1.0 mol) in 1.000 L of solution of density 1.0585 g mL⁻¹. What is its molality (in mol kg⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Mass of solution = 1058.5 g; solvent = 1058.5 − 58.5 = 1000 g = 1 kg; m = 1.0 ÷ 1 = 1.0 mol kg⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Uses the mass of the solution (1.0585 kg) as the mass of solvent

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Molality is preferred over molarity for accurate physical chemistry work at varying temperatures. Reason (R): Molality is defined per kilogram of solvent, and mass does not change with temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Molality is temperature independent precisely because it uses mass of solvent, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the temperature independence to the use of mass

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Molarity and molality sound like twins. What's the real difference between them?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Molarity per litre of solution changes with temperature; molality per kg of solvent doesn't. Twins no more!
teach.nudge: You gave one definition. What is in the denominator of the other, and which one is affected by temperature?

topics.title: Solubility of solids and Henry's law for gases

learn.hook: Pop open a chilled bottle of soda on a hot Delhi afternoon and it fizzes wildly. William Henry worked out the rule behind that fizz in 1803.
points: Solubility is the maximum amount of a substance that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. 'Like dissolves like': polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar in non-polar.
In a saturated solution, undissolved solute is in dynamic equilibrium with dissolved solute (rate of dissolution = rate of crystallisation). An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.

For solids, if dissolving is endothermic (Δsol H > 0) solubility rises with temperature; if exothermic (Δsol H < 0) it falls (Le Chatelier). Pressure has no significant effect because solids and liquids are nearly incompressible.
Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: p = K_H x. Solubility of a gas rises with its pressure.
K_H depends on the gas and the temperature. A larger K_H at the same pressure means a smaller mole fraction, i.e. lower solubility.

example.q: At 298 K, K_H for CO₂ in water is 1.67 kbar. Find the mole fraction of CO₂ in water when its partial pressure is 3.34 bar.

learn.reallife: Soft-drink bottling plants in India seal the bottles under high CO₂ pressure; Henry's law tells them how much gas stays dissolved until you twist the cap.

games.title: Solubility true or false
items: Pressure has no significant effect on the solubility of a solid in a liquid.
Solids and liquids are highly incompressible, so pressure barely matters.
A larger value of K_H means a gas is more soluble at the same pressure.
x = p/K_H, so a larger K_H gives a smaller mole fraction — lower solubility.
In a saturated solution, dissolution and crystallisation go on at equal rates.
This is the dynamic equilibrium of a saturated solution.
If dissolving a solid is exothermic, its solubility increases with temperature.
By Le Chatelier, raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, so solubility falls.
Naphthalene dissolves readily in benzene but not in water.
Like dissolves like: non-polar naphthalene suits non-polar benzene.
Henry's law says solubility of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure above the solution.
That is the law, written as p = K_H x.

items.text: Henry's law is written as p = ___ x.
Polar solutes dissolve best in ___ solvents.
A solution that can still dissolve more solute at that temperature is ___.
If Δsol H > 0, solubility ___ as temperature rises.

quiz.q: At 298 K, K_H for CO₂ is 1.67 kbar. If the partial pressure of CO₂ over water is 3.34 bar, the mole fraction of CO₂ is n × 10⁻³. What is n?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert kbar into bar, which shifts the answer by 1000

quiz.q: Gas A has K_H = 34.86 kbar and gas B has K_H = 144.97 kbar in water at 293 K. Which statement is correct?
options: Solubility does not depend on K_H
A is more soluble than B at the same partial pressure
B is more soluble than A at the same partial pressure
quiz.explain: x = p/K_H, so the gas with the smaller K_H (A) dissolves more at the same pressure.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a bigger Henry's constant means more solubility

quiz.q: The partial pressure of a gas over a solution is doubled at constant temperature. What happens to its mole fraction in the solution?
quiz.explain: p = K_H x with K_H constant at fixed temperature, so x is directly proportional to p.
quiz.mistake: Thinks K_H changes with pressure

quiz.q: Dissolving a certain salt in water is endothermic. What happens to its solubility as temperature increases?
options: It first increases then becomes zero
quiz.explain: For Δsol H > 0, Le Chatelier's principle says raising temperature shifts the equilibrium towards more dissolution.
quiz.mistake: Applies the gas rule (solubility falls with temperature) to solids

quiz.q: Why does pressure have no significant effect on the solubility of solids in liquids?
options: Solids and liquids are highly incompressible
Solids do not dissolve under pressure
quiz.explain: Because neither the solid nor the liquid changes volume noticeably with pressure, the equilibrium barely shifts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pressure affects all solubilities as it does for gases

quiz.q: Which pair best illustrates 'like dissolves like'?
options: Sugar in kerosene and wax in water
Sodium chloride in benzene and naphthalene in water
Sodium chloride in water and naphthalene in benzene
Glucose in petrol and iodine in water
quiz.explain: Ionic/polar NaCl dissolves in polar water; non-polar naphthalene dissolves in non-polar benzene.
quiz.mistake: Does not match polarity of solute with polarity of solvent

quiz.q: A gas has K_H = 100 kbar in water at 298 K. What partial pressure (in bar) is needed to make its mole fraction 1 × 10⁻⁵ in water?
quiz.explain: p = K_H x = 1.0 × 10⁵ bar × 1 × 10⁻⁵ = 1 bar.
quiz.mistake: Uses K_H in kbar without converting to bar

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In a saturated solution, the amount of dissolved solute stays constant. Reason (R): Dissolution has completely stopped in a saturated solution.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The amount stays constant because dissolution and crystallisation occur at equal rates — a dynamic equilibrium, not a stop.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equilibrium means the processes have stopped

teach.ask: Gappu peeks into a soda bottle: 'Why does opening the cap make it fizz? Explain using Henry's law.'
teach.praise: Pop! Lower partial pressure means lower solubility, so CO₂ escapes as bubbles. Henry would be proud!
teach.nudge: You mentioned the gas, but how is its solubility related to the pressure above the liquid?

topics.title: Henry's law in action: divers, mountaineers and temperature

learn.hook: An Indian Navy diver surfacing too fast can feel crippling joint pain called 'the bends', while soldiers posted at Siachen battle breathlessness. Both stories are Henry's law stories.
points: Soft drinks and soda water are sealed under high CO₂ pressure to increase its solubility; opening the bottle lowers the pressure and CO₂ bubbles out.

Scuba divers breathe air at high pressure underwater, so more N₂ dissolves in blood. On rapid ascent the pressure falls, N₂ forms bubbles in the blood and blocks capillaries: 'the bends', which is painful and dangerous.
To reduce this, diving tanks use air diluted with helium (about 11.7% He, 56.2% N₂ and 32.1% O₂), since helium is much less soluble in blood.
At high altitudes the partial pressure of O₂ is low, so less O₂ dissolves in blood and tissues: climbers become weak and cannot think clearly (anoxia).
Gas solubility in liquids decreases as temperature rises (dissolving a gas is exothermic). K_H increases with temperature — for O₂ in water it rises from 34.86 kbar at 293 K to 46.82 kbar at 303 K.

example.q: K_H for O₂ in water is 34.86 kbar at 293 K and 46.82 kbar at 303 K. At the same partial pressure, at which temperature is O₂ more soluble, and why do fish prefer cold water?
steps: x = p/K_H, so a smaller K_H gives a larger mole fraction
So more O₂ dissolves at 293 K; cold water carries more dissolved oxygen for aquatic life
example.answer: More soluble at 293 K; cold water holds more dissolved O₂

learn.reallife: In summer, fish kills are sometimes reported in shallow Indian ponds and lakes: warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, exactly as K_H increasing with temperature predicts.

games.title: Situation ↔ Henry's-law reason
pairs: N₂ bubbles form as pressure drops
He is much less soluble in blood
More O₂ dissolves at lower temperature

games.title: Diver's bends: put the chain of events in order
games.prompt: From the dive to the pain
items: Diver breathes compressed air at depth
Higher pressure dissolves more N₂ in blood
Diver rises quickly to the surface
Pressure drops and dissolved N₂ comes out as bubbles
Bubbles block capillaries causing the bends

quiz.q: Why are soda water bottles sealed under high pressure?
options: To prevent the glass from breaking
To lower the boiling point of water
To make CO₂ react with sugar
To increase the solubility of CO₂
quiz.explain: By Henry's law, a higher partial pressure of CO₂ dissolves more CO₂ in the drink.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pressure is only for packaging strength

quiz.q: The bends experienced by scuba divers are caused mainly by which gas coming out of the blood?
quiz.explain: Nitrogen, which dissolves at high pressure, forms bubbles when the pressure falls quickly.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the oxygen being breathed is the culprit

quiz.q: Why is air in scuba tanks diluted with helium?
options: Helium is more soluble in blood
Helium is much less soluble in blood than nitrogen
quiz.explain: Using a poorly soluble gas reduces the amount of gas dissolved in blood at depth, lowering the risk of the bends.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the solubility of helium

quiz.q: What is the main cause of anoxia in climbers at high altitudes?
options: Low partial pressure of oxygen at high altitude
quiz.explain: The partial pressure of O₂ is lower at altitude, so less O₂ dissolves in blood and tissues.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the percentage of oxygen in air falls instead of its partial pressure

quiz.q: K_H for O₂ in water is 34.86 kbar at 293 K and 46.82 kbar at 303 K. What does this show?
options: O₂ does not obey Henry's law
Solubility of O₂ increases as temperature increases
Solubility of O₂ decreases as temperature increases
quiz.explain: A larger K_H at higher temperature means a smaller mole fraction at the same pressure, so O₂ is less soluble when warmer.
quiz.mistake: Reads a bigger K_H as a bigger solubility

quiz.q: Why do aquatic species feel more comfortable in cold water than in warm water?
options: Cold water holds less dissolved oxygen
Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen
Cold water has a higher vapour pressure
quiz.explain: Gas solubility falls with rising temperature, so warm water carries less dissolved O₂.
quiz.mistake: Applies the rule for solids to gases

quiz.q: Dissolving a gas in a liquid is generally an exothermic process. On this basis, how does raising the temperature affect gas solubility?
options: It makes the gas react with the liquid
quiz.explain: For an exothermic process, Le Chatelier's principle says heating shifts the equilibrium backwards, releasing gas.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign of the enthalpy of dissolution

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A chilled soft drink goes flat more slowly than a warm one once opened. Reason (R): K_H for CO₂ increases with temperature.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: At low temperature K_H is smaller, so CO₂ stays more soluble and escapes more slowly. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the size of K_H to how much gas stays dissolved

teach.ask: Gappu wants to scuba dive: 'Why might I get the bends if I swim up too fast?'
teach.praise: Glug-glug! High pressure dissolves extra nitrogen, and a sudden drop makes bubbles. I'll rise slowly!
teach.nudge: Which gas is the problem, and what happens to its solubility when the pressure drops?

topics.title: Raoult's law for liquid–liquid solutions

learn.hook: Refineries at Jamnagar separate liquid mixtures by distillation. To predict what boils off first, you need François Raoult's law.
points: Raoult's law (volatile liquids): the partial vapour pressure of each component is proportional to its mole fraction in solution: p₁ = p₁° x₁ and p₂ = p₂° x₂, where p° is the vapour pressure of the pure liquid.
Dalton's law gives the total: p_total = p₁ + p₂ = p₁° x₁ + p₂° x₂ = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°) x₂. A plot of p_total against x₂ is a straight line joining p₁° and p₂°.
Composition of the vapour: y₁ = p₁ ÷ p_total. The vapour is richer in the more volatile component (the one with higher p°).
Raoult's law is a special case of Henry's law: both say partial pressure ∝ mole fraction, and for Raoult's law the constant K_H equals p₁°.

example.q: Liquids A (p_A° = 400 mm Hg) and B (p_B° = 600 mm Hg) form an ideal solution with x_A = 0.4. Find p_total and the mole fraction of A in the vapour.

learn.reallife: Petrol is a blend of volatile hydrocarbons. Indian refiners adjust its vapour pressure for summer and winter grades so that engines start easily without too much fuel evaporating — a direct use of Raoult-type thinking.

games.title: Find the vapour composition
games.prompt: Steps to calculate y₁ for an ideal binary solution
items: Find mole fractions x₁ and x₂ in the liquid
Use p₁ = p₁° x₁ and p₂ = p₂° x₂

items.q: p° = 300 mm Hg, x = 0.5. Partial pressure (mm Hg)?
p₁ = 120, p₂ = 80 mm Hg. Total pressure (mm Hg)?
x₁ = 0.35 in a binary liquid. x₂ = ?
In Raoult's law as a case of Henry's law, K_H equals?

quiz.q: Liquids A (p_A° = 400 mm Hg) and B (p_B° = 600 mm Hg) form an ideal solution with x_A = 0.4. What is the total vapour pressure (in mm Hg)?
quiz.mistake: Swaps the mole fractions (uses 0.4 for B), giving 480

quiz.q: For the solution in which p_A = 160 mm Hg and p_total = 520 mm Hg, what is the mole fraction of A in the vapour phase (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: y_A = p_A ÷ p_total = 160 ÷ 520 = 0.31. The vapour is poorer in A, the less volatile component.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the vapour has the same composition as the liquid (0.40)

quiz.q: At 298 K, pure chloroform and pure dichloromethane have vapour pressures of 200 and 415 mm Hg. In an ideal solution with x(dichloromethane) = 0.4, what is p_total (in mm Hg)?
quiz.explain: p_total = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°)x₂ = 200 + 215 × 0.4 = 286 mm Hg.
quiz.mistake: Uses the mole fraction of dichloromethane with chloroform's vapour pressure

quiz.q: In an ideal binary solution, how does the vapour composition compare with the liquid composition?
options: The vapour is richer in the less volatile component
The vapour always has the same composition as the liquid
The vapour contains only the more volatile component
The vapour is richer in the more volatile component
quiz.explain: The component with higher p° contributes a larger share of the vapour pressure, so its mole fraction in the vapour is higher.
quiz.mistake: Assumes liquid and vapour must have identical composition

quiz.q: What is the shape of the plot of total vapour pressure against mole fraction for an ideal binary solution?
options: A straight line joining p₁° and p₂°
quiz.explain: p_total = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°)x₂ is linear in x₂.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ideal behaviour with deviations from Raoult's law

quiz.q: Raoult's law becomes a special case of Henry's law when Henry's constant K_H is equal to:
options: the vapour pressure of the pure component, p₁°
the mole fraction of the component
quiz.explain: Both laws say p ∝ x. In Raoult's law the proportionality constant is p₁°, so K_H = p₁°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two laws have unrelated constants

quiz.q: Pure benzene and toluene have vapour pressures of 75 and 25 mm Hg at a certain temperature. For an equimolar ideal solution, what is the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour?
quiz.explain: p(benzene) = 37.5, p(toluene) = 12.5, total 50; y(benzene) = 37.5 ÷ 50 = 0.75.
quiz.mistake: Assumes an equimolar liquid gives an equimolar vapour

quiz.q: Assertion (A): For an ideal solution of two volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction. Reason (R): This follows from Raoult's law.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: p₁ = p₁° x₁ is exactly Raoult's law, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the proportionality comes from Dalton's law instead

teach.ask: Gappu sniffs a mixture: 'How do I work out the vapour pressure of a mixture of two volatile liquids?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Each partial pressure is p° times its mole fraction, then add them up. So neat!
teach.nudge: You named the law, but what do you multiply the pure liquid's vapour pressure by?

topics.title: Ideal and non-ideal solutions, azeotropes

learn.hook: Distil fermented sugarcane juice as long as you like, and the ethanol refuses to get purer than about 95% by volume. Meet the azeotrope.
points: Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law at all concentrations, with Δmix H = 0 and Δmix V = 0; A–B attractions equal A–A and B–B. Examples: n-hexane + n-heptane, bromoethane + chloroethane, benzene + toluene.

Positive deviation: A–B attractions weaker than A–A and B–B, so molecules escape more easily and vapour pressure is higher than Raoult's prediction; Δmix H > 0 and Δmix V > 0. Examples: ethanol + acetone, carbon disulphide + acetone.

Negative deviation: A–B attractions stronger, vapour pressure lower than predicted; Δmix H < 0 and Δmix V < 0. Example: chloroform + acetone (H-bond between CHCl₃ hydrogen and acetone oxygen); also phenol + aniline.
Azeotropes are binary mixtures that boil at a constant temperature with the same composition in liquid and vapour, so fractional distillation cannot separate them.

Minimum boiling azeotropes come from large positive deviation (ethanol–water at about 95% ethanol by volume). Maximum boiling azeotropes come from large negative deviation (nitric acid–water at about 68% HNO₃ by mass, boiling at 393.5 K).

example.q: When acetone and chloroform are mixed, the mixture warms up slightly and the final volume is a little less than the sum of the volumes. Classify the solution.
steps: Warming means heat is released: Δmix H < 0
Stronger A–B attraction (H-bond) means negative deviation
example.answer: Non-ideal solution with negative deviation from Raoult's law

learn.reallife: India's ethanol-blended petrol needs nearly water-free ethanol, but simple distillation of molasses wash stops near the ethanol–water azeotrope; distilleries use extra dehydration steps (like molecular sieves) to break past it.

games.title: Property ↔ type of solution
pairs: Δmix H > 0, vapour pressure higher than predicted
Δmix H < 0, vapour pressure lower than predicted

quiz.q: Which pair forms a nearly ideal solution?
quiz.explain: Benzene and toluene have very similar intermolecular forces, so A–B interactions match A–A and B–B and Raoult's law is obeyed.
quiz.mistake: Picks any two miscible liquids as ideal

quiz.q: For a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult's law, which is true?
quiz.explain: Weaker A–B attractions mean energy is absorbed on mixing and the molecules spread out a little: both changes are positive.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the signs for positive and negative deviation

quiz.q: Why does a chloroform–acetone mixture show negative deviation?
options: A hydrogen bond forms between chloroform's hydrogen and acetone's oxygen
Chloroform breaks the hydrogen bonds of acetone
quiz.explain: The new CHCl₃···O=C H-bond makes A–B attraction stronger than in the pure liquids, lowering escaping tendency.
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative deviation comes from breaking interactions

quiz.q: Ethanol mixed with acetone shows positive deviation. What is the main reason?
options: Both liquids have equal intermolecular forces
Acetone forms strong hydrogen bonds with ethanol
Acetone gets between ethanol molecules and breaks some of their hydrogen bonds
quiz.explain: Pure ethanol is held together by H-bonds; acetone disrupts them, so A–B attraction is weaker overall and vapour pressure rises.
quiz.mistake: Assumes mixing two polar liquids always strengthens attractions

quiz.q: A maximum boiling azeotrope is formed by solutions that show:
options: large negative deviation from Raoult's law
large positive deviation from Raoult's law
quiz.explain: Strong A–B attraction lowers vapour pressure the most at one composition, which therefore boils at the highest temperature.
quiz.mistake: Links 'maximum boiling' to positive deviation

quiz.q: Ethanol–water forms an azeotrope at about 95% ethanol by volume. What kind is it?
quiz.explain: Ethanol–water shows large positive deviation, so the azeotrope has a maximum vapour pressure and hence a minimum boiling point.
quiz.mistake: Confuses positive deviation with a higher boiling point

quiz.q: Why can an azeotropic mixture not be separated by fractional distillation?
options: It boils over a very wide range of temperature
It does not boil at all
Its liquid and vapour have the same composition when it boils
quiz.explain: Distillation relies on the vapour being richer in one component; at the azeotropic composition, it is not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks azeotropes are non-volatile

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The nitric acid–water azeotrope (about 68% HNO₃ by mass) boils at 393.5 K, higher than either pure component. Reason (R): Nitric acid–water solutions show large positive deviation from Raoult's law.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.explain: This azeotrope is maximum boiling, which comes from large negative deviation, so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Links a high boiling point to positive deviation

teach.ask: Gappu stirs two liquids: 'What makes a solution non-ideal, and why can't I purify ethanol past 95% by distillation?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Unequal A–B forces cause deviations, and at the azeotrope the vapour has the same composition as the liquid. Got it!
teach.nudge: You described the deviation, but what is special about the azeotropic mixture when it boils?

topics.title: Colligative properties: vapour pressure lowering and boiling point elevation

learn.hook: Add salt to the pressure cooker water and the dal takes a tiny bit longer to start boiling. The salt is just counting particles.
points: A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent because fewer solvent molecules are at the surface to escape.

Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.
Relative lowering of vapour pressure: (p₁° − p₁) ÷ p₁° = x₂. For dilute solutions x₂ ≈ n₂/n₁, so M₂ = (w₂ × M₁ × p₁°) ÷ (w₁ × Δp).

Boiling point elevation: ΔT_b = K_b m, where K_b is the ebullioscopic constant (unit K kg mol⁻¹; 0.52 for water, 2.53 for benzene). Molar mass: M₂ = (K_b × w₂ × 1000) ÷ (ΔT_b × w₁), with masses in grams.

example.q: 1.28 g of a non-volatile solute in 50 g of benzene raises its boiling point by 0.506 K. K_b for benzene is 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹. Find the molar mass of the solute.

learn.reallife: In Leh, water boils at a lower temperature because of low air pressure, which is why pressure cookers are essential there; dissolved salt nudges the boiling point up only a little, as ΔT_b = K_b m predicts.

games.title: Colligative or not?
items: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their identity.
That is the definition of a colligative property.
Adding a non-volatile solute raises the vapour pressure of a solvent.
It lowers it, because fewer solvent molecules occupy the surface.
A solution boils at a higher temperature than the pure solvent.
Its vapour pressure is lower, so it must be heated more to reach atmospheric pressure.
K_b of water is 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.
1.86 K kg mol⁻¹ is K_f of water; K_b of water is 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹.
The relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute.
This follows from Raoult's law for a non-volatile solute.

quiz.q: 0.5 mol of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 500 g of water (K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹). What is the boiling point of the solution (in K)? Pure water boils at 373.15 K.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts ΔT_b, treating it like freezing point depression

quiz.q: 1.28 g of a non-volatile solute in 50 g of benzene (K_b = 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹) raises the boiling point by 0.506 K. What is the molar mass (in g mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1000 for converting grams of solvent to kilograms, or halves the mass

quiz.q: The vapour pressure of a solvent falls from 100 mm Hg to 98 mm Hg on dissolving a non-volatile solute. What is the mole fraction of the solute?
quiz.explain: Relative lowering = (100 − 98) ÷ 100 = 0.02 = x₂.
quiz.mistake: Reports the mole fraction of the solvent or the absolute lowering

quiz.q: 6 g of a non-volatile solute in 90 g of water (5 mol) gives a relative lowering of vapour pressure of 0.02. Using n₂/n₁ for this dilute solution, what is the molar mass of the solute (in g mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Uses 90 g directly instead of 5 mol of water

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a colligative property?
quiz.explain: Viscosity depends on the nature of the solute and solvent, not just the number of particles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every property of a solution is colligative

quiz.q: Why is the boiling point of a solution of a non-volatile solute higher than that of the pure solvent?
options: Solutes make the solvent denser and heavier
The solute boils first and heats the solvent
Its vapour pressure is lower, so it must be heated more to equal atmospheric pressure
The solute increases the vapour pressure
quiz.explain: Boiling happens when vapour pressure equals external pressure; a lower vapour pressure needs a higher temperature.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect boiling to vapour pressure

quiz.q: Equal masses of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) and urea (M = 60 g mol⁻¹) are dissolved separately in equal masses of water. Which solution has the higher boiling point?
quiz.explain: Equal masses of urea give three times as many moles as glucose, so molality and ΔT_b are larger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the heavier molecule gives a larger effect

quiz.q: K_b depends on the solvent and can be expressed as K_b = R M₁ T_b² ÷ (1000 Δvap H). Which change in the solvent would give a larger K_b?
options: Higher boiling point with the same Δvap H and M₁
Larger enthalpy of vaporisation with the same T_b and M₁
Smaller molar mass with the same T_b and Δvap H
quiz.explain: K_b is proportional to T_b² and M₁ and inversely proportional to Δvap H; it is a property of the solvent only.
quiz.mistake: Thinks K_b changes with the amount of solute

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'How can just counting solute particles change the boiling point? Doesn't it matter what they are?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It's the number of particles that lowers vapour pressure, and ΔT_b = K_b m. Identity doesn't matter!
teach.nudge: You talked about boiling, but what happens to the vapour pressure first, and what does it depend on?

topics.title: Depression of freezing point

learn.hook: Every kulfi-wala knows the trick: pack the matka with ice and salt, and it gets colder than plain ice. That's freezing point depression at work.
points: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than the pure solvent because its vapour pressure is lower: ΔT_f = T_f° − T_f = K_f m.
K_f is the cryoscopic constant (unit K kg mol⁻¹): 1.86 for water and 5.12 for benzene. Molar mass: M₂ = (K_f × w₂ × 1000) ÷ (ΔT_f × w₁).
Both constants depend only on the solvent: K_b = R M₁ T_b² ÷ (1000 Δvap H) and K_f = R M₁ T_f² ÷ (1000 Δfus H), with M₁ in g mol⁻¹.
Uses: ethylene glycol is added to car radiators as antifreeze; salt (NaCl or CaCl₂) is spread on icy roads to melt the ice.

example.q: How many kelvin will the freezing point of water drop if 62 g of ethylene glycol (M = 62 g mol⁻¹) is added to 500 g of water? K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Army vehicles in Ladakh and Sikkim run with antifreeze (glycol-based coolant) in their radiators so the water does not freeze in sub-zero nights.

games.title: Molar mass from freezing point depression
items: Measure the freezing point of pure solvent and of the solution
Substitute masses in grams and K_f, then calculate

items.q: Water freezes at 273.15 K; ΔT_f = 1.86 K. New f.p. (K)?

quiz.q: 62 g of ethylene glycol (M = 62 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹). What is the depression in freezing point (in K)?
quiz.explain: m = 1 mol ÷ 0.5 kg = 2 mol kg⁻¹; ΔT_f = 1.86 × 2 = 3.72 K.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert 500 g to 0.5 kg, or uses moles as molality

quiz.q: 2 g of a non-electrolyte in 100 g of benzene lowers its freezing point by 0.32 K. K_f for benzene is 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹. What is the molar mass of the solute (in g mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Drops the factor 1000 or mixes up w₁ and w₂

quiz.q: A 0.2 molal aqueous solution of urea is cooled. At what temperature (in K) does it start to freeze? (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; pure water freezes at 273.15 K.)
quiz.mistake: Adds ΔT_f to the freezing point instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Why is salt spread on icy roads in winter?
options: It lowers the freezing point of water so ice melts
It raises the freezing point of water
It reacts with ice to release heat
It increases the vapour pressure of ice
quiz.explain: Dissolved salt makes a solution whose freezing point is below that of pure water, so the ice melts at sub-zero temperatures.
quiz.mistake: Thinks salt melts ice by a chemical reaction

quiz.q: The cryoscopic constant K_f of a solvent can be written as K_f = R M₁ T_f² ÷ (1000 Δfus H). On what does K_f depend?
options: On the amount of solute added
Only on the nature of the solvent
On the volume of the solution
Only on the nature of the solute
quiz.explain: All quantities in the expression (M₁, T_f, Δfus H) belong to the solvent.
quiz.mistake: Believes K_f changes from solute to solute

quiz.q: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point? (All solutes are non-electrolytes.)
quiz.explain: For non-electrolytes, ΔT_f = K_f m, so the highest molality gives the largest depression and the lowest freezing point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the solution with the heaviest solute freezes lowest

quiz.q: The freezing point of a solution is lower than that of the pure solvent. Which statement explains this best?
options: The solute raises the vapour pressure of the solvent
Freezing needs more heat when a solute is present
The solution's vapour pressure equals that of the solid solvent at a lower temperature
Solute particles freeze before the solvent
quiz.explain: Freezing occurs when liquid and solid phases have equal vapour pressure. Lowering the liquid's vapour pressure shifts this point to a lower temperature.
quiz.mistake: Does not link freezing to vapour pressure

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Kulfi makers mix salt with ice to cool their moulds below 0 °C. Reason (R): Salt solution has a lower freezing point than pure water.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The ice–salt mixture can stay liquid and keep melting below 0 °C, absorbing heat from the moulds; this is because of freezing point depression.
quiz.mistake: Thinks salt makes the mixture colder by a chemical reaction

teach.ask: Gappu shivers: 'Why does putting antifreeze in a car radiator stop the water from freezing?'
teach.praise: Brrr-avo! The dissolved solute lowers the freezing point by K_f m, so the coolant stays liquid. Warm wings!
teach.nudge: You said it stays liquid. What happens to the freezing point, and what formula tells us by how much?

topics.title: Osmosis, osmotic pressure and reverse osmosis

learn.hook: That RO purifier humming in your kitchen pushes water the 'wrong way' through a membrane. To understand it, first understand osmosis.
points: Osmosis: net flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent (or dilute solution) into a more concentrated solution. Osmotic pressure π is the extra pressure that must be applied to the solution to just stop this flow.
van't Hoff equation: π = CRT = (n₂/V)RT, where C is molarity, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T is in kelvin. Molar mass: M₂ = w₂RT ÷ (πV).

Osmotic pressure is the best method for macromolecules (proteins, polymers): it is measured at room temperature, uses molarity, and gives a large, measurable value even for very dilute solutions — useful for biomolecules that break down on heating.

Isotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressure. Blood cells are isotonic with 0.9% (w/V) NaCl (normal saline). In a hypertonic solution (more than 0.9%) cells lose water and shrink; in a hypotonic one (less than 0.9%) they swell and may burst.
Reverse osmosis: applying pressure greater than π on the solution side pushes pure solvent out through the membrane (e.g. cellulose acetate). It is used to desalinate sea water.

example.q: A 0.25 L solution contains 2 g of a polymer and shows π = 0.00166 bar at 300 K. Find the molar mass (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Chennai's Minjur and Nemmeli plants turn Bay of Bengal sea water into drinking water by reverse osmosis, and millions of Indian homes run small RO units under the kitchen sink.

games.title: Isotonic, hypertonic or hypotonic (relative to blood cells)?
Observation ↔ explanation
pairs: Water leaves cells into hypertonic brine
Wilted flowers revive in fresh water
Red blood cells burst in distilled water

quiz.q: What is the osmotic pressure (in bar) of a 0.1 M solution of a non-electrolyte at 300 K? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Slips a decimal place or forgets to multiply by C

quiz.q: 2 g of a polymer in 0.25 L of solution shows π = 0.00166 bar at 300 K. What is its molar mass (in g mol⁻¹)? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the volume (0.25 L), which gives 30000

quiz.q: Why is osmotic pressure preferred over other colligative properties for finding molar masses of proteins?
options: It depends on the nature of the protein
Proteins raise the boiling point strongly
It is measured at room temperature and gives a large value even for dilute solutions
quiz.explain: Proteins often decompose on heating, and their dilute solutions give tiny ΔT values; osmotic pressure avoids both problems.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the heat sensitivity of biomolecules

quiz.q: Red blood cells are placed in 2% (w/V) NaCl solution. What happens?
options: They shrink as water flows out
quiz.explain: 2% NaCl is hypertonic compared with 0.9% saline, so water leaves the cells by osmosis.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of water flow

quiz.q: In reverse osmosis used for desalination, which condition must be met?
options: The membrane must allow salt to pass
The sea water must be boiled first
Pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied on the sea water side
Pressure less than the osmotic pressure is applied on the sea water side
quiz.explain: Only a pressure exceeding π reverses the natural flow, pushing pure water out of the salt solution.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any applied pressure will reverse osmosis

quiz.q: Two solutions are isotonic. What does this mean?
options: They have the same osmotic pressure at the same temperature
They have the same mass percentage
quiz.explain: Isotonic means equal osmotic pressure, so there is no net osmosis between them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks isotonic solutions must contain the same substance

quiz.q: A solution of glucose at 300 K has an osmotic pressure of 4.98 bar. What is its molar concentration (in mol L⁻¹)? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by RT instead of dividing

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Raw mangoes shrivel when kept in concentrated salt solution for pickling. Reason (R): The salt solution is hypotonic with respect to the cell sap.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.explain: Mangoes shrivel because the brine is hypertonic, drawing water out. Calling it hypotonic is false.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the terms hypertonic and hypotonic

teach.ask: Gappu sips RO water: 'What is osmosis, and how does an RO purifier reverse it?'
teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! Water flows through a semipermeable membrane into the stronger solution, and pushing harder than π sends it back. Clean water for me!
teach.nudge: You described osmosis, but what must an RO unit apply on the salty side to reverse it?

topics.title: Abnormal molar masses and the van't Hoff factor

learn.hook: Measure the molar mass of table salt by freezing point depression and you get about 29 g mol⁻¹, not 58.5. Is the experiment wrong, or is salt splitting up?
points: When a solute dissociates (electrolytes in water) or associates (e.g. ethanoic acid dimerising in benzene via H-bonds), the number of particles changes, giving an 'abnormal' molar mass.
van't Hoff factor: i = normal molar mass ÷ abnormal molar mass = observed colligative property ÷ calculated colligative property = total moles of particles after ÷ moles before.
Dissociation gives i > 1 (KCl ≈ 2, K₂SO₄ ≈ 3 at infinite dilution); association gives i < 1 (ethanoic acid dimer in benzene ≈ 0.5); no change gives i = 1.
Modified equations: Δp/p₁° = i n₂/n₁; ΔT_b = i K_b m; ΔT_f = i K_f m; π = i CRT.
Degree of dissociation α = (i − 1) ÷ (n − 1), where n ions form per formula unit. Degree of association α = (1 − i) ÷ (1 − 1/n), where n molecules join together.

example.q: Ethanoic acid in benzene gives i = 0.6. Find its degree of association (it forms dimers).
example.answer: α = 0.8, i.e. 80% of the acid is dimerised

learn.reallife: The ORS packets distributed in Indian health programmes are designed around total particle count: the salts dissociate, so their osmotic effect depends on the van't Hoff factor, not just the grams of salt.

games.title: i greater than, less than or equal to 1?

items.q: Ethanoic acid fully dimerised in benzene

quiz.q: What is the depression in freezing point (in K) of a 0.1 m aqueous NaCl solution, assuming complete dissociation? (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
quiz.explain: NaCl gives 2 ions, so i = 2: ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.372 K.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the van't Hoff factor and uses i = 1

quiz.q: Ethanoic acid in benzene gives a van't Hoff factor of 0.6. What is its degree of association (as a fraction), assuming dimer formation?
quiz.mistake: Stops at 1 − i = 0.4 and forgets to divide by (1 − 1/n)

quiz.q: A weak monobasic acid HA in water has i = 1.2. What is its degree of dissociation?
quiz.mistake: Confuses i with α

quiz.q: The experimentally found molar mass of a solute is half its normal molar mass. What is i?
quiz.explain: i = normal molar mass ÷ abnormal molar mass = M ÷ (M/2) = 2: the solute has dissociated into two particles.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: Which 0.1 m aqueous solution has the highest boiling point? (Assume complete dissociation.)
quiz.explain: Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives 5 ions (i = 5), the most particles, so the largest ΔT_b.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the number of ions formed

quiz.q: Why does ethanoic acid show a molar mass close to 120 g mol⁻¹ in benzene instead of 60 g mol⁻¹?
options: It forms dimers through hydrogen bonding in benzene
It dissociates into ions in benzene
quiz.explain: In a non-polar solvent, two acid molecules hydrogen-bond into a dimer, halving the number of particles and doubling the apparent molar mass.
quiz.mistake: Thinks association lowers the apparent molar mass

quiz.q: A 0.1 M aqueous solution of K₂SO₄ is fully dissociated. What is its osmotic pressure (in bar) at 300 K? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
quiz.explain: i = 3 for K₂SO₄, so π = iCRT = 3 × 0.1 × 0.083 × 300 = 7.47 bar.
quiz.mistake: Takes i = 2 because there are two kinds of ions

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The van't Hoff factor for KCl in very dilute aqueous solution is close to 2. Reason (R): KCl dissociates into K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Each KCl gives two ions, doubling the particle count, so i approaches 2 at infinite dilution.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the ion count to i

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'Salt's molar mass came out as 29 g mol⁻¹ in my experiment. What went wrong?'
teach.praise: Tweet! NaCl dissociates into two ions, so i = 2 and the apparent molar mass halves. My experiment was fine!
teach.nudge: Nothing went wrong! But what happens to NaCl in water, and which factor corrects for it?

topics.title: Electrochemical cells and the Daniell cell

learn.hook: Your phone battery, the Ola electric scooter and the chrome plating on a bike handle all run on one idea: chemical energy and electrical energy can be swapped.
points: Electrochemistry studies the production of electricity from spontaneous chemical reactions and the use of electricity to drive non-spontaneous ones. It underpins batteries, fuel cells, electroplating and the industrial production of metals and chemicals such as NaOH and Cl₂.
A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to bring about a non-spontaneous reaction.
Daniell cell: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Zinc dips in ZnSO₄ and copper in CuSO₄, joined by a salt bridge; with 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions the cell gives 1.1 V.

If an opposing external voltage is applied: below 1.1 V electrons still flow from Zn to Cu; at exactly 1.1 V no current flows; above 1.1 V electrons flow from Cu to Zn and the cell works as an electrolytic cell (Zn deposits, Cu dissolves).
The salt bridge (e.g. KCl or KNO₃ in agar) completes the inner circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral.

example.q: A Daniell cell (1.1 V) is connected to an external source of 1.5 V opposing it. What happens at each electrode?
steps: External voltage 1.5 V > 1.1 V, so the reaction is reversed
Electrons now flow from Cu to Zn in the external circuit
Zn²⁺ is reduced: zinc deposits on the zinc electrode
Cu is oxidised: copper dissolves from the copper electrode
example.answer: The cell becomes electrolytic: zinc is deposited and copper dissolves

learn.reallife: Hindustan Zinc and Hindalco produce zinc and aluminium electrolytically, and the chlor-alkali plants of Gujarat make caustic soda and chlorine — giant electrolytic cells in action.

games.title: Galvanic or electrolytic?
items: Daniell cell working on its own
Daniell cell with external voltage above 1.1 V

games.title: Daniell cell checks
items: With 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions, a Daniell cell gives about 1.1 V.
When the opposing external voltage equals 1.1 V, no current flows.
In a galvanic cell, electrical energy is used to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
The salt bridge allows electrons to flow between the two solutions.
Ions, not electrons, move through the salt bridge; electrons travel in the external wire.
Above 1.1 V of opposing voltage, zinc gets deposited at the zinc electrode.
The reaction is reversed, so Zn²⁺ is reduced to Zn.

quiz.q: What is the overall reaction in a Daniell cell?
quiz.explain: Zinc, the stronger reducing agent, is oxidised and Cu²⁺ is reduced to copper.
quiz.mistake: Writes the reverse, non-spontaneous reaction

quiz.q: A Daniell cell is opposed by an external voltage of 0.8 V. In which direction do electrons flow in the outer circuit?
options: From the copper rod to the zinc rod
From the zinc rod to the copper rod
Electrons flow through the salt bridge
quiz.explain: 0.8 V is less than 1.1 V, so the cell still works normally: electrons leave zinc and go to copper.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any opposing voltage reverses the cell

quiz.q: What is the main function of a salt bridge?
options: It supplies Cu²⁺ ions to the cathode
It carries electrons between the electrodes
It completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality of the two solutions
quiz.explain: Ions migrate through the bridge to balance charges building up in the half-cells, keeping the current flowing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrons pass through the solution

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a galvanic cell from an electrolytic cell?
options: Both convert electrical energy into chemical energy
A galvanic cell needs an external battery
An electrolytic cell is driven by a spontaneous reaction
A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy; an electrolytic cell does the reverse
quiz.explain: Galvanic cells run on spontaneous reactions; electrolytic cells need external electricity to drive non-spontaneous ones.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the energy conversions

quiz.q: When the opposing external voltage on a Daniell cell is raised above 1.1 V, which process takes place at the copper electrode?
quiz.explain: The reaction reverses: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the copper electrode while Zn²⁺ is reduced at the zinc electrode.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the electrode reactions stay the same

quiz.q: Which industrial process is an application of electrolytic cells?
options: Production of sodium hydroxide and chlorine from brine
Burning coal in a thermal plant
quiz.explain: The chlor-alkali process electrolyses brine to give NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
quiz.mistake: Confuses electrolysis with ordinary thermal reactions

quiz.q: At what external opposing voltage does a standard Daniell cell stop delivering current?
quiz.explain: Current stops when the external voltage exactly equals the cell potential of 1.1 V.
quiz.mistake: Uses one electrode potential instead of the cell potential

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A Daniell cell can be made to work as an electrolytic cell. Reason (R): Applying an external voltage greater than 1.1 V in opposition reverses the cell reaction.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Above 1.1 V the reaction is driven backwards using external electricity, which is exactly what an electrolytic cell does.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that reversing the reaction makes it electrolytic

teach.ask: Gappu holds a battery: 'What is the difference between a galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell?'
teach.praise: Zap! Galvanic cells turn a spontaneous reaction into electricity; electrolytic cells use electricity to force a reaction. Got it!
teach.nudge: Which one makes electricity from a spontaneous reaction, and what does the other one need?

topics.title: Galvanic cells: half-cells, notation and the SHE

learn.hook: Cell notation is chemistry's shorthand. Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu tells an examiner the whole story in one line, if you know how to read it.
points: A galvanic cell has two half-cells (redox couples). Oxidation occurs at the anode, which is negative in a galvanic cell; reduction occurs at the cathode, which is positive.
Notation: anode on the left, cathode on the right, a single vertical line for a phase boundary and a double line for the salt bridge: Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Cu²⁺(aq)|Cu(s).
E_cell = E_right − E_left = E_cathode − E_anode, using reduction potentials for both.
Single electrode potentials cannot be measured alone. The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M), is assigned 0.00 V at all temperatures.
Measured against SHE: Pt|H₂(1 bar)|H⁺(1 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu gives 0.34 V, so E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; the zinc cell gives E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.

example.q: Write the cell for the reaction 2Ag⁺(aq) + Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) and find E°cell. E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.
steps: Zn is oxidised, so it is the anode (left); Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode (right)

learn.reallife: Chemistry labs at IISERs calibrate reference electrodes against the hydrogen electrode, the zero point on which every textbook E° value is built.

games.title: Read the cell notation left to right

quiz.q: What is E°cell for Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s)? E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V (in V).
quiz.explain: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Doubling for 2Ag⁺ does not change E°.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or doubles the silver potential

quiz.q: In a galvanic cell, where does oxidation take place and what is its polarity?
options: At the cathode, which is positive
At the anode, which is positive
At the cathode, which is negative
At the anode, which is negative
quiz.explain: Oxidation releases electrons at the anode, making it the negative terminal of a galvanic cell.
quiz.mistake: Uses the electrolytic-cell polarity for a galvanic cell

quiz.q: What potential is assigned to the standard hydrogen electrode?
quiz.explain: By convention, E°(H⁺/½H₂) = 0 at all temperatures; other potentials are measured against it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the SHE value is measured, not assigned

quiz.q: A cell is written Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M)||Cu²⁺(aq, 1 M)|Cu(s) and its emf is 0.34 V. What does this tell us?
options: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, and Cu²⁺ is reduced more easily than H⁺
Hydrogen ions are reduced at copper
quiz.explain: With SHE on the left as anode, E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − 0 = +0.34 V, so copper is the cathode.
quiz.mistake: Puts the electrode on the right as the anode

quiz.q: Which is the correct representation of the cell with the reaction Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)?
quiz.explain: The anode (Mg, oxidised) is written on the left, the cathode (Ag⁺/Ag) on the right, with || for the salt bridge.
quiz.mistake: Puts the cathode on the left

quiz.q: A cell made of Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) and SHE: which electrode is the cathode?
quiz.explain: Zinc has the lower reduction potential, so it is oxidised (anode); H⁺ is reduced at the SHE (cathode).
quiz.mistake: Assumes the metal electrode is always the cathode

quiz.q: Why can the absolute potential of a single electrode not be measured?
options: Only a potential difference between two electrodes can be measured
quiz.explain: A voltmeter needs two terminals, so potentials are measured relative to a reference like SHE.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a single electrode can be connected alone

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In a galvanic cell the cathode is the positive electrode. Reason (R): Electrons are consumed at the cathode by the reduction half-reaction.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Electrons flow towards the cathode where they are used up in reduction, making it positive relative to the anode.
quiz.mistake: Uses the electrolytic-cell sign convention

teach.ask: Gappu stares at Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu: 'What do all these lines mean, and how do I get the cell voltage?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Anode on the left, cathode on the right, salt bridge in the middle, and E_cell = E_right − E_left!
teach.nudge: Which electrode goes on the left, and how do you combine the two reduction potentials?

topics.title: Electrochemical series and predicting reactions

learn.hook: Can you store copper sulphate solution in a zinc pot from the market? The electrochemical series answers in one glance.
points: Standard reduction potentials (1 M, 1 bar, 298 K) listed in order form the electrochemical series: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V at the top, Li⁺/Li −3.05 V at the bottom.

The higher (more positive) E°, the stronger the oxidised form as an oxidising agent: F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. The lower (more negative) E°, the stronger the reduced form as a reducing agent: Li is the strongest reducing agent.
A redox reaction is feasible if E°cell = E°(species reduced) − E°(species oxidised) is positive. A metal with negative E° can liberate H₂ from dilute acids; Cu (+0.34 V) cannot.
Inert electrodes such as platinum or gold carry electrons for couples with no solid metal, e.g. Pt(s)|Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺ or Pt(s)|H₂|H⁺.
Useful values: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44, H⁺/H₂ 0.00, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34, I₂/I⁻ +0.54, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V.

example.q: Can CuSO₄ solution be stored in a zinc vessel? E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
steps: Possible reaction: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
Positive E°cell means the reaction occurs, so zinc would dissolve
example.answer: No — zinc reduces Cu²⁺ and the vessel would be eaten away

learn.reallife: Galvanised iron buckets and water tanks sold in Indian markets rely on zinc's lower E°: zinc corrodes first and protects the iron underneath.

games.title: Arrange by standard reduction potential
games.prompt: Most negative E° to most positive E°

games.title: Feasible or not?
items: Zinc liberates H₂ from dilute HCl.
E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) is negative, so E°cell with H⁺/H₂ is positive.
Copper liberates H₂ from dilute HCl.
E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) is +0.34 V, so the reaction has negative E°cell.
Fe³⁺ can oxidise I⁻ to I₂.
Silver nitrate solution can be safely stored in a copper vessel.
Cu (0.34 V) reduces Ag⁺ (0.80 V), so copper dissolves.
Li is the strongest reducing agent in the series.
It has the most negative reduction potential, −3.05 V.
F⁻ is a strong reducing agent.
F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent, so F⁻ is an extremely weak reducing agent.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent among these? E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V.
quiz.explain: The species with the highest reduction potential is most easily reduced, i.e. it is the strongest oxidising agent.
quiz.mistake: Chooses the metal with the lowest E°

quiz.q: Which metal is the strongest reducing agent? E°: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.36 V, Al³⁺/Al −1.66 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V.
quiz.explain: The most negative E° means the metal is most easily oxidised, so it is the best reducing agent.
quiz.mistake: Picks the least negative value

quiz.q: Can a solution of CuSO₄ be stored in a silver vessel? E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V.
options: Yes, because CuSO₄ reacts with silver to protect it
Yes, because Ag cannot reduce Cu²⁺
quiz.explain: For Ag + Cu²⁺ → Ag⁺ + Cu, E°cell = 0.34 − 0.80 = −0.46 V, so no reaction occurs.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every metal reacts with every salt solution

quiz.q: Will Fe³⁺ oxidise I⁻ to I₂ under standard conditions? E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. What is E°cell (in V)?
quiz.explain: E°cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V; positive, so the reaction is feasible.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order and gets a negative value
steps: Reduced species: Fe³⁺ (0.77 V); oxidised: I⁻ (0.54 V)

quiz.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Its standard reduction potential is negative
Its standard reduction potential is positive, higher than that of H⁺/H₂
HCl is too weak an acid
quiz.explain: With E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, the reaction Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂ has E°cell = −0.34 V.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all metals react with acids

quiz.q: Why is platinum used as the electrode in the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ half-cell?
options: It is inert and only provides a surface for electron transfer
quiz.explain: There is no solid metal in this couple, so an inert conductor like Pt is needed to carry electrons without reacting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the electrode metal must take part in the reaction

quiz.q: Arrange the metals in increasing order of reducing power: Ag (+0.80 V), Zn (−0.76 V), Cu (+0.34 V), Mg (−2.36 V).
quiz.explain: Reducing power increases as E° becomes more negative.
quiz.mistake: Ranks by the size of the number without considering the sign

quiz.q: Assertion (A): F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. Reason (R): F₂/F⁻ has the highest standard reduction potential in the electrochemical series.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The highest E° means F₂ has the greatest tendency to be reduced, so it oxidises others most strongly.
quiz.mistake: Does not link high reduction potential to oxidising strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I use the electrochemical series to tell if a metal will push hydrogen out of an acid?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Metals with negative E° sit below hydrogen and give positive E°cell with acid, so they release H₂!
teach.nudge: You mentioned the table, but what sign of E° does a metal need, and what must E°cell be?

topics.title: The Nernst equation

learn.hook: Standard conditions are rare outside the textbook. Walther Nernst's equation tells you the real voltage when concentrations are anything but 1 M.
points: For a reduction Mⁿ⁺(aq) + ne⁻ → M(s): E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(1/[Mⁿ⁺]). At 298 K this becomes E = E° − (0.059/n) log(1/[Mⁿ⁺]).
For a whole cell aA + bB → cC + dD: E_cell = E°cell − (0.059/n) log Q at 298 K, where Q = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ (pure solids and liquids are left out).
For the Daniell cell: E_cell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]). Raising [Cu²⁺] or lowering [Zn²⁺] increases E_cell.
Hydrogen electrode at 1 bar: E = −0.059 pH at 298 K.

example.q: Find E_cell at 298 K for Zn|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu. E°cell = 1.10 V.

learn.reallife: The pH meters used in Indian dairies and water-testing labs are electrochemical cells: their reading changes by 0.059 V for every pH unit, straight from the Nernst equation.

items.text: At 298 K, E_cell = E°cell − (___/n) log Q.
For Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, n = ___.
Pure solids such as Zn(s) are ___ from the reaction quotient Q.
For a hydrogen electrode at 1 bar and 298 K, E = −0.059 × ___.

quiz.q: Calculate E_cell at 298 K for Zn|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu, given E°cell = 1.10 V (answer in V).
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error with log Q, giving 1.041 V

quiz.q: What is the electrode potential (in V) of Cu²⁺(0.01 M)/Cu at 298 K? E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
quiz.mistake: Adds the correction instead of subtracting

quiz.q: What is the potential (in V) of a hydrogen electrode in a solution of pH 3 at 298 K (H₂ at 1 bar)?
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign

quiz.q: In the Daniell cell, how can E_cell be increased above 1.10 V?
options: Increase the length of the salt bridge
quiz.explain: E_cell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); a smaller ratio makes log Q negative and E_cell larger.
quiz.mistake: Gets the reaction quotient upside down

quiz.q: For Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(0.001 M)||Cu²⁺(0.1 M)|Cu(s), E°cell = 2.70 V. What is E_cell at 298 K (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Inverts Q (uses [Cu²⁺]/[Mg²⁺]), giving 2.641 V

quiz.q: Why are concentrations of Zn(s) and Cu(s) not written in the Nernst equation for the Daniell cell?
options: They cancel out with the salt bridge
They are too small to measure
Solids do not take part in the reaction
Pure solids have constant activity taken as 1
quiz.explain: The activity of a pure solid is unity, so it does not appear in Q.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solids are not reactants or products

quiz.q: For Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s), E° = 0.80 V. What is E (in V) at 298 K when [Ag⁺] = 0.1 M?
quiz.mistake: Divides 0.059 by 2 although n = 1

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The emf of a cell changes when the concentrations of ions are changed. Reason (R): E°cell depends on the concentrations of the ions.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: E_cell changes with concentration through the log Q term, but E° is fixed (defined at 1 M), so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Confuses E with E°

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Why isn't my cell giving exactly E°? What equation do I use for real concentrations?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The Nernst equation, E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q, corrects for concentrations. Real-world ready!
teach.nudge: Which equation, and what term in it carries the concentrations?

topics.title: Cell potential, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

learn.hook: A positive cell voltage is chemistry's green signal: it tells you the reaction is spontaneous and how far it will go before it stops.
points: Electrical work done by a cell = nFE_cell, so Δr G = −nFE_cell and Δr G° = −nFE°cell. F (Faraday constant) = 96487 C mol⁻¹, often taken as 96500 C mol⁻¹.
A positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G: the reaction is spontaneous.
At equilibrium E_cell = 0 and Q = K, so E°cell = (2.303RT/nF) log K_c = (0.059/n) log K_c at 298 K.
Also Δr G° = −2.303RT log K_c. A large positive E° means a very large K: the reaction goes nearly to completion.

example.q: Find Δr G° for the Daniell cell (E°cell = 1.10 V). Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Electrochemists at CSIR-CECRI, Karaikudi, use exactly these relations to screen new battery chemistries: a bigger E° means more energy stored per mole.

games.title: From E° to K at 298 K
items: Write the balanced cell reaction and find n
Take the antilog to find K

quiz.q: What is Δr G° (in kJ mol⁻¹) for the Daniell cell with E°cell = 1.10 V? Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Uses n = 1 or drops the negative sign

quiz.q: A cell reaction with n = 2 has E°cell = 0.295 V at 298 K. What is log K_c?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by n

quiz.q: What is the sign of Δr G for a reaction whose E_cell is positive?
options: Zero: the reaction is at equilibrium
quiz.explain: Δr G = −nFE_cell, so a positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G.
quiz.mistake: Assumes Δr G and E_cell have the same sign

quiz.q: What is E_cell for a galvanic cell whose reaction has reached equilibrium?
quiz.explain: At equilibrium Δr G = 0, so E_cell = 0; the battery is 'dead'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cell potential becomes E° at equilibrium

quiz.q: For a reaction with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.118 V at 298 K, what is K_c?
quiz.mistake: Stops at log K = 2 and reports it as K

quiz.q: Calculate Δr G° (in kJ mol⁻¹) for a cell with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.46 V. Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert J to kJ, or drops the sign

quiz.q: A cell reaction has a very large positive E°cell. What can you say about its equilibrium constant?
options: It is very large; the reaction goes nearly to completion
It cannot be predicted from E°
quiz.explain: log K = nE°/0.059, so a large positive E° gives a very large K.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect E° to K

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Electrical work done by a galvanic cell equals the decrease in its Gibbs energy. Reason (R): Δr G = −nFE_cell.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The maximum electrical work obtainable is nFE_cell, which equals −Δr G; R states this relation.
quiz.mistake: Does not see Δr G = −nFE as the work relation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a cell has a positive voltage, how do I know the reaction is spontaneous?'
teach.praise: Chirp! ΔG = −nFE, so positive E gives negative ΔG: spontaneous. Simple and powerful!
teach.nudge: Which thermodynamic quantity links to E_cell, and what sign does it take?

topics.title: Conductance, conductivity and molar conductivity

learn.hook: Tap water conducts electricity but distilled water barely does. Measuring that difference precisely is how labs check water purity.
points: Resistance R = ρ(l/A), where ρ is resistivity (Ω m). Conductance G = 1/R (siemens, S). Conductivity κ = 1/ρ (S m⁻¹, often S cm⁻¹; 1 S m⁻¹ = 0.01 S cm⁻¹).

Electronic (metallic) conduction depends on the metal's nature and structure and the number of valence electrons; it decreases as temperature rises. Electrolytic (ionic) conduction depends on the nature of the electrolyte, ion size and solvation, solvent viscosity, concentration and temperature; it increases as temperature rises.

Conductivity is measured in a conductivity cell (two Pt electrodes coated with Pt black) using a Wheatstone bridge with AC current, to avoid electrolysis and polarisation. Cell constant G* = l/A = R × κ.
Molar conductivity Λm = κ/c. In S cm² mol⁻¹: Λm = (κ in S cm⁻¹ × 1000) ÷ (molarity in mol L⁻¹). In SI it is S m² mol⁻¹.

example.q: A conductivity cell filled with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) has a resistance of 100 Ω. Find the cell constant and Λm.
example.answer: G* = 1.29 cm⁻¹; Λm = 129 S cm² mol⁻¹

learn.reallife: Pharma companies in Baddi and Hyderabad monitor the conductivity of 'purified water' continuously; a rise warns that ions have crept in.

quiz.q: A conductivity cell with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) has resistance 100 Ω. What is the cell constant (in cm⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Divides κ by R instead of multiplying

quiz.q: What is Λm (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of 0.1 M KCl with κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1000 that converts litres to cm³

quiz.q: The same cell (G* = 1.29 cm⁻¹) filled with a 0.02 M electrolyte shows R = 520 Ω. Its conductivity is n × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹. What is n (two decimals)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies G* by R instead of dividing (gives 670.8), or slips a power of ten

quiz.q: Why is alternating current (AC) used to measure the resistance of an electrolytic solution?
options: To prevent electrolysis and polarisation at the electrodes
Because AC heats the solution evenly
Because DC cannot pass through solutions
quiz.explain: DC would decompose the electrolyte and change its composition at the electrodes; AC avoids this.
quiz.mistake: Thinks AC is chosen only for safety or heating

quiz.q: How does the conductivity of a metal and of an electrolyte change on heating?
quiz.explain: Heating increases vibrations of metal ions, hindering electrons; in solutions it lowers viscosity and speeds up ions.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all conductors behave alike with temperature

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of molar conductivity?
quiz.explain: Λm = κ/c = (S m⁻¹) ÷ (mol m⁻³) = S m² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Confuses molar conductivity with conductivity

quiz.q: A solution has resistivity 50 Ω cm. What is its conductivity (in S cm⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Treats conductivity as equal to resistivity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The cell constant of a conductivity cell is found using a KCl solution of known conductivity. Reason (R): G* = κ × R, so knowing κ and measuring R gives G*.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Because l and A are hard to measure directly, a standard KCl solution is used with G* = κR.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the calibration to the formula

teach.ask: Gappu dips a probe: 'What's the difference between conductance, conductivity and molar conductivity?'
teach.praise: Bzzt! Conductance is 1/R, conductivity is 1/ρ, and molar conductivity is κ divided by concentration. Electrifying!
teach.nudge: You defined one of them. How is molar conductivity obtained from conductivity?

topics.title: Variation with concentration and Kohlrausch's law

learn.hook: Dilute a salt solution and its conductivity falls, yet its molar conductivity rises. It sounds like a contradiction until you count ions properly.
points: Conductivity κ decreases on dilution because the number of ions per unit volume falls. Molar conductivity Λm increases on dilution because Λm = κV, and V (volume containing 1 mol) increases more than κ falls.
Limiting molar conductivity Λ°m is the value as concentration approaches zero.

Strong electrolytes: Λm = Λ°m − A c^½ (Debye–Hückel–Onsager). Λm rises slowly on dilution; a plot of Λm vs √c is a straight line whose intercept gives Λ°m and whose slope is −A. A depends on the solvent, temperature and type of electrolyte (charges of ions: NaCl 1-1, CaCl₂ 2-1, MgSO₄ 2-2).
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: Λ°m of an electrolyte = sum of limiting molar conductivities of its ions, Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.

example.q: Find Λ°m of CaCl₂ using λ°(Ca²⁺) = 119.0 and λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Water-treatment engineers at Indian municipal plants track conductivity to estimate total dissolved salts, using the fact that each ion contributes its own share — Kohlrausch's idea.

games.title: Dilution and conductivity
items: Conductivity of a solution decreases on dilution.
There are fewer ions per unit volume.
Molar conductivity of a solution decreases on dilution.
It increases, because Λm = κV and V grows faster than κ falls.
For strong electrolytes Λm varies linearly with √c.
Λ°m of a weak electrolyte is easily found by extrapolating the Λm vs √c plot.
The plot is not linear for weak electrolytes; Kohlrausch's law is used instead.
The constant A is the same for NaCl and MgSO₄ in water at the same temperature.
A depends on the type of electrolyte (charges on the ions).

quiz.q: What is Λ°m (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of MgCl₂? λ°(Mg²⁺) = 106.0, λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 2 chloride ions per formula unit (gives 182.3)

quiz.q: What is Λ°m (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of Na₂SO₄? λ°(Na⁺) = 50.1, λ°(SO₄²⁻) = 160.0 S cm² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Adds just one sodium ion

quiz.q: Why does the conductivity (κ) of a solution decrease on dilution?
options: The number of ions per unit volume decreases
quiz.explain: κ measures conductance of a unit volume (1 cm³); dilution leaves fewer ions in that volume.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dilution reduces dissociation

quiz.q: Why does molar conductivity increase on dilution?
options: Λm = κV, and the volume V containing one mole increases more than κ decreases
quiz.explain: Although κ falls, the volume containing 1 mol of electrolyte rises faster, so their product Λm increases.
quiz.mistake: Confuses molar conductivity with conductivity

quiz.q: For a strong electrolyte, a graph of Λm against √c is a straight line. What does its intercept give?
quiz.explain: From Λm = Λ°m − A√c, the intercept at √c = 0 is Λ°m and the slope is −A.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slope and intercept

quiz.q: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
options: Λ°m of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion
All ions have the same molar conductivity
quiz.explain: At infinite dilution each ion moves independently and contributes its own λ°, so Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Kohlrausch's law with the definition of conductivity

quiz.q: Which electrolyte would have the largest constant A in Λm = Λ°m − A√c, in water at the same temperature?
quiz.explain: A depends on the charges of the ions; MgSO₄ is a 2-2 electrolyte, giving the strongest interionic effects.
quiz.mistake: Assumes A is the same for all electrolytes

quiz.q: Assertion (A): H⁺ has a much higher limiting molar conductivity than Na⁺. Reason (R): According to Kohlrausch's law, each ion contributes a definite share to Λ°m.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but Kohlrausch's law does not explain why H⁺ moves so fast; that is due to its special proton-hopping mechanism in water.
quiz.mistake: Treats any true statement about ions as the explanation
