teach.ask: Gappu dilutes a solution: 'Why does molar conductivity go up when conductivity goes down? And what did Kohlrausch say?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Λm = κV rises as V grows, and at infinite dilution each ion contributes independently. Kohlrausch nailed it!
teach.nudge: You explained one part. What does Kohlrausch's law say about the ions at infinite dilution?

topics.title: Weak electrolytes: degree of dissociation and Ka from conductivity

learn.hook: You cannot extrapolate acetic acid's conductivity curve to zero concentration — it shoots up wildly. Kohlrausch's law offers a clever detour.
points: Weak electrolytes (e.g. CH₃COOH) have low Λm at ordinary concentrations, which rises steeply on dilution as the degree of dissociation increases.
Their Λ°m cannot be obtained by extrapolation; instead use Kohlrausch's law with strong electrolytes: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(CH₃COONa) + Λ°(HCl) − Λ°(NaCl).
Degree of dissociation at concentration c: α = Λm ÷ Λ°m.
Dissociation constant: Ka = cα² ÷ (1 − α).

example.q: Λ°m of HCl, NaCl and CH₃COONa are 425.9, 126.4 and 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹. Find Λ°m of acetic acid.

learn.reallife: Vinegar (about 5% acetic acid) used in Indian pickles is a weak electrolyte; its conductivity is far lower than that of an HCl solution of the same concentration.

games.title: Find Ka of acetic acid by conductivity
items: Measure κ of the acid solution of known c
Find Λ°m using Kohlrausch's law with HCl, CH₃COONa and NaCl

quiz.q: Λ°m values: HCl 425.9, NaCl 126.4, CH₃COONa 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is Λ°m of CH₃COOH (in S cm² mol⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹: the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ contributions cancel.
quiz.mistake: Adds all three values instead of subtracting NaCl

quiz.q: 0.01 M acetic acid has Λm = 39.05 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is its degree of dissociation?
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: For 0.01 M acetic acid with α = 0.1, Ka = n × 10⁻⁴. What is n (two decimals)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the approximation Ka = cα² (gives 1.00) when α is not negligible

quiz.q: Why can Λ°m of acetic acid not be found by extrapolating its Λm vs √c graph?
options: The graph is a straight line with zero slope
Acetic acid is a strong electrolyte
Acetic acid does not conduct electricity
Λm rises very steeply at low concentrations, so the curve cannot be extrapolated reliably
quiz.explain: For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation keeps increasing sharply on dilution, so the curve is steep near zero concentration.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all electrolytes give a straight-line plot

quiz.q: Why does the molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte increase sharply on dilution?
options: Its degree of dissociation increases a lot on dilution
quiz.explain: On dilution more molecules ionise, greatly increasing the number of ions per mole.
quiz.mistake: Applies the strong-electrolyte reason (reduced interionic attraction) instead

quiz.q: Using λ°(H⁺) = 349.6 and λ°(HCOO⁻) = 54.6 S cm² mol⁻¹, what is Λ°m of formic acid (in S cm² mol⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Λ°m(HCOOH) = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2 S cm² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the ionic conductivities

quiz.q: A 0.001 M solution of a weak acid HA has Λm = 78.1 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is α?
quiz.mistake: Divides Λ°m by Λm

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Kohlrausch's law helps find the dissociation constant of a weak acid from conductivity data. Reason (R): It allows Λ°m of the weak acid to be calculated from Λ°m values of strong electrolytes.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: With Λ°m known, α = Λm/Λ°m and then Ka = cα²/(1 − α); R is exactly why A works.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that Λ°m is the missing piece

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How can I find how much acetic acid has dissociated just by measuring conductivity?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Get Λ°m from Kohlrausch's law, then α = Λm/Λ°m and Ka = cα²/(1 − α). Elegant!
teach.nudge: You measured Λm. What ratio gives α, and where does Λ°m come from?

topics.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's laws

learn.hook: The silver-plated thali at a wedding and copper refined to 99.9% purity for wiring both depend on counting electrons — Faraday's way.
points: In electrolysis of CuSO₄ with copper electrodes, Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) while the copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). This is the basis of electrorefining (impure Cu as anode) and electroplating.
In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode is negative (opposite of a galvanic cell); oxidation is still at the anode.
Faraday's first law: mass deposited m ∝ charge Q, so m = Z × I × t, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent, I is current (A) and t is time (s).
Faraday's second law: for the same charge, masses of different substances liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights (atomic mass ÷ number of electrons needed).
Charge on 1 mol of electrons = 1 F = 96487 C mol⁻¹ (≈ 96500). Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag needs 1 F per mol, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 F, Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 3 F.

example.q: A current of 2 A is passed through CuSO₄ solution for 965 s. What mass of copper is deposited? (Cu = 63.5 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
steps: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles of Cu = 0.01 mol

learn.reallife: Electrorefining at Hindustan Copper's plants produces high-purity copper for India's power cables, and Moradabad artisans electroplate brassware with silver and nickel.

items.q: Faradays needed for 1 mol Al from Al³⁺?
Mass of Ag (g) deposited by 1 F? (Ag = 108)
Faradays to deposit 1 mol Cu from Cu²⁺?

games.title: Silver-plating a spoon
games.prompt: Arrange the set-up and process in order
items: Make the spoon the cathode and a silver bar the anode
Dip both in a silver salt solution
Silver dissolves from the anode as Ag⁺
Ag⁺ is reduced and silver deposits on the spoon

quiz.q: A current of 2 A flows through CuSO₄ solution for 965 s. What mass of Cu (in g) is deposited? (Cu = 63.5 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
quiz.explain: Q = 1930 C = 0.02 mol e⁻; Cu needs 2 e⁻, so 0.01 mol Cu = 0.635 g.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that Cu²⁺ needs two electrons (gives 1.27 g)

quiz.q: How much charge (in C) is needed to deposit 1.08 g of silver from AgNO₃ solution? (Ag = 108 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Uses 2 electrons per silver ion

quiz.q: How long (in s) must a 5 A current flow to deposit 2.7 g of aluminium from molten Al₂O₃? (Al = 27 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Uses one electron per Al instead of three

quiz.q: The same charge deposits 1.08 g of Ag in one cell and some copper in a second cell connected in series. What mass of Cu (in g) is deposited? (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5)
quiz.explain: 1.08 g Ag means 0.01 mol e⁻ passed; Cu²⁺ needs 2e⁻, so 0.005 mol Cu = 0.3175 g.
quiz.mistake: Assumes equal moles of Ag and Cu are deposited

quiz.q: In the electrolysis of CuSO₄ solution using copper electrodes, what happens at the anode?
quiz.explain: The copper anode is oxidised, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, replacing the Cu²⁺ deposited at the cathode.
quiz.mistake: Applies the inert-electrode result (O₂ at anode) to copper electrodes

quiz.q: In electrorefining of copper, which is made the anode?
quiz.explain: Impure copper dissolves at the anode, and pure copper deposits on the cathode; impurities settle as anode mud.
quiz.mistake: Swaps anode and cathode roles

quiz.q: How many faradays are needed to reduce 1 mol of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺?
quiz.explain: Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons per ion, so 5 F per mole.
quiz.mistake: Uses the oxidation number +7 directly

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In an electrolytic cell the anode is the positive electrode. Reason (R): Oxidation always occurs at the anode.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Both are true. The anode is positive because it is connected to the positive terminal of the external source; the fact that oxidation happens there holds in all cells and does not explain the sign.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the place of oxidation decides the polarity

teach.ask: Gappu wants a silver medal: 'How do I calculate how much silver gets plated if I pass current for some time?'
teach.praise: Ding! Charge = current × time, divide by F for moles of electrons, then use the electrons per ion. Shiny!
teach.nudge: You found the charge. What constant converts it into moles of electrons?

topics.title: Products of electrolysis

learn.hook: Electrolyse molten salt and you get sodium metal; electrolyse brine and you get hydrogen instead. Same ions, different stories.
points: Products depend on the state of the electrolyte, the nature of the electrodes (inert Pt or reactive Cu), the standard potentials of competing reactions and overpotential (extra voltage needed for some reactions, especially gas evolution).
Molten NaCl: cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(l); anode Cl⁻ → ½Cl₂(g) + e⁻.

Aqueous NaCl: at the cathode water is reduced instead of Na⁺ (E° of H₂O/H₂ = −0.83 V vs Na⁺/Na −2.71 V): H₂O + e⁻ → ½H₂ + OH⁻. At the anode Cl₂ is evolved rather than O₂ (although E° Cl₂/Cl⁻ 1.36 V > O₂ 1.23 V) because of the overpotential of oxygen. Net: NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) + ½H₂(g) + ½Cl₂(g).
Dilute H₂SO₄ (Pt electrodes): O₂ at the anode, 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (E° 1.23 V). At higher concentration, peroxodisulphate forms: 2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ (E° 1.96 V). H₂ is evolved at the cathode.

example.q: Predict the products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl using inert electrodes.
steps: Cathode: compare Na⁺/Na (−2.71 V) with H₂O/H₂ (−0.83 V); water is reduced → H₂ + OH⁻
Anode: Cl₂ (1.36 V) vs O₂ (1.23 V); O₂ has a high overpotential, so Cl₂ forms
Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain in solution as NaOH
example.answer: H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode, NaOH in solution

learn.reallife: This is the chlor-alkali process run at large plants in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; the NaOH goes into soaps and paper, and the Cl₂ into water disinfection and PVC.

quiz.q: What is obtained at the cathode when molten NaCl is electrolysed?
quiz.explain: In the melt there is no water, so Na⁺ is the only species reduced: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.
quiz.mistake: Applies the aqueous result to the molten salt

quiz.q: Why is H₂ and not Na formed at the cathode during electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
options: Water has a higher (less negative) reduction potential than Na⁺
Na⁺ is reduced but immediately evaporates
Na⁺ has a higher reduction potential than water
quiz.explain: E°(H₂O/H₂) = −0.83 V is less negative than E°(Na⁺/Na) = −2.71 V, so water is reduced preferentially.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cation in the salt is always the one reduced

quiz.q: Why is chlorine rather than oxygen liberated at the anode in the electrolysis of brine?
options: Cl₂/Cl⁻ has a lower E° than O₂
Oxygen is not present in brine
Chloride ions are reduced at the anode
Oxygen evolution has a high overpotential
quiz.explain: Thermodynamics favours O₂ slightly (1.23 V vs 1.36 V), but the extra voltage needed for O₂ makes Cl₂ formation faster in practice.
quiz.mistake: Ignores overpotential and uses E° alone

quiz.q: Which substance is left in the solution after electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
quiz.explain: Na⁺ ions remain and OH⁻ forms at the cathode, giving NaOH in solution.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sodium metal collects in water

quiz.q: Which product forms at the anode on electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid with platinum electrodes?
quiz.explain: In dilute acid water is oxidised: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
quiz.mistake: Gives the concentrated-acid product

quiz.q: At higher concentrations of H₂SO₄, what is the anode product?
quiz.explain: With more sulphate ions available, 2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ becomes the anode reaction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the anode product never changes with concentration

quiz.q: Aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed with platinum electrodes. What forms at the anode?
quiz.explain: Pt is inert, so water is oxidised to O₂; copper deposits at the cathode.
quiz.mistake: Confuses inert electrodes with copper electrodes

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The products of electrolysis can differ for the same electrolyte. Reason (R): Products depend on whether the electrolyte is molten or aqueous and on the electrode material.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Molten vs aqueous NaCl, and Pt vs Cu electrodes with CuSO₄, give different products, as R explains.
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrolysis products are fixed for a salt

teach.ask: Gappu splashes in brine: 'Why don't I get sodium when I electrolyse salt water, but I do with molten salt?'
teach.praise: Chirp! In water, H₂O is reduced more easily than Na⁺, giving H₂; in the melt there's no water, so Na forms!
teach.nudge: What competes with Na⁺ at the cathode in brine, and why does it win?

topics.title: Batteries and fuel cells

learn.hook: The dry cell in a TV remote, the lead battery under an auto-rickshaw seat and the fuel cell that powered Apollo astronauts share the same physics but very different chemistry.
points: Primary batteries cannot be recharged. Dry (Leclanché) cell: zinc container anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), carbon (graphite) rod cathode in MnO₂ + carbon, NH₄Cl/ZnCl₂ paste; cathode: MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃. About 1.5 V.

Mercury cell: zinc–mercury amalgam anode, HgO + carbon paste cathode, KOH + ZnO paste electrolyte. Anode: Zn(Hg) + 2OH⁻ → ZnO(s) + H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode: HgO + H₂O + 2e⁻ → Hg(l) + 2OH⁻. About 1.35 V, constant because no ion appears in the overall reaction Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l). Used in hearing aids and watches.
Secondary (rechargeable) lead storage battery: Pb anode, grid of lead packed with PbO₂ as cathode, 38% H₂SO₄. Discharge: Pb(s) + PbO₂(s) + 2H₂SO₄(aq) → 2PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l); charging reverses it.
Nickel–cadmium cell: Cd(s) + 2Ni(OH)₃(s) → CdO(s) + 2Ni(OH)₂(s) + H₂O(l); longer life than the lead cell but more expensive.

H₂–O₂ fuel cell (used in the Apollo programme): porous carbon electrodes with Pt/Pd catalyst in concentrated aqueous NaOH. Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; anode: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻; overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Efficiency about 70%, versus about 40% for thermal power plants, and it is pollution free.

example.q: Why does a mercury cell give a constant voltage throughout its life, unlike a dry cell?
steps: Overall reaction: Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l)
No ion in solution appears in the overall reaction
So the reaction quotient, and hence E, does not change as the cell is used
example.answer: Its overall reaction involves no ions whose concentration changes, so the voltage stays about 1.35 V

learn.reallife: Indian Oil and ISRO have tested hydrogen fuel-cell technology (ISRO demonstrated a fuel-cell power system on its POEM platform in space), and hydrogen fuel-cell buses have begun trials on Indian roads.

quiz.q: What is the anode in a dry (Leclanché) cell?
quiz.explain: Zinc is oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), so the zinc container is the anode.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the central rod is the anode

quiz.q: What is the cathode reaction of a dry cell?

quiz.q: Why does a mercury cell give a constant voltage during its life?

quiz.explain: Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l) has only solids and a liquid, so Q stays constant.

quiz.q: What is the overall discharge reaction of a lead storage battery?
quiz.explain: Both electrodes turn into PbSO₄ while sulphuric acid is used up during discharge.

quiz.q: Why is the density of the acid in a lead storage battery a measure of its charge?
options: Lead dissolves in the acid on charging
H₂SO₄ is consumed during discharge, so the acid becomes less dense
quiz.explain: Discharge uses up H₂SO₄ and forms water, lowering density; charging restores it.

quiz.q: What is the cathode reaction in an H₂–O₂ fuel cell with alkaline electrolyte?
quiz.explain: Oxygen is reduced at the cathode in alkaline medium, giving hydroxide ions.
quiz.mistake: Gives the anode reaction

quiz.q: What is the approximate efficiency of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
quiz.explain: Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electricity at about 70%, compared with about 40% for thermal power plants.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the efficiency of thermal plants

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A nickel–cadmium cell is a secondary cell. Reason (R): Its cell reaction can be reversed by passing current through it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Secondary cells are rechargeable, i.e. their reaction can be reversed by an external current, which is true for Ni–Cd cells.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'secondary' means 'less important'

teach.ask: Gappu shakes a remote: 'What's the difference between a primary cell, a secondary cell and a fuel cell?'
teach.praise: Beep! Primary cells can't be recharged, secondary ones can, and fuel cells run as long as fuel keeps flowing!
teach.nudge: Which type can be recharged, and what is special about how a fuel cell gets its reactants?

topics.title: Corrosion: an electrochemical enemy

learn.hook: Mumbai's sea air is brutal on iron: railings, ships and bridges rust fast. Rusting is a tiny galvanic cell on the metal's surface.
points: Corrosion slowly destroys a metal by forming oxides or other salts; rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver and the green coating on copper are examples.

At an anodic spot on iron: 2Fe(s) → 2Fe²⁺ + 4e⁻ (E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V). Electrons move through the metal to a cathodic spot where O₂ is reduced in the presence of H⁺ (from H₂CO₃ formed by dissolved CO₂): O₂(g) + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (E° = 1.23 V).
Overall: 2Fe(s) + O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l), E°cell = 1.67 V. Fe²⁺ is further oxidised by air to Fe³⁺, forming rust, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

Prevention: barrier coatings (paint, oil, chemicals like bisphenol); covering with a more reactive metal that corrodes instead (galvanising with zinc); sacrificial electrodes of Mg or Zn connected to the iron; and anti-rust solutions.

example.q: Calculate E°cell for the rusting reaction 2Fe + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + 2H₂O.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways uses galvanised steel and special paints on bridges and overhead line masts in coastal areas, and ships docked at Visakhapatnam carry zinc or magnesium sacrificial anodes on their hulls.

quiz.q: Which reaction occurs at the anodic spot during rusting of iron?
quiz.explain: Iron is oxidised at the anodic spot; oxygen is reduced at the cathodic spot.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up anode and cathode reactions

quiz.q: What is the chemical formula of rust?
quiz.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
quiz.mistake: Gives an iron(II) or anhydrous oxide

quiz.q: Why does iron rust faster near the sea coast?
options: Salt in the moist air makes the surface water a better electrolyte
quiz.explain: Dissolved salts increase ionic conduction between anodic and cathodic spots, speeding the electrochemical reaction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks salt protects metals

quiz.q: How does galvanising protect iron?
options: Zinc is more reactive and gets oxidised in preference to iron
Zinc makes iron a cathode by absorbing oxygen only
Zinc is less reactive than iron
Zinc reacts with rust to remove it
quiz.explain: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V is more negative than Fe's, so zinc corrodes first even if the coating is scratched.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coating works only as a paint-like barrier

quiz.q: A magnesium block is connected to an underground iron pipeline. What is it called?
quiz.explain: Magnesium is oxidised instead of iron, so it is sacrificed to protect the pipe.
quiz.mistake: Thinks magnesium acts as the cathode

quiz.q: Why does corrosion of iron need both moisture and oxygen?
options: Only oxygen is needed; water is optional
Water acts as the electrolyte and O₂ is reduced at the cathodic spot
quiz.explain: Without an electrolyte the electrochemical cell cannot work, and without O₂ there is no cathode reaction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rusting is a simple combination of iron with oxygen

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A scratch on a galvanised iron sheet does not lead to rusting of the exposed iron. Reason (R): Zinc has a lower (more negative) reduction potential than iron and corrodes preferentially.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Even when exposed, iron is protected because zinc acts as the anode and is oxidised first.
quiz.mistake: Thinks protection is lost the moment the coating is scratched

teach.ask: Gappu sees a rusty gate: 'Why is rusting called an electrochemical process, and how can we stop it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Iron is oxidised at anodic spots, oxygen reduced at cathodic spots, and zinc or paint protects it. Shiny gate!
teach.nudge: You described the rust, but what happens at the anodic and cathodic spots, and how can we prevent it?

topics.title: Rate of a reaction: average and instantaneous

learn.hook: Diamond turning into graphite is thermodynamically favourable, yet your grandmother's diamond nose-pin is safe for millions of years. Feasibility is not speed — kinetics is.
points: Chemical kinetics studies reaction rates, the factors affecting them and the mechanism (the steps by which reactants become products). Thermodynamics tells whether a reaction is feasible; kinetics tells how fast it goes.
Average rate = change in concentration ÷ time interval: r_av = −Δ[R]/Δt = +Δ[P]/Δt. Units: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (for gases, atm s⁻¹).
Instantaneous rate is the average rate as Δt → 0: r = −d[R]/dt = d[P]/dt, found from the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that instant.
For aA + bB → cC + dD: rate = −(1/a) d[A]/dt = −(1/b) d[B]/dt = (1/c) d[C]/dt = (1/d) d[D]/dt, so that every species gives the same rate.

example.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, hydrogen is used up at 0.03 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find the rate of formation of NH₃ and the rate of the reaction.
example.answer: NH₃ forms at 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; rate of reaction = 0.01 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹

learn.reallife: Food technologists at CFTRI, Mysuru, study how fast vitamins and colours in packaged foods break down to set 'best before' dates — that is reaction kinetics.

Instantaneous rate of formation of product

items.q: [R] falls from 0.50 to 0.30 M in 4 min. Average rate (M min⁻¹)?

quiz.q: The concentration of a reactant falls from 0.50 M to 0.30 M in 4 minutes. What is the average rate (in mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Reports the change in concentration without dividing by time

quiz.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, −d[H₂]/dt = 0.03 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is d[NH₃]/dt (in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Rate = −(1/3) d[H₂]/dt = 0.01 = (1/2) d[NH₃]/dt, so d[NH₃]/dt = 0.02.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all species change at the same speed

quiz.q: For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂, which expression correctly gives the rate of reaction?
quiz.explain: Each rate is divided by its stoichiometric coefficient so they all become equal; reactants carry a minus sign.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by coefficients instead of dividing

quiz.q: How is the instantaneous rate found from a concentration–time graph?
options: By dividing total change by total time
From the slope of the tangent at that instant
From the area under the curve
From the intercept on the concentration axis
quiz.explain: Instantaneous rate is d[R]/dt, the gradient of the tangent at that point.
quiz.mistake: Confuses instantaneous rate with average rate

quiz.q: What is the unit of rate for a gaseous reaction when concentration is expressed as pressure?
quiz.explain: Rate = change in pressure ÷ time, so the unit is atm s⁻¹ (or bar s⁻¹).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the unit of rate with that of a rate constant

quiz.q: Why does a reaction that is thermodynamically feasible sometimes not occur noticeably?
options: The reaction has no activation energy
Thermodynamics shows feasibility but not speed; the rate may be extremely slow
Its Gibbs energy change must be positive
quiz.explain: ΔG < 0 says the reaction can occur; kinetics (activation energy) decides how fast. Diamond to graphite is very slow.
quiz.mistake: Assumes negative ΔG means fast

quiz.q: For 2A → B, the product forms at 0.15 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the rate of disappearance of A (in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The rate of a reaction usually decreases with time. Reason (R): Reactant concentrations decrease as the reaction proceeds.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Rate depends on reactant concentrations, which fall as they are consumed, so the rate generally slows.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rate of a reaction is constant

teach.ask: Gappu watches a reaction: 'What's the difference between average rate and instantaneous rate?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Average rate is the change over a time interval; instantaneous rate is the tangent's slope at one moment!
teach.nudge: You described the average. How do you get the rate at one exact moment?

topics.title: Factors affecting rate; rate law and rate constant

learn.hook: Milk curdles faster on a hot day in Chennai than in a cool Shimla kitchen. Concentration, temperature and catalysts are the three big dials of reaction speed.
points: Rate depends on concentration of reactants (pressure for gases), temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
Rate law (rate expression): rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ, where x and y are found by experiment and need not equal the stoichiometric coefficients.
k is the rate constant: the rate when all reactant concentrations are 1 mol L⁻¹. It is constant at a fixed temperature but changes with temperature.
Examples (experimental): 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), rate = k[NO]²[O₂]; CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½; CH₃CHO → CH₄ + CO, rate = k[CH₃CHO]^(3/2).

example.q: For 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. How does the rate change if [NO] is doubled and [O₂] is halved?

learn.reallife: Indian refineries use catalysts and high temperatures to speed up cracking of heavy oil — all about turning up the 'rate dials'.

games.title: Does it change the value of k?
items: Halving the volume of the container (gas)

games.title: Rate law checks
items: The powers in a rate law are always equal to the coefficients in the balanced equation.
They are found experimentally and may differ.
The rate constant k depends on temperature.
k equals the rate when all reactant concentrations are 1 mol L⁻¹.
Substituting unit concentrations gives rate = k.
For CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, the rate law is rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂].
A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction.
It provides a path of lower activation energy.

quiz.q: For rate = k[NO]²[O₂], by what factor does the rate change if [NO] is doubled and [O₂] is halved?
quiz.mistake: Treats both concentration changes as cancelling

quiz.q: For rate = k[A][B]², by what factor does the rate change if [B] is tripled at constant [A]?
quiz.explain: Rate ∝ [B]², so tripling [B] multiplies the rate by 3² = 9.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the square on [B]

quiz.q: Which statement about the rate law is correct?
options: It does not include the rate constant
It can always be written from the balanced equation
quiz.explain: Exponents in the rate law come from experiment; for example CHCl₃ + Cl₂ has an order of ½ in Cl₂.
quiz.mistake: Assumes stoichiometric coefficients give the exponents

quiz.q: What is the physical meaning of the rate constant k?
options: The time taken for half the reactant to react
The rate at the end of the reaction
The rate of reaction when every reactant concentration is 1 mol L⁻¹
The equilibrium constant of the reaction
quiz.explain: Putting [A] = [B] = 1 M in rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ gives rate = k.
quiz.mistake: Confuses k with half-life or equilibrium constant

quiz.q: Which change will NOT change the rate constant of a reaction?
options: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
quiz.explain: Concentration changes the rate but not k; k changes only with temperature or catalyst.
quiz.mistake: Thinks k changes whenever the rate changes

quiz.q: For CH₃CHO → CH₄ + CO, rate = k[CH₃CHO]^(3/2). By what factor does the rate change if [CH₃CHO] is made 4 times?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 4 by 3/2 instead of raising it to that power

quiz.q: For a reaction A + B → C, the rate law is rate = k[A]. Which statement is correct?
options: Changing [A] does not affect the rate
B is not consumed in the reaction
Changing [B] does not affect the rate
quiz.explain: The rate law shows no dependence on [B], though B is still consumed; its order is zero.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a reactant missing from the rate law is not used up

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The rate of a gaseous reaction increases when the reaction mixture is compressed. Reason (R): Compression increases the concentration (partial pressure) of the gaseous reactants.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Higher pressure means more molecules per unit volume, i.e. higher concentration, which raises the rate.
quiz.mistake: Does not link pressure of gases to concentration

teach.ask: Gappu peers at rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ: 'Where do x and y come from, and what is this k?'
teach.praise: Chirp! x and y come from experiments, and k is the rate at unit concentrations, fixed at a given temperature!
teach.nudge: You said what k is called, but how are x and y found, and what changes k?

topics.title: Order of reaction and units of k

learn.hook: Exam favourite: a table of initial concentrations and rates. Spot how the rate responds and the order falls out like a puzzle.
points: Order of a reaction = sum of the powers of concentration terms in the rate law (x + y for rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ). It can be 0, 1, 2, 3 or even fractional.
Zero order: rate independent of concentration; first order: rate ∝ [A]; second order: rate ∝ [A]² or [A][B].
Units of k = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹ for order n: zero order mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; first order s⁻¹; second order L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Initial-rate method: change one concentration at a time. If doubling [A] doubles the rate, order in A is 1; if it quadruples the rate, order is 2; if the rate is unchanged, order is 0.

example.q: For A + B → products: doubling [A] at fixed [B] doubles the rate; doubling [B] at fixed [A] makes the rate 4 times. Find the rate law and overall order.

learn.reallife: Pharmacologists at Indian drug companies find the order of a drug's decomposition to decide shelf life: most tablets degrade by first-order kinetics.

items.q: Doubling [A] makes rate 8 times. Order in A?
Doubling [A] leaves rate unchanged. Order in A?

quiz.q: In an experiment, doubling [A] at constant [B] doubles the rate, and doubling [B] at constant [A] increases the rate 4 times. What is the overall order?
quiz.explain: Order in A = 1 and in B = 2, so overall order = 1 + 2 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the orders or adds the rate factors

quiz.q: The rate constant of a reaction is 2.0 × 10⁻³ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the order of the reaction?
quiz.explain: L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−2) s⁻¹, which matches n = 2.
quiz.mistake: Reads the unit backwards

quiz.q: What is the unit of the rate constant of a zero order reaction?
quiz.explain: For n = 0, unit = (mol L⁻¹)¹ s⁻¹ — the same as the unit of rate.
quiz.mistake: Gives the first-order unit

quiz.q: Initial rates: [A] = 0.1 M gives 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; [A] = 0.2 M gives 8.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹. What is the order with respect to A?
quiz.explain: Doubling [A] increases the rate 4 times: 2ˣ = 4, so x = 2.
quiz.mistake: Reports the rate ratio (4) as the order

quiz.q: For CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½. What is the overall order?
quiz.explain: Order = 1 + ½ = 1.5; orders can be fractional.
quiz.mistake: Uses the stoichiometric coefficients (1 + 1)

quiz.q: The rate of a reaction is unchanged when the concentration of reactant X is tripled. What is the order with respect to X?
quiz.explain: If 3ˣ = 1, x = 0: the rate does not depend on [X].
quiz.mistake: Assumes every reactant must have order at least 1

quiz.q: Which of these values is possible for the order of a reaction but impossible for the molecularity of an elementary step?
quiz.explain: Order is experimental and can be fractional; molecularity counts colliding species, so it must be a whole number (1, 2 or 3).
quiz.mistake: Confuses order with molecularity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The unit of k for a first order reaction does not involve concentration. Reason (R): For n = 1, (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) becomes (mol L⁻¹)⁰.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: For first order the concentration unit cancels, leaving s⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Does not apply the general unit formula

teach.ask: Gappu looks at k = 4 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹: 'How can a unit tell me the order of a reaction?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Unit of k = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹, so s⁻¹ means first order. Units are clues!
teach.nudge: Which general formula connects the unit of k with the order n?

topics.title: Molecularity, elementary and complex reactions

learn.hook: Three molecules bumping into each other at exactly the same moment, in the right way? Rare — which is why termolecular reactions are so uncommon.
points: An elementary reaction occurs in a single step. A complex reaction occurs through a sequence of elementary steps (the mechanism).
The slowest step is the rate-determining step; it controls the overall rate.

Molecularity = number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) colliding at the same time in an elementary step: unimolecular (NH₄NO₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O), bimolecular (2HI → H₂ + I₂), termolecular (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂). Molecularity above 3 is very unlikely.
Molecularity applies only to elementary reactions and cannot be zero or fractional. Order applies to any reaction and can be zero or fractional; for a complex reaction, molecularity has no meaning.
Example: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ in alkaline medium with I⁻: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]. Step 1 (slow): H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻; step 2 (fast): H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + I⁻ + O₂.

example.q: For the I⁻-catalysed decomposition of H₂O₂, the slow step is H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻. What are the order and the molecularity of this step?
steps: Two species collide in this elementary step: molecularity 2
example.answer: Order 2, molecularity 2 (bimolecular) for the slow step

learn.reallife: Traffic on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway moves only as fast as the narrowest toll booth — just as a reaction goes only as fast as its rate-determining step.

games.title: Order or molecularity?
items: Number of species colliding in one step

quiz.q: What is the molecularity of the elementary reaction 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g)?
quiz.explain: Two HI molecules collide simultaneously, so it is bimolecular.
quiz.mistake: Counts the products instead of the colliding reactants
steps: Reacting species in the step: 2 HI

quiz.q: Which statement about molecularity is correct?
options: It cannot be zero or fractional
It applies to the overall complex reaction
It is found only from experiment
quiz.explain: Molecularity counts colliding species in an elementary step, which must be a whole number of 1, 2 or 3.
quiz.mistake: Confuses molecularity with order

quiz.q: Why are reactions with molecularity greater than three very rare?
options: The chance of more than three molecules colliding at once with the right orientation is extremely small
quiz.explain: Simultaneous effective collisions of many species are statistically very unlikely.
quiz.mistake: Gives an unrelated reason

quiz.q: In a complex reaction, which step determines the overall rate?
quiz.explain: The overall rate can be no faster than its slowest step, the rate-determining step.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the fastest step controls the rate

quiz.q: For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (catalysed by I⁻ in alkaline medium), the rate law is rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]. What is the order with respect to H₂O₂?
quiz.explain: The power of [H₂O₂] in the experimental rate law is 1, even though its coefficient in the overall equation is 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the stoichiometric coefficient as the order

quiz.q: Which reaction is unimolecular?
quiz.explain: A single species (NH₄NO₂) decomposes in this elementary step.
quiz.mistake: Counts product molecules

quiz.q: The order of a reaction is 1.5. What can you conclude?
options: It is a complex reaction, not an elementary one
It is a zero order reaction
It is a termolecular elementary reaction
quiz.explain: A fractional order cannot arise from a single elementary step, so the reaction must have a multi-step mechanism.
quiz.mistake: Thinks order and molecularity are always equal

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Order and molecularity are the same for every reaction. Reason (R): Molecularity has meaning only for elementary reactions.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Order and molecularity often differ (and molecularity is meaningless for complex reactions), so A is false; R is true.
quiz.mistake: Assumes order always equals molecularity

teach.ask: Gappu counts molecules: 'Is molecularity just another name for order?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Molecularity counts colliding species in an elementary step and is a whole number; order comes from experiment!
teach.nudge: You said they differ. Which applies only to elementary steps, and which is found experimentally?

topics.title: Zero order reactions and half-life

learn.hook: Ammonia decomposing on a hot platinum surface ignores how much ammonia you add — the surface is already full. That's a zero order reaction.
points: Zero order: rate = k[R]⁰ = k. Integrated form: [R] = [R]₀ − kt, so k = ([R]₀ − [R]) ÷ t. A plot of [R] vs t is a straight line with slope −k and intercept [R]₀.
Examples: decomposition of NH₃ on a hot Pt surface at high pressure, 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) (rate = k because the surface is saturated); thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface.
Half-life t½ is the time for the concentration to fall to half its initial value. Zero order: t½ = [R]₀ ÷ 2k, directly proportional to the initial concentration.
First order: t½ = 0.693 ÷ k, independent of initial concentration. For the zero order case, time for complete reaction = [R]₀ ÷ k.

example.q: A zero order reaction has k = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ and [R]₀ = 0.8 mol L⁻¹. Find the half-life and the time for completion.

learn.reallife: Catalytic converters in BS-VI vehicles work on hot metal surfaces; when the surface is saturated with exhaust gas, the conversion behaves like a zero order process.

items.q: [R]₀ = 0.5 M, k = 0.025 M s⁻¹. Time to finish (s)?
[R] falls from 0.9 to 0.5 M in 40 s (zero order). k (M s⁻¹)?

quiz.q: A zero order reaction has [R]₀ = 0.8 mol L⁻¹ and k = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is its half-life (in s)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the first-order formula 0.693/k

quiz.q: For a zero order reaction with [R]₀ = 0.6 M and k = 0.01 M s⁻¹, what is [R] (in M) after 20 s?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only k without multiplying by time

quiz.q: What is obtained when [R] is plotted against t for a zero order reaction?
options: A straight line with slope −k and intercept [R]₀
A straight line with slope k/2.303
A straight line through the origin with slope k
quiz.explain: From [R] = −kt + [R]₀, the graph is linear with slope −k.
quiz.mistake: Uses the first-order log plot

quiz.q: Why is the decomposition of NH₃ on a hot platinum surface at high pressure zero order?
options: The reaction has no activation energy
NH₃ does not adsorb on platinum
The metal surface is saturated with NH₃, so more gas cannot increase the rate
quiz.explain: Once all active sites are covered, the rate is fixed by the surface, not by the gas concentration.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the catalyst is consumed

quiz.q: How does the half-life of a zero order reaction depend on the initial concentration?
quiz.explain: t½ = [R]₀/2k, so doubling [R]₀ doubles t½.
quiz.mistake: Uses the first-order result for all orders

quiz.q: A first order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. What is its half-life (in min)?
quiz.mistake: Divides 1 by k or uses 2.303/k

quiz.q: How long (in s) will a zero order reaction with [R]₀ = 0.5 M and k = 0.025 M s⁻¹ take to go to completion?
quiz.explain: At completion [R] = 0, so t = [R]₀/k = 0.5 ÷ 0.025 = 20 s.
quiz.mistake: Gives the half-life instead

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is a zero order reaction. Reason (R): For zero order reactions, the rate depends on the concentration of the reactant.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: HI decomposition on gold is zero order, but zero order means the rate does NOT depend on concentration, so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Misremembers what zero order means

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'How can a reaction's speed not depend on how much reactant there is?'
teach.praise: Chirp! When a catalyst surface is saturated, rate = k regardless of concentration, and t½ = [R]₀/2k!
teach.nudge: You said it's zero order. Why doesn't the concentration matter, and what's its half-life formula?

topics.title: First order reactions

learn.hook: Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from Harappan sites, radioactive iodine therapy at Tata Memorial, and how quickly a medicine leaves your body: all follow first order kinetics.
points: First order: rate = k[R]. Integrated form: ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt, i.e. k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]). Also [R] = [R]₀e^(−kt).
Plots: ln[R] vs t is a straight line with slope −k; log([R]₀/[R]) vs t is a straight line through the origin with slope k/2.303.
Half-life t½ = 0.693/k, independent of initial concentration. After n half-lives, the fraction left = (½)ⁿ.
Useful results: time for 75% completion = 2 t½; time for 99.9% completion ≈ 10 t½. Examples: hydrogenation of ethene, decomposition of N₂O₅ and N₂O, and all natural radioactive decay.

example.q: A first order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. How long will it take for 75% of the reactant to react?

learn.reallife: Archaeologists at the Birbal Sahni Institute, Lucknow, date ancient charcoal using the first order decay of carbon-14 (half-life about 5730 years).

games.title: Fraction remaining after each half-life
games.prompt: Starting from 100% of a first order reactant

items.q: Is t½ of a first order reaction dependent on [R]₀?

quiz.q: A first order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. How long (in min) does it take for 75% completion?
quiz.explain: 75% completion = 2 half-lives; t½ = 0.693/0.0231 = 30 min, so t = 60 min.
quiz.mistake: Gives one half-life (50% completion)

quiz.q: The concentration of a reactant in a first order reaction falls from 0.1 M to 0.01 M in 46.06 s. What is k (in s⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Uses ln without the factor 2.303, or misplaces the decimal

quiz.q: What fraction of a first order reactant remains after 4 half-lives?
quiz.explain: Each half-life halves the amount: (½)⁴ = 1/16.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 instead of halving four times

quiz.q: Which plot gives a straight line for a first order reaction?
quiz.explain: ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt is linear in t with slope −k.
quiz.mistake: Uses the zero-order plot

quiz.q: Why is the half-life of a first order reaction independent of the initial concentration?
options: Because the reaction stops at half-life
Because t½ = 0.693/k, which contains no concentration term
quiz.explain: Substituting [R] = [R]₀/2 into k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]) gives t½ = 2.303 log 2/k = 0.693/k.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all half-lives depend on concentration

quiz.q: A first order reaction is 50% complete in 30 minutes. How long (in min) will it take to be 87.5% complete?
quiz.explain: 87.5% complete means 12.5% = (½)³ remains, so 3 half-lives = 90 min.
quiz.mistake: Takes the percentage proportionally (gives 52.5 min)

quiz.q: The half-life of a first order reaction is 10 min. What is k (in min⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Uses k = 1/t½

quiz.q: Assertion (A): All natural radioactive decays follow first order kinetics. Reason (R): The rate of radioactive decay is proportional to the number of nuclei present.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Decay rate ∝ N is the first order rate law, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect proportional rate with first order

teach.ask: Gappu holds a carbon-dated bone: 'What's special about first order reactions and their half-life?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Rate ∝ [R], t½ = 0.693/k and it's independent of starting amount. Ancient bones confirm it!
teach.nudge: You mentioned half-life. What is its formula, and does it depend on how much you start with?

topics.title: Gas-phase first order reactions and pseudo first order reactions

learn.hook: When a gas decomposes in a sealed flask, chemists just watch the pressure gauge. And when water is in huge excess, a second order reaction behaves like first order.
points: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g) at constant volume: if pᵢ is the initial pressure and pₜ the total pressure at time t, then p_A = 2pᵢ − pₜ.
k = (2.303/t) log[pᵢ ÷ (2pᵢ − pₜ)]. The decomposition of N₂O₅ (2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂) is a classic first order gas-phase reaction studied this way.
Pseudo first order reactions are of higher molecularity/order but behave as first order because one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration barely changes.
Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O →(H⁺) CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH; rate = k[CH₃COOC₂H₅] since water is in excess.
Inversion of cane sugar: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O →(H⁺) C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose); rate = k[C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁].

example.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), pᵢ = 0.5 atm. After 100 s the total pressure is 0.95 atm. Find k.

learn.reallife: Gur and jaggery makers in Kolhapur see sucrose slowly 'invert' when cane juice is acidic — the inversion of cane sugar is the textbook pseudo first order reaction.

games.title: Pressure method for A(g) → B(g) + C(g)
items: Note the initial pressure pᵢ of A
Measure the total pressure pₜ at time t

games.title: Pseudo first order?
items: Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate is pseudo first order.
Water is in large excess, so rate = k[ester].
Inversion of cane sugar is truly first order in both sucrose and water.
Water is in excess; it is pseudo first order, rate = k[sucrose].
In a pseudo first order reaction, one reactant is present in large excess.
For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), the total pressure decreases as the reaction proceeds.
One mole of gas gives two, so total pressure increases.
Decomposition of N₂O₅ is a first order reaction.
It is a standard example of first order kinetics.

quiz.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), pᵢ = 0.5 atm and pₜ = 0.95 atm after 100 s. k is n × 10⁻² s⁻¹. What is n?
quiz.mistake: Uses pₜ instead of p_A = 2pᵢ − pₜ

quiz.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), what is the partial pressure of A in terms of pᵢ and the total pressure pₜ?
quiz.explain: If x atm of A reacts, pₜ = pᵢ + x, so p_A = pᵢ − x = 2pᵢ − pₜ.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the pressure of products with that of A

quiz.q: Why is the acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate called a pseudo first order reaction?
options: Water is a catalyst and is not consumed
Ethyl acetate is in large excess
Water is in large excess, so its concentration remains almost constant
The acid is the only reactant
quiz.explain: Rate = k[ester][H₂O] becomes k′[ester] because [H₂O] barely changes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks water does not react

quiz.q: What are the products of the acid-catalysed inversion of cane sugar?
quiz.explain: Sucrose + water → glucose + fructose (in the presence of H⁺).
quiz.mistake: Confuses sucrose with maltose or lactose

quiz.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g) at constant volume, what happens to the total pressure as the reaction proceeds?
options: It first rises then falls to zero
quiz.explain: One mole of gas gives two moles, so total pressure rises towards 2pᵢ.
quiz.mistake: Assumes pressure falls as reactant is used up

quiz.q: A pseudo first order reaction has rate = k′[ester], where k′ = k[H₂O]. If k′ = 0.0050 min⁻¹ and [H₂O] = 50 M, what is the true rate constant k (in L mol⁻¹ min⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by [H₂O] instead of dividing

quiz.q: Which reaction is a standard example of a first order gas-phase decomposition followed by pressure measurements?
quiz.explain: Decomposition of N₂O₅ is first order and changes the total pressure, which makes it easy to follow.
quiz.mistake: Picks a reaction that is not first order

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Inversion of cane sugar is a pseudo first order reaction. Reason (R): Its rate law is rate = k[C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁] because water is present in large excess.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The large excess of water makes its concentration constant, so the rate depends only on sucrose.
quiz.mistake: Does not realise water is a reactant

teach.ask: Gappu splashes water: 'What makes a reaction pseudo first order? Give me an example!'
teach.praise: Chirp! When one reactant like water is in large excess, its concentration stays constant and the reaction behaves first order!
teach.nudge: You named it, but why does one reactant's concentration effectively drop out of the rate law?

topics.title: Temperature, activation energy and the Arrhenius equation

learn.hook: Food in a refrigerator stays fresh for days; in a Rajasthan summer it spoils in hours. Svante Arrhenius explained why temperature has such a strong effect.
points: For many reactions, the rate constant nearly doubles for a 10 K rise in temperature. Temperature coefficient = k(T + 10)/k(T), usually about 2 to 3.
Arrhenius equation: k = A e^(−Ea/RT), where A is the pre-exponential (frequency) factor, Ea is the activation energy (J mol⁻¹) and R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Reactants must reach an unstable, high-energy activated complex at the top of the energy barrier before forming products. Ea is the energy needed to reach this complex from the reactants.

The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the fraction of molecules with each kinetic energy. At a higher temperature the curve broadens and shifts towards higher energy, and the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases a lot (the area beyond Ea roughly doubles for a 10 K rise).
The factor e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of molecules with kinetic energy equal to or greater than Ea.

example.q: A reaction's rate constant doubles for every 10 K rise. By what factor does it increase from 300 K to 330 K?

learn.reallife: Indian cold-chain logistics for vaccines (like the eVIN-tracked supply network) keep vials at 2–8 °C precisely because degradation rates climb steeply with temperature.

games.title: Term ↔ meaning
pairs: Fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea
Unstable intermediate at the top of the barrier

games.title: Temperature effects
items: For many reactions, the rate constant nearly doubles for a 10 K rise in temperature.
This is the common rule of thumb; the temperature coefficient is about 2–3.
At higher temperature the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve becomes narrower and taller.
It broadens and its peak shifts to higher energy and becomes lower.
The total area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve stays the same at different temperatures.
It represents the total number of molecules, which is unchanged.
Raising the temperature lowers the activation energy.
It increases the fraction of molecules that have at least Ea; Ea itself is unchanged.
A larger Ea means a smaller rate constant at the same temperature (same A).
k = A e^(−Ea/RT) decreases as Ea increases.

quiz.q: A reaction's rate doubles for every 10 K rise. By what factor does the rate increase when temperature rises from 300 K to 340 K?
quiz.explain: 40 K = 4 steps of 10 K, so the factor is 2⁴ = 16.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 2 by 4 instead of raising 2 to the power 4

quiz.q: In the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT), what does e^(−Ea/RT) represent?
options: The fraction of molecules with kinetic energy equal to or greater than Ea
quiz.explain: The exponential term gives the fraction of collisions energetic enough to cross the barrier.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the exponential factor with the frequency factor A

quiz.q: What is the activated complex?
options: An unstable, high-energy arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy barrier
The catalyst used in the reaction
A reactant molecule at low energy
quiz.explain: It forms when reactants gain energy equal to Ea and exists only momentarily before giving products or reactants.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the activated complex is a product

quiz.q: How does the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve change when temperature increases?
options: It broadens and shifts towards higher energies
It becomes narrower and shifts to lower energies
quiz.explain: Higher temperature spreads energies more widely, with more molecules at high energy; total area stays constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of molecules increases with temperature

quiz.q: Why does a small rise in temperature increase the rate of reaction so much?
options: The fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases greatly
quiz.explain: Because of the exponential term, a modest temperature rise sharply increases the number of molecules that can cross the barrier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks temperature changes Ea

quiz.q: Two reactions have the same A at the same temperature, but reaction X has a higher Ea than reaction Y. Which is faster?
quiz.explain: k = A e^(−Ea/RT): a lower Ea gives a larger k.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a higher Ea gives a faster reaction

quiz.q: If the rate constant increases from k to 3k for a 10 K rise, what is the temperature coefficient?
quiz.explain: Temperature coefficient = k(T + 10)/k(T) = 3k/k = 3.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 10 K

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Increasing temperature increases the rate of a reaction. Reason (R): Increasing temperature decreases the activation energy of the reaction.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: A is true, but temperature does not change Ea; it increases the fraction of molecules having energy ≥ Ea. R is false.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the effect of temperature with that of a catalyst

teach.ask: Gappu sweats in the heat: 'Why does warming a reaction speed it up so dramatically?'
teach.praise: Chirp! More molecules gain energy ≥ Ea at higher temperature — Arrhenius's exponential makes it a big jump!
teach.nudge: You mentioned temperature. What barrier must molecules cross, and what happens to the number that can?

topics.title: Finding Ea and the effect of a catalyst

learn.hook: Two rate constants at two temperatures — that's all you need to measure the height of a reaction's energy hill. And a catalyst simply digs a tunnel through it.
points: Taking logs: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope −Ea/R (or log k vs 1/T has slope −Ea/(2.303R)).
Two temperatures: log(k₂/k₁) = [Ea ÷ (2.303R)] × [(T₂ − T₁) ÷ (T₁T₂)].
A catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy (often via an intermediate complex), and is regenerated at the end.

A catalyst does not change ΔG of the reaction or the equilibrium constant; it speeds up forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster. It cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction occur.

example.q: The rate constant of a reaction doubles from 300 K to 310 K. Find Ea. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, log 2 = 0.3010)

learn.reallife: The Haber process at fertiliser plants like those of IFFCO uses an iron catalyst so that ammonia forms fast enough at a workable temperature — the catalyst changes speed, not the equilibrium yield.

items.text: Slope of ln k vs 1/T = ___.
Slope of log k vs 1/T = ___.
Intercept of ln k vs 1/T = ___.
A catalyst lowers the ___ energy.

quiz.q: A reaction's rate constant doubles when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K. What is Ea (in kJ mol⁻¹)? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, log 2 = 0.3010)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2.303 when converting ln to log (gives 23.27)

quiz.q: A plot of ln k against 1/T has a slope of −6000 K. What is Ea (in kJ mol⁻¹)? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
quiz.explain: Slope = −Ea/R, so Ea = 6000 × 8.314 = 49884 J mol⁻¹ ≈ 49.88 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Also multiplies by 2.303 though the plot uses ln k

quiz.q: A plot of log k against 1/T has a slope of −5000 K. What is Ea (in kJ mol⁻¹)? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2.303 for the log k plot

quiz.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
It shifts the equilibrium towards products
It increases the kinetic energy of molecules
quiz.explain: The catalyst forms a different route (often via an intermediate) with a lower energy barrier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a catalyst adds energy to the system

quiz.q: What effect does a catalyst have on the equilibrium constant of a reversible reaction?
quiz.explain: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so K is unchanged; equilibrium is just reached sooner.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a catalyst increases product yield at equilibrium

quiz.q: Can a catalyst make a reaction with positive ΔG occur spontaneously?
options: No; it only speeds up reactions that are already spontaneous
Only if it is used in large amounts
quiz.explain: A catalyst does not change ΔG, so it cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction spontaneous.
quiz.mistake: Believes a catalyst can change thermodynamics

quiz.q: In the Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T, what does the intercept on the ln k axis give?
quiz.explain: From ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T), the intercept at 1/T = 0 is ln A.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slope and intercept

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A catalyst does not alter the equilibrium constant of a reaction. Reason (R): A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and backward reactions by the same amount.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Equal lowering of both barriers speeds both directions equally, so the equilibrium position and K stay the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lowering Ea must shift the equilibrium

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a catalyst speed things up without changing the final equilibrium?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A catalyst opens a lower-Ea pathway for both directions, so equilibrium comes faster but K stays the same!
teach.nudge: You said it lowers something. What does it lower, and why doesn't the equilibrium shift?

topics.title: Collision theory of reaction rates

learn.hook: Billions of collisions happen every second in a gas, yet only a tiny fraction cause a reaction. Like a perfect cover drive, it needs both power and the right angle.
points: Collision theory (Max Trautz and William Lewis): reactant molecules are hard spheres, and reaction happens only when they collide. Collision frequency Z is the number of collisions per second per unit volume.
Effective collisions need enough energy (at least the threshold energy, i.e. Ea above the ground state) and proper orientation.
Rate = Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT) for energy alone; including orientation, rate = P Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT), where P is the probability (steric) factor.
Example of orientation: CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻ happens only when OH⁻ approaches the carbon from the side opposite to Br.
Limitation: atoms and molecules are treated as hard spheres, ignoring their structure.

example.q: In collision theory, which two conditions must a collision satisfy to be effective, and where do they appear in the rate expression?
steps: Energy at least equal to the threshold (Ea): e^(−Ea/RT) term

learn.reallife: A bowler at Eden Gardens needs pace and the right seam angle to take a wicket; molecules need energy and orientation to react.

games.title: Collision theory term ↔ meaning
pairs: Collision frequency of A and B

games.title: Collision facts
items: Every collision between reactant molecules leads to a reaction.
Only collisions with enough energy and proper orientation are effective.
The probability factor P accounts for proper orientation.
It corrects Z e^(−Ea/RT) for orientation.
Collision theory treats molecules as hard spheres.
In CH₃Br + OH⁻, OH⁻ must approach from the same side as Br.
It must attack from the side opposite to the Br atom.
Raising temperature increases the fraction of effective collisions.
More molecules have energy at least equal to Ea.

quiz.q: According to collision theory, which two factors decide whether a collision is effective?
quiz.explain: Molecules must have at least the threshold energy and collide in the right orientation to form products.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any collision leads to reaction

quiz.q: In the expression rate = P Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT), what does P represent?
options: The probability or steric factor for proper orientation
quiz.explain: P accounts for the fraction of energetic collisions that also have correct orientation.
quiz.mistake: Reads P as pressure

quiz.q: What is collision frequency (Z)?
options: The number of products formed per second
The fraction of collisions that are effective
The number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture
quiz.explain: Z counts all collisions, effective or not, per unit time per unit volume.
quiz.mistake: Confuses all collisions with effective collisions

quiz.q: What is the main limitation of collision theory?
options: It cannot explain the effect of temperature
It treats atoms and molecules as hard spheres and ignores their structure
quiz.explain: Real molecules have shapes and internal structure that the hard-sphere model ignores.
quiz.mistake: Thinks collision theory has no energy factor

quiz.q: For CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻, why do many energetic collisions still fail to give products?
options: CH₃Br is too small to collide
Br⁻ is a poor leaving group
OH⁻ must attack carbon from the side opposite to Br, and many collisions are wrongly oriented
quiz.explain: Proper orientation is needed; only attack opposite to Br leads to the product.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the orientation requirement

quiz.q: Why does an increase in temperature increase the number of effective collisions?
options: More molecules possess energy equal to or greater than the threshold energy
quiz.explain: Higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with sufficient energy; Ea and P are unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Thinks temperature changes P or Ea

quiz.q: Who proposed the collision theory of reaction rates?
quiz.explain: Collision theory was developed by Max Trautz and William Lewis (1916–18).
quiz.mistake: Credits the theory to Arrhenius

quiz.q: Assertion (A): All collisions between reactant molecules do not lead to the formation of products. Reason (R): Only collisions with sufficient energy and proper orientation are effective.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Effective collisions need both energy and orientation, which explains why most collisions fail.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect effectiveness to energy and orientation

teach.ask: Gappu bumps into a wall: 'Molecules collide all the time, so why don't they always react?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation are effective. I'll aim better next time!
teach.nudge: You said they collide. Which two conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?

topics.title: Position, definition and electronic configuration

learn.hook: The iron in Delhi's Mehrauli pillar, the copper in your house wiring and the zinc on a galvanised bucket all sit in the same block of the periodic table, yet zinc is not called a transition metal. Why?
points: The d-block occupies groups 3–12, where d orbitals are progressively filled. It has four transition series: 3d (Sc to Zn), 4d (Y to Cd), 5d (La and Hf to Hg) and 6d (Ac and Rf to Cn).
The f-block (placed separately at the bottom) has two series: lanthanoids (4f, Ce to Lu) and actinoids (5f, Th to Lr).

A transition element has an incompletely filled d subshell in its ground state or in any of its common oxidation states. Zn, Cd and Hg have full d¹⁰ configurations in the ground state and in their common oxidation states, so they are not regarded as transition elements (though they are studied with them).
General configuration: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²; Pd is an exception with 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰.
Exceptions in the 3d series due to the extra stability of half-filled and fully filled d orbitals: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (not 3d⁴ 4s²) and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (not 3d⁹ 4s²).

example.q: Copper has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell in its ground state. Why is it still called a transition element?
steps: 3d⁹ is incompletely filled in a common oxidation state
example.answer: Because Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has an incomplete d subshell

learn.reallife: India's Hindustan Zinc and the stainless-steel industry of Jindal both work with d-block metals; nickel and chromium make the steel in your kitchen 'stainless'.

quiz.q: What is the ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
quiz.explain: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.
quiz.mistake: Applies the simple filling order without the half-filled exception

quiz.q: Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not regarded as transition elements?
options: They have incompletely filled d orbitals
They have completely filled d¹⁰ orbitals in the ground state and in their common oxidation states
quiz.explain: Zn²⁺, Cd²⁺ and Hg²⁺ are all d¹⁰, so these elements never have a partly filled d subshell in common states.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they lack d electrons

quiz.q: Which series of transition elements starts with lanthanum?
quiz.explain: La and then Hf to Hg make up the 5d series.
quiz.mistake: Confuses La with the start of the 4f lanthanoid series

quiz.q: What is the general outer electronic configuration of the d-block elements?
quiz.explain: The d orbitals of the penultimate shell, (n−1)d, are being filled.
quiz.mistake: Writes the d subshell in the same shell as s

quiz.q: How many unpaired electrons are present in Cu²⁺ (Z of Cu = 29)?
quiz.explain: Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹, which has one unpaired electron.
quiz.mistake: Removes electrons from 3d before 4s

quiz.q: Which element of the d-block has the configuration 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰?
quiz.explain: Pd is the notable exception with an empty 5s orbital.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every d-block element has at least one ns electron

quiz.q: Silver has the configuration [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s¹. Why is it considered a transition element?
options: In its +2 oxidation state it has an incomplete 4d⁹ subshell
Its ground state has an incomplete d subshell
quiz.explain: Ag²⁺ (4d⁹) has an incompletely filled d subshell, satisfying the definition.
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the ground state

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Copper has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s². Reason (R): A completely filled d subshell has extra stability.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Moving one electron from 4s to 3d gives the more stable full 3d¹⁰ subshell.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the exception to filled-subshell stability

teach.ask: Gappu pecks at zinc: 'Zinc is in the d-block, so why isn't it a transition element?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Transition elements need a partly filled d subshell in the atom or a common ion; Zn is always d¹⁰!
teach.nudge: What kind of d subshell defines a transition element, and what does zinc have?

topics.title: Physical properties, atomic sizes and ionisation enthalpies

learn.hook: Tungsten in an old filament bulb stays solid above 3600 K, while mercury in a thermometer is liquid at room temperature. Both are d-block metals.
points: Transition elements are typically hard, lustrous metals with high melting and boiling points, high densities and high enthalpies of atomisation, due to strong metallic bonding that involves (n−1)d as well as ns electrons. Melting points rise to a maximum around the middle (d⁵) of each series, apart from anomalous values for Mn and Tc.
Zn, Cd and Hg have no unpaired d electrons, weaker metallic bonding, and hence low melting points; Hg is a liquid.

Across a series, atomic radius decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant because each added d electron shields the outer electrons poorly while nuclear charge increases. Density increases from Ti to Cu.

4d and 5d elements of the same group have almost identical radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) because of lanthanoid contraction: the poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before the 5d series pull the 5d atoms in.

Ionisation enthalpy rises across a series but irregularly. The second ionisation enthalpies of Cr and Cu are unusually high (removing an electron from stable d⁵ and d¹⁰ ions), and the third ionisation enthalpies of Mn (Mn²⁺ is d⁵) and Zn (Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰) are high.

example.q: Explain why Zr and Hf have almost the same atomic radius even though Hf has 32 more electrons.
steps: Between Zr (4d) and Hf (5d) come the 14 lanthanoids, filling 4f
4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly
Effective nuclear charge rises, cancelling the expected increase in size: lanthanoid contraction
example.answer: Lanthanoid contraction makes their radii nearly equal (160 pm and 159 pm)

learn.reallife: Zr and Hf are so alike that separating them for India's nuclear reactors (zirconium alloy tubes must be nearly hafnium-free) is a specialised job done at the Nuclear Fuel Complex, Hyderabad.

quiz.q: Why do transition metals have high melting points and enthalpies of atomisation?
options: Strong metallic bonding involving both (n−1)d and ns electrons
They have only s electrons for bonding
quiz.explain: Unpaired d electrons add to metallic bonding, which is strongest around the middle of a series.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only ns electrons take part in metallic bonding

quiz.q: Which 3d metal has the lowest melting point?
quiz.explain: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell and no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weakest.
quiz.mistake: Picks a metal from the middle of the series

quiz.q: Why are the atomic radii of Zr (160 pm) and Hf (159 pm) almost equal?
options: Hf has fewer electrons than Zr
quiz.explain: The poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before Hf cause a contraction that cancels the expected size increase.
quiz.mistake: Credits actinoid contraction, which affects later elements

quiz.q: Why is the second ionisation enthalpy of chromium unusually high?
options: Removing the second electron breaks the stable 3d⁵ configuration of Cr⁺
Chromium has a very large atomic radius
quiz.explain: Cr⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a stable half-filled subshell; removing another electron needs extra energy.
quiz.mistake: Writes the wrong configuration for Cr⁺

quiz.q: Why is the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese unusually high?
options: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
quiz.explain: Removing a third electron from Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) destroys the extra-stable half-filled subshell.
quiz.mistake: Confuses half-filled with fully filled

quiz.q: How does atomic radius generally change across the 3d series?
options: It decreases sharply all the way
It decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant
quiz.explain: Increasing nuclear charge contracts the atom, but poor shielding by d electrons soon balances the effect.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the trend is as steep as in s- and p-block

quiz.q: Which property increases from titanium to copper in the 3d series?
quiz.explain: Atoms get slightly smaller while atomic mass increases, so density rises from Ti to Cu.
quiz.mistake: Assumes size also increases

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Reason (R): Mercury has no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weak.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: With a full 5d¹⁰ 6s² configuration, Hg has weak metallic bonding and a very low melting point.
quiz.mistake: Does not link unpaired electrons to metallic bond strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is lanthanoid contraction, and why do zirconium and hafnium look like twins?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Poor shielding by 4f electrons shrinks the 5d atoms, so Zr and Hf end up nearly the same size!
teach.nudge: You named it. Which electrons cause it, and what do they fail to do?

topics.title: Oxidation states and stability of higher oxidation states

learn.hook: Manganese can show every oxidation state from +2 to +7. Potassium permanganate's purple and manganese dioxide's black are just two of its many faces.
points: Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the (n−1)d and ns electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be lost or shared; oxidation states usually differ by one.
The number of oxidation states is greatest in the middle of the 3d series: Mn shows +2 to +7. At the ends there are few: Sc mainly +3, Zn only +2.
Highest oxidation states rise up to Mn (Sc +3, Ti +4, V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7) and then fall. Low oxidation states (0, +1) appear in complexes with π-acceptor ligands like CO, e.g. Ni(CO)₄ and Fe(CO)₅.
Fluorine and oxygen stabilise high oxidation states. Oxygen does it better because it can form multiple bonds to the metal: Mn's highest fluoride is MnF₄ but its highest oxide is Mn₂O₇.

Halides: Cu(II) halides exist except the iodide, because Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂. In water, Cu⁺ disproportionates (2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu) because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy.

example.q: Find the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄, K₂MnO₄ and MnO₂.

learn.reallife: The Mn in the MnO₂ of a dry cell (+4) and in KMnO₄ used to disinfect village wells in India (+7) shows how one element can play many redox roles.

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇?

quiz.q: Which 3d element shows the largest number of oxidation states?
quiz.explain: Mn has the most electrons available in 3d and 4s and shows +2 to +7.
quiz.mistake: Picks an element at the end of the series

quiz.q: Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal often found in its oxide rather than its fluoride?
options: Oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine
Oxygen can form multiple bonds with the metal
Fluorine cannot form bonds with metals
quiz.explain: Multiple M=O bonding lets oxygen stabilise very high oxidation states, e.g. Mn₂O₇ versus MnF₄.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine

quiz.q: Why does CuI₂ not exist while CuCl₂ and CuBr₂ do?
options: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is reduced to Cu(I)
Iodine is too small to bond with copper
quiz.explain: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂: iodide is a good reducing agent.
quiz.mistake: Does not consider redox between Cu²⁺ and I⁻

quiz.q: Why is Cu⁺ unstable in aqueous solution?
options: It disproportionates to Cu²⁺ and Cu because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy
It is oxidised by water to Cu³⁺
It has an incomplete d subshell
quiz.explain: The large hydration energy of the smaller, more highly charged Cu²⁺ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy.
quiz.mistake: Ignores hydration enthalpy

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of nickel in Ni(CO)₄?
quiz.explain: CO is a neutral ligand, so nickel is in the zero oxidation state.
quiz.mistake: Treats CO as carrying a charge

quiz.q: Which is the highest oxidation state shown by vanadium?
quiz.explain: V has 3d³ 4s², so it can use all five electrons, as in V₂O₅.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all metals reach +7

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Transition elements show variable oxidation states. Reason (R): The energies of (n−1)d and ns orbitals are very close.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because the two sets of electrons are close in energy, varying numbers can be used in bonding.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link to orbital energies

teach.ask: Gappu counts on his feathers: 'Why does manganese show so many oxidation states, from +2 to +7?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Mn's 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy, so it can use 2 up to all 7 of them!
teach.nudge: You said it varies. Which electrons are involved, and why can different numbers be used?

topics.title: Electrode potentials and chemical reactivity

learn.hook: Most 3d metals fizz in dilute acid, but copper sits calmly in it. The answer lies in a positive standard electrode potential and the energy accounting behind it.
points: E°(M²⁺/M) is generally negative across the 3d series (e.g. Mn −1.18, Fe −0.44, Ni −0.25, Zn −0.76 V), so these metals liberate H₂ from dilute acids.

Copper is unique with E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V: its high enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation enthalpies are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy, so it does not liberate H₂ from acids (only oxidising acids like HNO₃ react).
Values for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than the general trend: Mn²⁺ (d⁵) and Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) are extra stable, and Ni²⁺ has a very negative hydration enthalpy.

E°(M³⁺/M²⁺): Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ = +1.57 V and Co³⁺/Co²⁺ = +1.97 V are high, so Mn³⁺ and Co³⁺ are strong oxidising agents. The comparatively low value for Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V) reflects the stability of Fe³⁺ (d⁵). Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ = −0.41 V, so Cr²⁺ is a strong reducing agent (it becomes stable d³).
Chemical reactivity: apart from copper, 3d metals are fairly reactive and are oxidised by 1 M H⁺, although some (like Ti and V) are passive due to protective oxide films.

example.q: Cr²⁺ and Mn³⁺ are both d⁴. Why is Cr²⁺ reducing while Mn³⁺ is oxidising?
steps: Cr²⁺ (d⁴) → Cr³⁺ (d³): loses an electron to reach the stable half-filled t₂g³ arrangement — acts as a reducing agent
Mn³⁺ (d⁴) → Mn²⁺ (d⁵): gains an electron to reach the extra-stable half-filled d⁵ — acts as an oxidising agent
This matches E°: Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V
example.answer: Cr²⁺ is oxidised to stable d³; Mn³⁺ is reduced to stable d⁵

learn.reallife: Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids, but in air sour foods slowly attack it; that is why traditional copper and brass cookware in Indian kitchens is lined with tin (kalai) before acidic dishes are cooked in it.

games.title: Oxidising or reducing agent in water?

quiz.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute HCl?
options: Copper has a very negative E°
Copper forms a protective oxide in HCl
