learn.reallife: Gold mines such as Hutti in Karnataka extract gold by cyanide leaching, and today Indian hospitals use cisplatin for testicular, ovarian and other cancers.

quiz.q: Which metal is present in chlorophyll?
quiz.explain: Chlorophyll is a magnesium complex; haemoglobin contains iron and vitamin B₁₂ contains cobalt.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up chlorophyll with haemoglobin

quiz.q: Which metal is present in vitamin B₁₂?
quiz.explain: Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex.
quiz.mistake: Guesses iron because of its link to anaemia

quiz.q: How is the hardness of water estimated using coordination chemistry?
options: By adding AgNO₃ to precipitate Ca²⁺
By titration with Na₂EDTA, which complexes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
quiz.explain: EDTA forms stable 1:1 complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, allowing their estimation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses hardness estimation with chloride testing

quiz.q: What is the role of cyanide ions in extracting gold?
options: They reduce gold ions to metal
quiz.explain: Gold dissolves as [Au(CN)₂]⁻ in the presence of oxygen, and is then recovered by adding zinc.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cyanide is the reducing agent

quiz.q: What is Wilkinson's catalyst used for?
quiz.explain: [(Ph₃P)₃RhCl] catalyses the addition of H₂ to alkenes.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up different applications

quiz.q: What is chelate therapy?
options: Removal of excess or toxic metals from the body using chelating ligands
quiz.explain: For example, EDTA removes lead, and D-penicillamine and desferrioxamine B remove excess copper and iron.
quiz.mistake: Thinks chelates are only industrial

quiz.q: Which complex is used as an anticancer drug?
quiz.explain: cis-Platin inhibits the growth of tumours; the trans isomer is much less effective.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the importance of the cis arrangement

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In black-and-white photography, the developed film is fixed by washing with hypo solution. Reason (R): Hypo dissolves undecomposed AgBr by forming the complex [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Removing unexposed AgBr as a soluble complex stops further darkening, fixing the image.
quiz.mistake: Does not link fixing to complex formation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Name some ways coordination compounds help us in daily life.'
teach.praise: Chirp! Haemoglobin, chlorophyll and B₁₂ in biology, EDTA in analysis and medicine, and cisplatin against cancer!
teach.nudge: You named one example. Can you give one from biology and one from medicine?

topics.title: Classification and nomenclature of halo compounds

learn.hook: PVC water pipes start from vinyl chloride, chloroquine treats malaria, and the halothane once used in operation theatres is a haloalkane. Naming and classifying them is step one.
points: By number of halogen atoms: mono-, di-, tri- or polyhalo compounds.

Compounds with an sp³ C–X bond: alkyl halides (1°, 2° or 3°, by the carbon bearing X), allylic halides (X on an sp³ carbon next to C=C, e.g. CH₂=CH–CH₂Br) and benzylic halides (X on an sp³ carbon attached to a benzene ring, e.g. C₆H₅CH₂Cl).
Compounds with an sp² C–X bond: vinylic halides (X on a C=C carbon, e.g. CH₂=CHCl) and aryl halides (X directly on an aromatic ring, e.g. C₆H₅Cl).
IUPAC names treat halogens as prefixes: CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃ is 2-chlorobutane, (CH₃)₃CBr is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, CH₂=CHCH₂Br is 3-bromoprop-1-ene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl is (chloromethyl)benzene.

Dihalides: geminal (gem) have both X on the same carbon, e.g. CH₃CHCl₂ (1,1-dichloroethane, ethylidene chloride); vicinal (vic) have X on adjacent carbons, e.g. ClCH₂CH₂Cl (1,2-dichloroethane, ethylene dichloride).

example.q: Give the IUPAC name and classify (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl.
steps: Longest chain containing C–Cl: 3 carbons, Cl on C-1, CH₃ on C-2
The carbon bearing Cl is attached to only one other carbon → primary

learn.reallife: The antimalarial chloroquine and the antiseptic chloroxylenol are halogen compounds, and PVC pipes laid under Indian cities are polymers of chloroethene (vinyl chloride).

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CBr?
quiz.explain: The longest chain is propane with Br and CH₃ both on C-2.
quiz.mistake: Numbers the chain to give Br the position 1

quiz.q: CH₂=CH–CH₂–Cl is an example of which type of halide?
quiz.explain: Cl is on an sp³ carbon next to a C=C double bond.
quiz.mistake: Confuses allylic with vinylic

quiz.q: Which is a vinylic halide?
quiz.explain: In a vinylic halide, the halogen is bonded directly to an sp² carbon of C=C.
quiz.mistake: Picks the allylic compound

quiz.q: Which dihalide is a geminal dihalide?
quiz.explain: Both chlorines are on the same carbon (gem = twins).
quiz.mistake: Confuses gem with vic

quiz.q: Classify CH₃CH₂CH(Br)CH₃.
quiz.explain: The carbon bearing Br is bonded to two other carbons.
quiz.mistake: Counts all carbons in the molecule instead of those on the C–X carbon

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of C₆H₅CH₂Cl?
quiz.explain: The Cl is on the CH₂ group attached to the ring, named as a chloromethyl substituent.
quiz.mistake: Puts the Cl on the ring

quiz.q: In which compound is the C–X carbon sp² hybridised?
quiz.explain: In aryl halides, X is attached to an sp² carbon of the aromatic ring.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any compound with a ring or double bond has sp² C–X

quiz.q: Assertion (A): ClCH₂CH₂Cl is a vicinal dihalide. Reason (R): Its two chlorine atoms are on adjacent carbon atoms.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: vic dihalides have halogens on neighbouring carbons, exactly as in 1,2-dichloroethane.
quiz.mistake: Confuses vicinal with geminal

teach.ask: Gappu gets confused: 'What's the difference between allylic, vinylic and benzylic halides?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Allylic: X on sp³ C next to C=C; vinylic: X on the C=C itself; benzylic: X on sp³ C next to a benzene ring!
teach.nudge: Where exactly is the halogen in each type — on the double-bonded carbon or next to it?

topics.title: Nature of the C–X bond and physical properties

learn.hook: Chloroform is so dense that it sinks under water in a test tube. Halogens make molecules heavier, more polar and stickier.
points: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar (Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻). From F to I the halogen gets larger, so bond length increases (CH₃F 139 pm → CH₃I 214 pm) and bond enthalpy decreases (452 → 234 kJ mol⁻¹).
Dipole moments: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) > CH₃F (1.847 D) > CH₃Br (1.830 D) > CH₃I (1.636 D); CH₃F is lower than CH₃Cl because of its very short bond.

Boiling points: higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass (polarity, greater mass); RI > RBr > RCl > RF; for isomers, bp decreases with branching (1-bromobutane > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane).
para-Dihalobenzenes have higher melting points than ortho and meta isomers because their symmetry lets them pack better in the crystal lattice.

Bromo, iodo and polychloro compounds are denser than water. Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water (the energy needed to break water's hydrogen bonds is not recovered) but dissolve well in organic solvents.

example.q: Arrange 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in decreasing order of boiling point.
steps: All three have the formula C₄H₉Br (same mass)
More branching → more compact shape → smaller surface area → weaker van der Waals forces

learn.reallife: Mothballs used in Indian wardrobes are often 1,4-dichlorobenzene; being the symmetric para isomer, it is a solid that slowly sublimes.

games.title: C–X bond and properties
items: The C–I bond is longer than the C–Cl bond.
C–F has the lowest bond enthalpy among C–X bonds.
C–F is the strongest; C–I is the weakest.
CH₃Cl has a higher dipole moment than CH₃F.
1.860 D versus 1.847 D, because the C–F bond is much shorter.
Haloalkanes are highly soluble in water.
1,4-Dichlorobenzene melts at a higher temperature than 1,2-dichlorobenzene.
The para isomer is more symmetric and packs better.
Polychloro compounds are denser than water.

quiz.q: Which compound has the highest dipole moment?
quiz.explain: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) beats CH₃F (1.847 D) because the C–F bond is very short, reducing charge × distance.
quiz.mistake: Picks CH₃F because F is most electronegative

quiz.q: How do C–X bond length and bond enthalpy change from C–F to C–I?
options: Bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases
Bond length decreases and bond enthalpy increases
quiz.explain: Larger halogen atoms form longer, weaker bonds with carbon.
quiz.mistake: Thinks larger atoms bond more strongly

quiz.q: Which has the highest boiling point?
quiz.explain: Boiling point increases with molar mass and polarisability: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
quiz.mistake: Picks the most electronegative halogen

quiz.q: Why does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane boil at a lower temperature than 1-bromobutane?
options: It has a larger molar mass
Branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals forces
It has a more polar C–Br bond
quiz.explain: Isomers have equal mass, so the shape decides intermolecular contact.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of branching on surface area

quiz.q: Why is the melting point of p-dichlorobenzene higher than that of its o- and m-isomers?
options: Its symmetrical shape fits better in the crystal lattice
It has a larger dipole moment
It has a higher molar mass
quiz.explain: The para isomer is symmetric and packs closely, so more energy is needed to melt it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the isomers have different masses

quiz.q: Why are haloalkanes only slightly soluble in water even though they are polar?
options: They are less dense than water
Energy released by new attractions with water is less than that needed to break water's hydrogen bonds
quiz.explain: Haloalkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds as strong as those between water molecules.
quiz.mistake: Thinks polarity alone guarantees water solubility

quiz.q: Which is denser than water?
quiz.explain: Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives are denser than water.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all organic liquids float on water

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Haloalkanes have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass. Reason (R): The C–X bond is polar, and haloalkanes have stronger intermolecular attractions.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Dipole–dipole attractions plus greater polarisability make haloalkane molecules stick together more.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the polar C–X bond to intermolecular forces

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does branching lower the boiling point of bromobutanes even though they have the same mass?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Branching makes molecules compact, cutting surface area and van der Waals forces, so they boil lower!
teach.nudge: You said branching matters. What does it do to the molecule's surface area and intermolecular forces?

topics.title: Preparation of haloalkanes

learn.hook: Thionyl chloride is a chemist's favourite for turning alcohols into chlorides. Its by-products simply bubble away as gases, leaving a pure product behind.
points: From alcohols with HX: R–OH + HCl →(ZnCl₂) R–Cl + H₂O. ZnCl₂ is needed for primary and secondary alcohols; tertiary alcohols react with concentrated HCl at room temperature. Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°.
With phosphorus halides: 3R–OH + PX₃ → 3R–X + H₃PO₃ (PBr₃, PI₃ generated in situ from red P and Br₂/I₂); R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl.
With thionyl chloride: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑. Preferred, because both by-products are gases that escape, leaving pure alkyl chloride.
These methods are not used for aryl halides because the C–O bond in phenols has partial double bond character and is hard to break.

Halogen exchange: Finkelstein reaction R–X + NaI →(dry acetone) R–I + NaX (X = Cl, Br); NaCl or NaBr precipitates in acetone, driving the reaction forward. Swarts reaction: CH₃–Br + AgF → CH₃–F + AgBr (also with Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃).

example.q: Why is thionyl chloride preferred for converting ethanol into chloroethane?
steps: Both by-products are gases and escape
No separation is needed, giving pure chloroethane
example.answer: Because its by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, leaving the product pure

learn.reallife: India's pharmaceutical industry, the 'pharmacy of the world', uses thionyl chloride and halogen-exchange reactions in many drug syntheses.

quiz.q: What are the by-products when an alcohol reacts with thionyl chloride?
quiz.explain: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl; both are gases.
quiz.mistake: Gives the PCl₅ by-products

quiz.q: What is the role of anhydrous ZnCl₂ when a primary alcohol reacts with HCl?
options: It acts as a Lewis acid catalyst
quiz.explain: ZnCl₂ coordinates with the OH group, making it a better leaving group.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ZnCl₂ is a reactant consumed in the reaction

quiz.q: Which reaction converts C₂H₅Br into C₂H₅I?
options: Finkelstein reaction with NaI in dry acetone
quiz.explain: NaI swaps Br for I; NaBr is insoluble in acetone and precipitates.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Finkelstein with Swarts

quiz.q: Why does the Finkelstein reaction go to completion in dry acetone?
options: NaCl or NaBr formed is insoluble in acetone and precipitates out
Acetone reacts with the alkyl halide
quiz.explain: Removing the product salt by precipitation shifts the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the iodide precipitates

quiz.q: Which reagent is used to prepare alkyl fluorides by the Swarts reaction?
quiz.explain: Heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metallic fluoride such as AgF gives the alkyl fluoride.
quiz.mistake: Picks direct fluorination

quiz.q: Which alcohol reacts fastest with concentrated HCl at room temperature without ZnCl₂?
quiz.explain: Tertiary alcohols react readily because they form stable carbocations; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary alcohols are most reactive

quiz.q: Why are aryl halides not prepared by treating phenol with HCl or PCl₅?
options: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double bond character and is difficult to break
quiz.explain: Resonance gives the C–O bond in phenol partial double bond character, so OH cannot be easily replaced.
quiz.mistake: Assumes phenols behave like alcohols

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Thionyl chloride is the preferred reagent for preparing alkyl chlorides from alcohols. Reason (R): Both by-products of the reaction are gases that escape easily.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Gaseous SO₂ and HCl leave the reaction, so the alkyl chloride obtained is pure.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the gaseous by-products to purity

teach.ask: Gappu needs alkyl iodide: 'How can I swap a bromine for an iodine in an alkyl bromide?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Finkelstein: NaI in dry acetone, and the NaBr precipitates, pushing the swap forward!
teach.nudge: Which reagent and solvent, and why does the reaction go to completion?

topics.title: Preparation of haloarenes

learn.hook: You can't chlorinate benzene the way you'd chlorinate methane; it needs a Lewis acid helper, or a clever detour through a diazonium salt.
points: Electrophilic substitution: benzene + Cl₂ (or Br₂) with a Lewis acid catalyst (Fe or anhydrous FeCl₃/FeBr₃) in the dark gives chlorobenzene (or bromobenzene). Methylbenzene gives a mixture of ortho and para isomers, which can be separated (the para isomer has a higher melting point).
Iodination is reversible and needs an oxidising agent (HNO₃ or HIO₄) to remove the HI formed. Fluorination is too violent to control, so fluoroarenes are not made this way.
Sandmeyer reaction: an arenediazonium salt (from aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K) is treated with CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr, replacing –N₂⁺ by Cl or Br: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + CuCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂.
Iodobenzene is made simply by shaking the diazonium salt with potassium iodide: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + KI → C₆H₅I + KCl + N₂.

example.q: How would you prepare iodobenzene from aniline?
steps: Diazotise: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K → benzenediazonium chloride
example.answer: Diazotisation followed by treatment with KI

learn.reallife: Chlorobenzene from plants in Gujarat's chemical clusters is a starting material for pesticides and dyes.

games.title: Benzene to bromobenzene
items: Take dry benzene in the dark
Add anhydrous FeBr₃ (or Fe filings) as Lewis acid

quiz.q: What is the role of anhydrous FeCl₃ in the chlorination of benzene?
options: It is a Lewis acid that generates the Cl⁺ electrophile
quiz.explain: FeCl₃ polarises Cl₂, producing Cl⁺ (as FeCl₄⁻ forms), which attacks the ring.
quiz.mistake: Thinks FeCl₃ is a source of chlorine atoms by itself

quiz.q: Which reagent converts benzenediazonium chloride into chlorobenzene in the Sandmeyer reaction?
quiz.explain: Cuprous chloride replaces the diazonium group by Cl, releasing N₂.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the iodide method

quiz.q: How is iodobenzene prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
options: By shaking it with potassium iodide solution
By heating with CuI and HCl only
By direct reaction with I₂ and FeCl₃
quiz.explain: KI readily replaces the diazonium group by iodine without needing a copper catalyst.
quiz.mistake: Applies Sandmeyer conditions unnecessarily

quiz.q: Why is an oxidising agent like HNO₃ needed for direct iodination of benzene?
options: It acts as a Lewis acid
Iodination is reversible; the oxidising agent removes the HI formed
Iodine is not reactive at all
quiz.explain: HI is a strong reducing agent that would reverse the reaction; oxidising it drives iodination forward.
quiz.mistake: Thinks HNO₃ is a catalyst like FeCl₃

quiz.q: Why are fluoroarenes not made by direct fluorination of benzene?
options: The reaction with fluorine is too violent to control
Fluorine does not react with benzene
quiz.explain: Fluorine is so reactive that direct reaction cannot be controlled.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fluorine is unreactive

quiz.q: What is formed when methylbenzene (toluene) is chlorinated with Cl₂ and FeCl₃ in the dark?
quiz.explain: The methyl group is ortho/para directing; in the dark with a Lewis acid, substitution occurs on the ring.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ring substitution with side-chain substitution in light

quiz.q: At what temperature range is benzenediazonium chloride prepared from aniline?
quiz.explain: Diazonium salts are unstable and must be made and used in the cold (0–5 °C).
quiz.mistake: Assumes room temperature is fine

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The ortho and para isomers formed on chlorinating toluene can be separated easily. Reason (R): The para isomer has a much higher melting point than the ortho isomer.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because of the large difference in melting points, the para isomer can be crystallised out.
quiz.mistake: Does not link melting point difference to separation

teach.ask: Gappu wants iodobenzene: 'Why can't I just add iodine to benzene? What's the better way?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Direct iodination is reversible, so I'll diazotise aniline and add KI for iodobenzene. Smart!
teach.nudge: Why is direct iodination tricky, and which salt do you convert first?

topics.title: Nucleophilic substitution: products and ambident nucleophiles

learn.hook: A haloalkane is like a kabaddi raider with a weak hold: a nucleophile tags the carbon and the halide is pushed out. Swap the nucleophile and you get a whole family of products.
points: In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile (electron-rich species) attacks the partially positive carbon of C–X and the halide leaves: Nu⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X⁻.

Products: OH⁻ (aq KOH) → alcohol; R′O⁻ → ether; I⁻ → alkyl iodide; NH₃ → amine; KCN → alkyl cyanide (nitrile); AgCN → isocyanide; KNO₂ → alkyl nitrite; AgNO₂ → nitroalkane; R′COOAg → ester; LiAlH₄ → hydrocarbon.

Ambident nucleophiles can attack through two different atoms. Cyanide: KCN is ionic, giving free CN⁻ that attacks through carbon (C–C bond is more stable), forming R–CN. AgCN is mainly covalent, so only nitrogen's lone pair is available, forming R–NC.
Nitrite: KNO₂ attacks through oxygen to give alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O; AgNO₂ attacks through nitrogen to give nitroalkane R–NO₂.
Reaction with KCN is useful for increasing the carbon chain by one carbon.

example.q: What products form when bromoethane reacts with (i) KCN and (ii) AgCN?
steps: KCN is ionic: CN⁻ attacks through C → CH₃CH₂CN (propanenitrile)
AgCN is covalent: N attacks → CH₃CH₂NC (ethyl isocyanide)

learn.reallife: Many Indian drug syntheses use cyanide substitution to add one carbon to a chain, followed by converting the nitrile into an acid or amine.

games.title: Ambident nucleophiles
items: KCN reacts with alkyl halides mainly to give alkyl cyanides.
The free CN⁻ attacks through carbon.
AgCN reacts with alkyl halides mainly to give alkyl cyanides.
It gives isocyanides because only N's lone pair is free.
AgNO₂ gives nitroalkanes with alkyl halides.
KNO₂ gives nitroalkanes with alkyl halides.
Reaction of R–X with KCN increases the carbon chain by one.
The CN group adds a carbon atom.

quiz.q: What is the main product when CH₃CH₂Br reacts with alcoholic KCN?
quiz.explain: Ionic KCN gives CN⁻, which attacks through carbon to form propanenitrile.
quiz.mistake: Gives the AgCN product

quiz.q: Why does AgCN give isocyanides with alkyl halides?
options: AgCN is mainly covalent, so only the lone pair on nitrogen is available for attack
AgCN is ionic and gives free CN⁻
Isocyanides are more stable than cyanides
quiz.explain: With the carbon bonded to silver, the nitrogen lone pair attacks, giving R–NC.
quiz.mistake: Assumes AgCN behaves like KCN

quiz.q: What forms when bromoethane reacts with AgNO₂?
quiz.explain: AgNO₂ attacks through nitrogen to give the nitroalkane.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the KNO₂ and AgNO₂ products

quiz.q: Which reagent converts an alkyl halide into an ether?
quiz.explain: R′O⁻ replaces X, giving R–O–R′ (Williamson synthesis).
quiz.mistake: Picks the reagent that gives an alcohol

quiz.q: What is formed when an alkyl halide is treated with LiAlH₄?
quiz.explain: LiAlH₄ supplies hydride ions (H⁻), which replace the halogen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks LiAlH₄ always gives alcohols

quiz.q: Which is an ambident nucleophile?
quiz.explain: Cyanide can attack through C or through N.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ambident with strong nucleophiles

quiz.q: How many carbon atoms does the product have when 1-chloropropane reacts with KCN?
quiz.explain: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN (butanenitrile), with one extra carbon.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the cyanide adds a carbon

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Alkyl halides react with KCN to form alkyl cyanides as the main product. Reason (R): The C–C bond formed is more stable than a C–N bond.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Free CN⁻ prefers to attack through carbon because the resulting C–C bond is more stable.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why carbon attack is preferred

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does KCN give a cyanide but AgCN give an isocyanide with the same alkyl halide?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Ionic KCN lets CN⁻ attack via carbon; covalent AgCN leaves only nitrogen's lone pair free. Same ion, two outcomes!
teach.nudge: What is different about the bonding in KCN and AgCN, and which atom attacks in each?

topics.title: SN2 and SN1 mechanisms and reactivity

learn.hook: Two routes, one goal: SN2 is a single swift tackle from behind; SN1 waits for the halide to leave first. Which route a molecule takes depends on its crowding.
points: SN2 (substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular): one step; the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to X (backside attack) as X leaves; the transition state has carbon partly bonded to both. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order). Configuration is inverted (Walden inversion). Example: CH₃Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Cl⁻.
SN2 reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°, because bulky groups hinder the backside approach (steric hindrance).

SN1 (unimolecular): two steps — slow ionisation of R–X to a carbocation (rate-determining), then fast attack by the nucleophile. Rate = k[RX] (first order). Favoured in polar protic solvents (water, alcohol, acetic acid). Example: (CH₃)₃CBr + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH + Br⁻.
SN1 reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°, following carbocation stability. Allylic and benzylic halides are very reactive in SN1 because their carbocations are stabilised by resonance.
For the same alkyl group, reactivity of the halide in both mechanisms: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (weaker C–X bond, better leaving group).

example.q: Arrange CH₃Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr and (CH₃)₃CBr in order of increasing SN2 reactivity, and in order of increasing SN1 reactivity.
steps: SN2 is slowed by crowding: (CH₃)₃CBr < (CH₃)₂CHBr < CH₃Br
SN1 depends on carbocation stability: CH₃Br < (CH₃)₂CHBr < (CH₃)₃CBr

learn.reallife: Medicinal chemists in Indian labs choose SN2 routes when a drug molecule needs one specific inverted 3D arrangement, since enzymes in the body can tell mirror-image forms apart.

games.title: SN1 reactivity
games.prompt: Least reactive to most reactive in SN1

quiz.q: What is the rate law for an SN2 reaction of R–X with OH⁻?
quiz.explain: Both the substrate and nucleophile are in the single rate-determining step.
quiz.mistake: Gives the SN1 rate law

quiz.q: Which alkyl bromide reacts fastest by the SN2 mechanism?
quiz.explain: The methyl carbon is least hindered, so backside attack is easiest.
quiz.mistake: Uses the SN1 order

quiz.q: Which alkyl bromide reacts fastest by the SN1 mechanism?
quiz.explain: It forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation.
quiz.mistake: Uses the SN2 order

quiz.q: Why are benzyl chloride and allyl chloride very reactive towards SN1?
options: Their carbocations are stabilised by resonance
They have very strong C–Cl bonds
quiz.explain: The positive charge is delocalised over the ring or the double bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are tertiary

quiz.q: Which solvent favours the SN1 mechanism?
options: A polar protic solvent such as water or ethanol
A non-polar solvent such as hexane
quiz.explain: Polar protic solvents stabilise the carbocation and leaving halide ion by solvation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solvent has no effect

quiz.q: Arrange in decreasing order of reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution (same alkyl group): R–F, R–Cl, R–Br, R–I.
quiz.explain: C–I is the weakest and longest bond, so iodide leaves most easily.
quiz.mistake: Uses electronegativity instead of bond strength

quiz.q: Why does the rate of SN2 reaction decrease from methyl to tertiary halides?
options: Increasing steric hindrance blocks the backside attack of the nucleophile
quiz.explain: Bulky alkyl groups crowd the carbon, making the five-coordinate transition state harder to reach.
quiz.mistake: Explains SN2 with carbocation stability

quiz.q: Assertion (A): (CH₃)₃CBr undergoes hydrolysis mainly by the SN1 mechanism. Reason (R): The tertiary carbocation formed is highly stable, while backside attack is sterically hindered.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Both factors favour SN1 for tertiary halides, so R correctly explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect structure with mechanism

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do tertiary halides prefer SN1 while primary ones prefer SN2?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Tertiary halides form stable carbocations (SN1) and are too crowded for backside attack; primary ones are open for SN2!
teach.nudge: What does a tertiary halide form easily, and what stops backside attack?

topics.title: Stereochemistry: optical activity, chirality and configuration

learn.hook: Your left and right hands are mirror images that never superimpose. Many molecules are 'handed' too, and they twist polarised light in opposite directions.
points: Optically active compounds rotate the plane of plane-polarised light (measured in a polarimeter): dextrorotatory (d or +) to the right, laevorotatory (l or −) to the left.

A carbon bonded to four different groups is an asymmetric carbon (stereocentre); a molecule that is not superimposable on its mirror image is chiral. Butan-2-ol and 2-chlorobutane are chiral; propan-2-ol and 2-chloropropane are achiral.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. They have identical physical properties (mp, bp, solubility) except the direction of rotation of plane-polarised light.

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers and shows zero rotation (external compensation); it is written dl or (±). Converting an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is racemisation.

Retention: the spatial arrangement around the stereocentre is preserved. SN2 gives inversion of configuration; SN1 gives mostly racemisation, because the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

example.q: Optically active 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed by aqueous KOH via (i) SN2 and (ii) SN1. What is the stereochemistry of butan-2-ol in each case?
steps: (i) SN2: backside attack → inverted configuration, still optically active
(ii) SN1: planar carbocation → attack from both faces
Equal amounts of both enantiomers → racemic mixture, optically inactive
example.answer: SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives racemisation

learn.reallife: Some medicines are sold as a single enantiomer because one mirror form works better in the body; for example, the acid-reducer esomeprazole is the single-enantiomer form of omeprazole.

games.title: Term ↔ meaning
pairs: Not superimposable on its mirror image
Equal amounts of d and l forms
Rotates plane-polarised light to the right
Conversion of an enantiomer into a racemic mixture

quiz.q: Which compound is chiral?
quiz.explain: C-2 of butan-2-ol carries H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅ — four different groups.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any secondary carbon is a stereocentre

quiz.q: What is a racemic mixture?
options: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers with zero optical rotation
A compound with a plane of symmetry
quiz.explain: The rotations of the d and l forms cancel exactly (external compensation).
quiz.mistake: Confuses racemic mixture with a single enantiomer

quiz.q: What stereochemical outcome is typical of an SN2 reaction at a chiral carbon?
quiz.explain: Backside attack flips the configuration, like an umbrella turning inside out.
quiz.mistake: Gives the SN1 result

quiz.q: Why does an SN1 reaction of an optically active halide usually give a racemic product?
options: The planar carbocation can be attacked equally from both sides
The nucleophile attacks only from the back
quiz.explain: Attack from either face gives both configurations in nearly equal amounts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks SN1 gives inversion

quiz.q: Which property differs between two enantiomers?
options: Direction of rotation of plane-polarised light
quiz.explain: Enantiomers share all physical properties except the sign of optical rotation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks enantiomers differ in boiling point

quiz.q: How many asymmetric carbon atoms are present in 2-chlorobutane?
quiz.explain: Only C-2 has four different groups: H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅.
quiz.mistake: Counts every carbon bearing a substituent

quiz.q: What does the symbol (±) before a name indicate?
quiz.explain: (±) or dl shows equal amounts of the + and − enantiomers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it denotes charge

quiz.q: Assertion (A): 2-Chloropropane is optically inactive. Reason (R): It does not have any carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: C-2 carries two identical CH₃ groups, so there is no stereocentre and the molecule is achiral.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every halo compound with a secondary carbon is chiral

teach.ask: Gappu looks at his feet: 'What makes a molecule chiral, and how do SN1 and SN2 treat it differently?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Four different groups make a chiral carbon; SN2 inverts it and SN1 racemises it. My feet agree!
teach.nudge: You said chiral. What must the carbon carry, and what happens to it in SN2 versus SN1?

topics.title: Elimination, and reactions with metals

learn.hook: Heat 2-bromopentane with alcoholic KOH and two alkenes form, but one wins by a big margin. Zaitsev's rule predicts the winner.
points: Dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination): a haloalkane with a β-hydrogen, heated with alcoholic KOH, loses H and X from adjacent carbons to form an alkene.
Zaitsev (Saytzeff) rule: the preferred alkene is the one with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons. E.g. 2-bromopentane gives pent-2-ene (81%) rather than pent-1-ene (19%).

Substitution vs elimination: a strong, bulky base favours elimination; primary halides prefer SN2; secondary give SN2 or elimination depending on the base/nucleophile; tertiary give SN1 or elimination depending on carbocation stability and alkene substitution.

Grignard reagent: R–X + Mg →(dry ether) R–MgX. The C–Mg bond is highly polar, so R behaves as a carbanion and reacts with any proton source: RMgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X. Hence it must be made under anhydrous conditions. (Victor Grignard, Nobel Prize 1912.)
Wurtz reaction: 2R–X + 2Na →(dry ether) R–R + 2NaX, doubling the alkyl group.

example.q: Predict the major product when 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH.
steps: β-hydrogens are on C-1 and C-3
Loss of H from C-3 gives but-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃, more substituted)
Loss of H from C-1 gives but-1-ene (less substituted)
By Zaitsev's rule, the more substituted alkene is major

learn.reallife: Grignard reactions are workhorses in API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) plants in Hyderabad, where moisture is kept out carefully because water destroys the reagent.

items.text: The rule that the more substituted alkene forms preferentially is ___ rule.
Dehydrohalogenation needs a hydrogen on the ___ carbon.
Grignard reagents must be prepared in ___ ether.
2CH₃Br + 2Na → ___ + 2NaBr

quiz.q: What is the major product when 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic KOH?
quiz.explain: By Zaitsev's rule, the more substituted alkene (pent-2-ene, 81%) is the major product.
quiz.mistake: Gives the less substituted alkene

quiz.q: Which reagent favours elimination over substitution for an alkyl halide?
quiz.explain: In alcohol, OH⁻/alkoxide acts more as a base, abstracting a β-hydrogen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks aqueous and alcoholic KOH give the same product

quiz.q: What is formed when CH₃MgBr reacts with water?
quiz.explain: The carbanion-like CH₃ takes a proton from water: CH₃MgBr + H₂O → CH₄ + Mg(OH)Br.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Grignard reagents give alcohols with water

quiz.q: Why must Grignard reagents be prepared under anhydrous conditions?
options: They react with water (any proton source) to form hydrocarbons
quiz.explain: The highly polar C–Mg bond makes R a strong base that grabs protons from water.
quiz.mistake: Gives a vague safety reason

quiz.q: What is the product of the Wurtz reaction of CH₃CH₂Br with sodium in dry ether?
quiz.explain: Two ethyl groups join: 2C₂H₅Br + 2Na → C₄H₁₀ + 2NaBr.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the product keeps the same number of carbons

quiz.q: Which type of alkyl halide is most likely to undergo elimination rather than SN2 with a strong base?
quiz.explain: Tertiary halides are too hindered for SN2 and give stable, substituted alkenes.
quiz.mistake: Assumes primary halides eliminate most

quiz.q: How many different alkenes can form when 2-bromobutane undergoes dehydrohalogenation (ignoring cis–trans isomers)?
quiz.explain: Removal of H from C-1 gives but-1-ene; from C-3 gives but-2-ene.
quiz.mistake: Ignores one of the β-carbons

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Elimination from 2-bromobutane gives but-2-ene as the major product. Reason (R): The alkene with more alkyl groups on the double-bonded carbons is more stable.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: This is Zaitsev's rule, which follows from the greater stability of more substituted alkenes.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why the more substituted alkene is favoured

teach.ask: Gappu holds alcoholic KOH: 'How do I know which alkene will be the major product?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Remove a β-hydrogen so that the double bond carries the most alkyl groups — that's Zaitsev's rule!
teach.nudge: Which hydrogen is removed, and which alkene does Zaitsev favour?

topics.title: Reactions of haloarenes

learn.hook: Boil chlorobenzene with aqueous NaOH and almost nothing happens. Industry had to use 623 K and 300 atmospheres to make phenol from it — the Dow process.
points: Haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophiles because: (i) resonance gives the C–X bond partial double bond character; (ii) the sp² carbon holds the bond more tightly (C–Cl 169 pm in chlorobenzene vs 177 pm in CH₃Cl); (iii) the phenyl cation is not resonance stabilised, so SN1 is ruled out; (iv) the electron-rich ring repels nucleophiles and blocks backside attack.
Dow process: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm gives sodium phenoxide, which is acidified to phenol.

Electron-withdrawing groups like –NO₂ at ortho and para positions make substitution much easier (1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, then 2,4-dinitro, then 2,4,6-trinitro react under progressively milder conditions); a meta –NO₂ has no such effect.

Electrophilic substitution: the halogen is deactivating (–I effect) but ortho/para directing (+R effect). Chlorination, nitration, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation of chlorobenzene give mainly the para product with some ortho.
Wurtz–Fittig: Ar–X + R–X + 2Na → Ar–R + 2NaX (dry ether). Fittig: 2Ar–X + 2Na → Ar–Ar + 2NaX, e.g. diphenyl from chlorobenzene.

example.q: Why does 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene react with NaOH much more easily than chlorobenzene?
steps: OH⁻ attacks the carbon bearing Cl
The negative charge of the intermediate is delocalised onto the para –NO₂ group
This stabilises the intermediate and lowers the activation energy
example.answer: The para nitro group withdraws electrons and stabilises the intermediate

learn.reallife: Dyes and pesticides made in Indian chemical hubs such as Ankleshwar often start from nitrochlorobenzenes, which react easily because of their activating nitro groups.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason for the low reactivity of haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution?
options: The C–X bond in haloarenes is longer than in haloalkanes
The electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile
Resonance gives the C–X bond partial double bond character
The phenyl cation is not stabilised by resonance
quiz.explain: The C–X bond in haloarenes is actually shorter (169 pm vs 177 pm), making it stronger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the aryl C–X bond is longer

quiz.q: What are the conditions of the Dow process for converting chlorobenzene into phenol?
options: NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm, then acidification
quiz.explain: Drastic conditions are needed because chlorobenzene resists nucleophilic attack.
quiz.mistake: Assumes haloarenes hydrolyse as easily as haloalkanes

quiz.q: What is the major product of nitration of chlorobenzene?
quiz.explain: Cl is ortho/para directing; the para product is major for steric reasons.
quiz.mistake: Thinks deactivating groups are always meta directing

quiz.q: Why is chlorine deactivating yet ortho/para directing in electrophilic substitution?
options: It donates electrons by both effects
It withdraws electrons only from the meta position
It forms hydrogen bonds with the electrophile
Its –I effect reduces ring electron density, while its +R effect increases it at ortho and para positions
quiz.explain: Overall the ring is deactivated (–I wins), but resonance directs electrophiles to ortho/para.
quiz.mistake: Mixes the two effects

quiz.q: What is formed when chlorobenzene and methyl chloride react with sodium in dry ether?
quiz.explain: This is the Wurtz–Fittig reaction: C₆H₅Cl + CH₃Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅CH₃ + 2NaCl.
quiz.mistake: Gives the Fittig product

quiz.q: What is formed when chlorobenzene alone is treated with sodium in dry ether?
quiz.explain: Fittig reaction: 2C₆H₅Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Fittig with Wurtz–Fittig

quiz.q: Which compound undergoes nucleophilic substitution with aqueous NaOH most readily?
quiz.explain: Three o/p nitro groups strongly stabilise the intermediate; meta nitro and methyl do not help.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a meta nitro group activates as well

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Chlorobenzene does not undergo SN1 reactions easily. Reason (R): The phenyl cation formed by loss of Cl⁻ is not stabilised by resonance.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: SN1 needs a stable carbocation; the phenyl cation is unstable, so the SN1 route is ruled out.
quiz.mistake: Does not link SN1 to carbocation stability

teach.ask: Gappu struggles: 'Why won't chlorobenzene react with NaOH the way chloroethane does?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Resonance and sp² carbon make the C–Cl bond strong, and the phenyl cation is unstable. So it needs the Dow process!
teach.nudge: Give one reason the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is hard to break.

topics.title: Polyhalogen compounds: dichloromethane, chloroform and iodoform

learn.hook: Chloroform was once the anaesthetic of choice in operating rooms. Then doctors noticed something deadly could form from it if bottles were left in the light.
points: Dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂): used as a solvent (paint remover), aerosol propellant, process solvent in drug manufacture and for metal cleaning and finishing. It harms the central nervous system: low exposure can slightly impair hearing and vision; higher levels cause dizziness, nausea and tingling or numbness in fingers and toes; on the skin it causes intense burning, and it can burn the cornea.

Trichloromethane (chloroform, CHCl₃): solvent for fats, alkaloids and iodine; used to make the refrigerant R-22; once a general anaesthetic, now replaced by safer ones. Breathing its vapour depresses the central nervous system; chronic exposure can damage the liver and kidneys.

In air and light, chloroform is slowly oxidised to the extremely poisonous gas phosgene: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ →(light) 2COCl₂ + 2HCl. So it is stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim to keep out air.

Triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃) was used as an antiseptic; its action is due to the free iodine it releases, not iodoform itself. Because of its objectionable smell it has been replaced by other iodine-based preparations.
Lab safety: handle these volatile liquids only in a fume hood, with gloves and goggles, and never sniff them directly.

example.q: Why is chloroform stored in closed dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim?
steps: Light and air oxidise chloroform: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl
Dark glass blocks light and a full bottle leaves no air
example.answer: To prevent its oxidation to poisonous phosgene

learn.reallife: Industrial safety rules under India's Factories Act require proper ventilation where solvents like dichloromethane are used, for example in paint-stripping and pharma units.

games.title: Compound ↔ use or hazard
pairs: Paint remover; harms the nervous system
Solvent for fats and alkaloids; forms phosgene in light

quiz.q: Why is chloroform stored in dark bottles filled to the brim?
options: To keep out light and air that oxidise it to phosgene
To stop it from absorbing water
quiz.explain: Both light and oxygen are needed for the oxidation to phosgene.
quiz.mistake: Gives an unrelated reason

quiz.q: To what is the antiseptic property of iodoform due?
quiz.explain: Iodoform releases iodine, which kills microbes.
quiz.mistake: Credits the compound rather than the iodine

quiz.q: Which of these is a use of dichloromethane?
options: Paint remover and process solvent in drug manufacture
quiz.explain: Its solvent power makes it useful for stripping paint and in pharmaceutical processes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with iodoform or DDT

quiz.q: Which health effect is associated with exposure to dichloromethane?
options: Damage to the central nervous system, with dizziness and impaired hearing and vision
quiz.explain: CH₂Cl₂ harms the CNS; higher doses cause dizziness, nausea and numbness.
quiz.mistake: Assumes common solvents are harmless

quiz.q: Why was chloroform replaced as a general anaesthetic?
options: Safer anaesthetics became available; chloroform is toxic to the liver and can form phosgene
quiz.explain: Toxicity and the risk of phosgene formation led to its replacement.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it was ineffective

quiz.q: Which refrigerant is manufactured from chloroform?
quiz.explain: Chloroform is a raw material for R-22 (a hydrochlorofluorocarbon); Freon-12 is made from CCl₄.
quiz.mistake: Confuses R-22 with Freon-12

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Iodoform was once used as an antiseptic. Reason (R): It liberates free iodine.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The antiseptic action comes from the free iodine released, which is why iodoform worked.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link between iodine release and antiseptic action

teach.ask: Gappu sniffs a bottle: 'Why is chloroform kept in dark bottles, and what is iodoform good for?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Dark, full bottles stop light and air turning chloroform into phosgene; iodoform's iodine fights germs!
teach.nudge: What does light and air turn chloroform into, and what does iodoform release?

topics.title: CCl₄, freons and DDT: uses and environmental effects

learn.hook: The Montreal Protocol, which India signed, phased out CFCs to heal the ozone hole. The same chlorine chemistry that made freons useful made them dangerous up in the stratosphere.
points: Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄): used to make refrigerants, aerosol propellants and CFCs, in pharmaceutical manufacture and as a solvent; earlier used as a cleaning fluid, spot remover and fire extinguisher. Exposure can cause liver cancer, nerve damage, dizziness and nausea. Released into air, it rises to the stratosphere and depletes the ozone layer.

Freons are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) of methane and ethane: stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive and easily liquefied. Freon-12 (CCl₂F₂) is the most common, made from CCl₄ by the Swarts reaction; used in refrigeration, air conditioning and aerosols.

In the stratosphere, UV light breaks CFCs into chlorine radicals that start chain reactions destroying ozone, letting more harmful UV reach Earth (risk of skin cancer, eye disease and weakened immunity).

DDT (p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) was the first chlorinated organic insecticide. It was first made in 1873; its insecticidal power was discovered by Paul Müller in 1939 (Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1948). It was widely used against mosquitoes spreading malaria and lice carrying typhus.

Problems with DDT: insects developed resistance; it is highly toxic to fish; it is chemically stable and fat-soluble, so it is not metabolised quickly, gets stored in fatty tissues and builds up along food chains. It was banned in the USA in 1973.

example.q: Why does DDT become more concentrated in animals higher up a food chain?
steps: DDT is chemically stable and fat-soluble
It is not broken down quickly and is stored in fatty tissue
Each predator eats many contaminated organisms, accumulating more
example.answer: Because it is persistent and fat-soluble, it accumulates along the food chain

learn.reallife: Under the Montreal Protocol, India completed its CFC phase-out ahead of the Protocol's 2010 deadline and is now phasing out HCFCs used in air conditioners; DDT use in India is restricted to public-health vector control.

teach.ask: Gappu flies high: 'How do freons in my fridge harm the ozone layer so far up in the sky?'

topics.title: Classification, nomenclature and structures

learn.hook: The sanitiser on your hands (ethanol or propan-2-ol), the glycerol in your soap and the phenol-based disinfectant in a hospital corridor all carry an –OH group. Naming them right is half the battle.
points: By number of –OH groups: monohydric (ethanol), dihydric (ethane-1,2-diol, glycol), trihydric (propane-1,2,3-triol, glycerol) and polyhydric compounds.

Alcohols with sp³ C–OH: 1°, 2°, 3° (by the carbon bearing OH), allylic (CH₂=CH–CH₂OH, prop-2-en-1-ol) and benzylic (C₆H₅CH₂OH, phenylmethanol). With sp² C–OH: vinylic alcohols (CH₂=CH–OH) and phenols (OH on a benzene ring).

IUPAC: replace -e of the alkane by -ol: (CH₃)₂CHOH is propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Phenols: o-cresol is 2-methylphenol; catechol, resorcinol and quinol (hydroquinone) are benzene-1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-diol.

Ethers R–O–R′ are simple (symmetrical, same groups: C₂H₅OC₂H₅, ethoxyethane) or mixed (unsymmetrical: CH₃OC₂H₅, methoxyethane). IUPAC names them as alkoxyalkanes; C₆H₅OCH₃ is methoxybenzene (anisole).

Structures: C–O–H angle in methanol is 108.9° (lone pair repulsion); C–O–C in methoxymethane is 111.7° (bulky groups). In phenol the C–O bond (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm) because of partial double bond character from resonance and the sp² carbon.

example.q: Name (CH₃)₂CH–CH(OH)–CH₃ and classify it.
steps: Longest chain with C–OH: 4 carbons, numbered so OH gets the lower number
OH on C-2, CH₃ on C-3
The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons

learn.reallife: Hand sanitisers approved in India contain ethanol or propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol), and glycerol is added to keep skin moist.

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃C–OH?
quiz.explain: The longest chain through the C–OH carbon is propane with OH and CH₃ on C-2.
quiz.mistake: Numbers the chain to put OH on C-1

quiz.q: Which is a benzylic alcohol?
quiz.explain: The OH is on an sp³ carbon attached directly to a benzene ring.
quiz.mistake: Confuses benzylic alcohols with phenols

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of resorcinol?
quiz.explain: Resorcinol has two OH groups meta to each other.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up catechol, resorcinol and quinol

quiz.q: Why is the C–O–C bond angle in methoxymethane (111.7°) larger than the tetrahedral angle?
options: Repulsion between the two bulky methyl groups
quiz.explain: The bulky CH₃ groups push apart, slightly widening the angle.
quiz.mistake: Uses the lone-pair argument, which would narrow the angle

quiz.q: Why is the C–O bond in phenol shorter than in methanol?
options: Resonance gives it partial double bond character and the carbon is sp² hybridised
The oxygen in phenol is sp³
quiz.explain: Delocalisation of oxygen's lone pair into the ring and sp² carbon both shorten the bond (136 pm vs 142 pm).
quiz.mistake: Credits hydrogen bonding with bond length

quiz.q: C₂H₅–O–CH₃ is an example of a:
quiz.explain: The two groups on oxygen are different (ethyl and methyl).
quiz.mistake: Confuses ethers with alcohols

quiz.q: What is the C–O–H bond angle in methanol?
quiz.explain: Repulsion between oxygen's lone pairs makes it slightly less than the tetrahedral angle.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a perfect tetrahedral angle

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Phenols are not classified as alcohols although they contain an –OH group. Reason (R): In phenols the –OH is bonded to an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Alcohols have OH on sp³ carbon; phenols have it on an aromatic sp² carbon, which changes their properties.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the importance of carbon hybridisation

quiz.q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is classified as a:
quiz.explain: Alcohols are classified by the number of –OH groups. Glycerol has three, so it is trihydric; ethane-1,2-diol (glycol) is dihydric.
quiz.mistake: Counts carbon atoms or names instead of –OH groups

teach.ask: Gappu sees C₆H₅OH and C₆H₅CH₂OH: 'Both have a benzene ring and OH. Why is one a phenol and the other an alcohol?'
teach.praise: Chirp! In phenol the OH sits on the ring's sp² carbon; in benzyl alcohol it's on an sp³ CH₂. Different families!
teach.nudge: Where exactly is the OH attached in each, and what is that carbon's hybridisation?

topics.title: Preparation of alcohols

learn.hook: Propene can give two different alcohols depending on the route: acid-catalysed hydration or hydroboration–oxidation. Your choice of reagent decides the product.
points: Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes follows Markovnikov's rule: CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O →(H⁺) CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Mechanism: (1) protonation of the alkene by H₃O⁺ to form a carbocation; (2) nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation; (3) loss of a proton to give the alcohol.

Hydroboration–oxidation: diborane adds to the alkene, and the trialkylborane is oxidised by H₂O₂ in aqueous NaOH. The product looks like anti-Markovnikov addition of water: propene → propan-1-ol, in excellent yield.

Reduction of carbonyl compounds with H₂ (Pt, Pd or Ni), NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄: aldehydes give 1° alcohols and ketones give 2° alcohols. Carboxylic acids are reduced to 1° alcohols by LiAlH₄; industrially, acids are first converted to esters, which are then hydrogenated catalytically.
Grignard reagents add to carbonyl compounds, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives alcohols: methanal → 1° alcohol, other aldehydes → 2° alcohols, ketones → 3° alcohols.

example.q: Which carbonyl compound and Grignard reagent would you use to make 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
example.answer: Propanone with methylmagnesium bromide, followed by hydrolysis

learn.reallife: Propan-2-ol used in Indian sanitiser factories is made mainly by hydration of propene from refinery cracking units.

quiz.q: What is the main product of acid-catalysed hydration of propene?
quiz.explain: Markovnikov addition puts OH on the more substituted carbon via the more stable 2° carbocation.

quiz.q: What is the product of hydroboration–oxidation of propene?
quiz.explain: The overall result looks like anti-Markovnikov addition of water, putting OH on the terminal carbon.

quiz.q: Which type of alcohol is obtained when a ketone reacts with a Grignard reagent followed by hydrolysis?
quiz.explain: The carbonyl carbon of a ketone already has two alkyl groups; adding a third gives a 3° alcohol.
quiz.mistake: Confuses aldehyde and ketone outcomes

quiz.q: What is obtained when methanal reacts with CH₃CH₂MgBr followed by hydrolysis?
quiz.explain: Methanal gives a 1° alcohol with one more carbon than the Grignard alkyl group: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the carbon from methanal

Protonation of the alkene to form a carbocation
Attack of water on the alkene

quiz.mistake: Starts with nucleophilic attack by water

quiz.explain: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols at the carbonyl carbon.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ketones give primary alcohols

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Industrially, carboxylic acids are converted to esters before reduction to alcohols. Reason (R): LiAlH₄ is an expensive reagent.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because LiAlH₄ is costly, industry hydrogenates esters catalytically instead.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect cost with the industrial route

teach.ask: Gappu has propene: 'How can I make propan-1-ol instead of propan-2-ol from it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Hydroboration–oxidation with B₂H₆ then H₂O₂/OH⁻ puts the OH on the end carbon: propan-1-ol!
teach.nudge: Which reagent sequence gives the OH on the terminal carbon?

topics.title: Preparation of phenols and physical properties

learn.hook: Most of the world's phenol comes from cumene, and the same process gives acetone as a valuable bonus. Two products for the price of one!
points: From haloarenes: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm → sodium phenoxide → acidify → phenol.
From benzenesulphonic acid: sulphonate benzene with oleum, fuse the sulphonic acid with molten NaOH to get sodium phenoxide, then acidify.
From diazonium salts: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K gives benzenediazonium chloride, which on warming with water (or dilute acid) gives phenol.
From cumene (isopropylbenzene): air oxidation gives cumene hydroperoxide, which with dilute acid gives phenol and acetone (propanone). Most phenol worldwide is made this way.

Physical properties: alcohols and phenols have much higher boiling points than hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of similar mass because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Boiling point rises with more carbon atoms and falls with branching. Lower alcohols are miscible with water (H-bonding); solubility falls as the alkyl group grows.

example.q: Outline the cumene process for making phenol.
example.answer: Phenol, with acetone as a co-product

learn.reallife: Phenol from Indian petrochemical plants goes into making bakelite switches, epoxy resins and the antiseptic 'carbolic' soaps once common in Indian homes.

games.title: Starting material ↔ route to phenol
pairs: NaOH at 623 K, 300 atm, then H⁺

quiz.q: Which by-product is obtained along with phenol in the cumene process?

quiz.q: How is phenol prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
quiz.explain: Warm water replaces –N₂⁺ by –OH, releasing N₂.

quiz.q: Why does ethanol have a much higher boiling point than methoxymethane, though both have M = 46?

quiz.q: How does branching affect the boiling point of isomeric alcohols?
quiz.explain: Branched molecules have smaller surface area and weaker van der Waals forces.
quiz.mistake: Thinks branching strengthens intermolecular forces

quiz.q: Why does the solubility of alcohols in water decrease with increasing molar mass?
options: The larger hydrophobic alkyl part hinders hydrogen bonding with water
quiz.explain: As the alkyl chain grows, it dominates and the molecule behaves more like a hydrocarbon.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the OH group changes

quiz.q: Which reagent is used to convert benzene into benzenesulphonic acid for making phenol?
quiz.explain: Sulphonation with oleum introduces the –SO₃H group, which is later replaced by –OH.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sulphonation with chlorination

quiz.q: Under what conditions does chlorobenzene give sodium phenoxide with NaOH?
quiz.explain: Drastic conditions are needed because aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution.
quiz.mistake: Assumes mild conditions are enough

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Lower alcohols are miscible with water. Reason (R): Alcohols form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The –OH group of small alcohols forms H-bonds with water, so they dissolve completely.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect H-bonding to solubility

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does ethanol boil so much higher than an ether or hydrocarbon of the same size?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Ethanol's O–H groups form hydrogen bonds between molecules, so it needs more heat to boil!
teach.nudge: Which bond holds ethanol molecules together that ethers and alkanes lack?

topics.title: Reactions with metals and acidity of alcohols and phenols

learn.hook: Phenol (carbolic acid) is about a million times more acidic than ethanol, yet it still can't fizz with baking soda. Resonance explains both facts.
points: Alcohols and phenols react with active metals to give H₂: 2R–OH + 2Na → 2R–O⁻Na⁺ + H₂; phenol also reacts with aqueous NaOH to form sodium phenoxide (alcohols do not react appreciably with NaOH).

Alcohols are very weak Brønsted acids, weaker than water: R–O⁻ + H₂O → R–OH + OH⁻ (alkoxide is a stronger base than hydroxide). Acidity order: 1° > 2° > 3°, because electron-releasing alkyl groups increase electron density on oxygen.

Phenol is more acidic (pKa ≈ 10.0) than ethanol (pKa ≈ 15.9): the OH is on an electron-withdrawing sp² carbon, and the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge over the ring.
Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. –NO₂) increase phenol's acidity, especially at ortho and para positions: p-nitrophenol pKa 7.1, o-nitrophenol 7.2, m-nitrophenol 8.3, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol 0.5.
Electron-releasing groups (e.g. –CH₃) decrease acidity: o-, m- and p-cresols have pKa about 10.1–10.2. Phenol is too weak to react with NaHCO₃.

example.q: Arrange phenol, p-nitrophenol, p-cresol and ethanol in increasing order of acidity.

learn.reallife: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol), as acidic as a strong acid, was historically used as an explosive and in burn ointments; today it is handled only under strict safety rules.

quiz.q: Which is the most acidic?

quiz.q: Why is m-nitrophenol (pKa 8.3) less acidic than p-nitrophenol (pKa 7.1)?

m-Nitrophenol has no nitro group on the ring

quiz.q: Why are alcohols weaker acids than water?

quiz.q: What is formed when ethanol reacts with sodium metal?
quiz.explain: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂.

quiz.q: Arrange in increasing order of acidity: propan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, propan-2-ol.

quiz.q: What is the pKa of phenol?

quiz.mistake: Confuses phenol with ethanol or acetic acid

quiz.q: Assertion (A): o-Cresol is less acidic than phenol. Reason (R): The methyl group is electron releasing and destabilises the phenoxide ion.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Electron donation increases negative charge density on the phenoxide oxygen, making it less stable, so acidity falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any substituent increases acidity

teach.ask: Gappu peers at a bar of carbolic soap: 'Why is phenol acidic while ethanol hardly is?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The phenoxide ion spreads its negative charge over the ring by resonance, so phenol gives up H⁺ more easily!
teach.nudge: What happens to the negative charge after phenol loses H⁺?

topics.title: Esterification, C–O cleavage and dehydration

learn.hook: Turn salicylic acid into aspirin, find whether an alcohol is 1°, 2° or 3° in five minutes, or turn ethanol into ethene: three reactions every Class 12 student must know.
points: Esterification: R–OH + R′COOH ⇌(conc. H₂SO₄) R′COOR + H₂O (water is removed as it forms to shift the equilibrium). With acid anhydrides (H⁺) or acid chlorides (in pyridine, which neutralises HCl). Acetylation of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride gives aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid).
With HX: R–OH + HX → R–X + H₂O. Lucas test (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂): tertiary alcohols give turbidity immediately, secondary after a few minutes, primary not at room temperature.
With phosphorus trihalides: 3R–OH + PBr₃ → 3R–Br + H₃PO₃.

Dehydration to alkenes with conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ (or anhydrous ZnCl₂, alumina): ethanol at 443 K with conc. H₂SO₄ gives ethene; 2° alcohols need 85% H₃PO₄ at 440 K; 3° alcohols only 20% H₃PO₄ at 358 K. Ease: 3° > 2° > 1°.
Mechanism of dehydration: (1) protonation of the alcohol (fast); (2) loss of water to form a carbocation (slow, rate-determining); (3) loss of H⁺ from an adjacent carbon to form the alkene.

example.q: Why do tertiary alcohols give the Lucas test immediately while primary alcohols do not at room temperature?
steps: The test involves forming an alkyl chloride via a carbocation
Tertiary carbocations are very stable and form quickly
The insoluble alkyl chloride makes the solution cloudy (turbid) at once
example.answer: Because 3° alcohols form stable carbocations rapidly, giving insoluble chlorides immediately

learn.reallife: Aspirin, made by acetylating salicylic acid, is among the most widely produced drugs in India's pharmaceutical sector.

games.title: Lucas test result at room temperature
Mechanism of acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol
items: Ethanol is protonated by H⁺ to form an oxonium ion
Water leaves, forming a carbocation (slow step)
A β-hydrogen is lost as H⁺

quiz.q: What are the reagents in the Lucas test?
quiz.explain: Lucas reagent converts alcohols into insoluble alkyl chlorides at rates depending on their class.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the FeCl₃ or iodoform test

quiz.q: Which alcohol gives turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent?
quiz.explain: Tertiary alcohols react fastest because they form stable 3° carbocations.

quiz.q: What is the product when ethanol is heated with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K?
quiz.explain: At 443 K, intramolecular dehydration gives ethene; at 413 K, ethoxyethane forms.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the temperatures for alkene and ether

quiz.q: Which step is rate-determining in the acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols?
options: Loss of H⁺ to form the alkene
quiz.explain: Loss of water from the protonated alcohol to form the carbocation is slow.
quiz.mistake: Picks the fast protonation step

quiz.q: Arrange in order of ease of dehydration: 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
quiz.explain: Dehydration goes via carbocations, and 3° carbocations are most stable.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order

quiz.q: Why is pyridine used when an alcohol reacts with an acid chloride?
options: To neutralise the HCl formed, shifting the equilibrium forward
To act as an oxidising agent
quiz.explain: Removing HCl drives the esterification towards the ester.
