Strong H-bonds are not fully broken even in vapour.

quiz.q: An acid has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its pKa?
quiz.explain: pKa = −log Ka = −log(10⁻⁵) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign in the definition

quiz.q: Why do carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alcohols of similar molar mass?
options: They form more extensive hydrogen bonds, often existing as dimers
quiz.explain: Two H-bonds hold acid molecules in pairs, needing more energy to separate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks alcohols form stronger H-bonds

quiz.q: Which test distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a phenol?
options: Colour with litmus is the same for both
quiz.explain: Acids release CO₂ with bicarbonate; phenols are too weak to do so.
quiz.mistake: Uses a test that both pass

quiz.q: Which is the strongest acid?
quiz.explain: Three highly electronegative F atoms give the strongest electron-withdrawing effect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Cl is more electron-withdrawing than F

quiz.q: Why is a carboxylic acid more acidic than phenol?
options: Carboxylate has two equivalent resonance structures with the charge on two oxygen atoms, while phenoxide places charge on less electronegative carbon
Carboxylic acids have more hydrogen atoms
quiz.explain: Better delocalisation over electronegative atoms makes carboxylate more stable.
quiz.mistake: Thinks phenoxide has no resonance at all

quiz.q: Arrange in increasing order of acidity: 4-chlorobutanoic acid, 2-chlorobutanoic acid, butanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid.
quiz.explain: The –I effect of Cl decreases with distance from –COOH.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of distance

quiz.q: Why is benzoic acid nearly insoluble in cold water while ethanoic acid is miscible?
options: The large hydrophobic benzene ring outweighs the hydrogen bonding of –COOH
quiz.explain: As the hydrocarbon part grows, water solubility falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ring increases polarity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Benzoic acid (pKa 4.19) is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76). Reason (R): A phenyl group directly attached to –COOH increases acidity compared with a methyl group.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The sp² carbon of the phenyl ring is more electronegative than the methyl carbon, and CH₃ releases electrons, so benzoic acid is stronger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks phenyl always decreases acidity

teach.ask: Gappu sips vinegar: 'Why are carboxylic acids more acidic than alcohols and phenols?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Carboxylate spreads its charge equally over two oxygens by resonance, so acids give up H⁺ easily!
teach.nudge: What happens to the negative charge in the carboxylate ion?

topics.title: Reactions involving C–OH cleavage and the –COOH group

learn.hook: Fruity smells of esters, the pain-relief paracetamol (an amide) and the nylon in your schoolbag straps all come from reactions where the –OH of an acid is replaced.
points: Anhydride formation: heating with a dehydrating agent such as P₂O₅ or conc. H₂SO₄ gives acid anhydrides: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O.

Esterification: R–COOH + R′–OH ⇌(H⁺) R–COOR′ + H₂O. Mechanism: (1) protonation of the carbonyl oxygen; (2) nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the carbonyl carbon; (3) proton transfer in the tetrahedral intermediate, making –OH₂⁺ a good leaving group; (4) loss of water; (5) loss of H⁺ from the protonated ester.
Acid chlorides: R–COOH + PCl₅ → R–COCl + POCl₃ + HCl; 3R–COOH + PCl₃ → 3R–COCl + H₃PO₃; R–COOH + SOCl₂ → R–COCl + SO₂ + HCl (preferred: gaseous by-products).
Amides: R–COOH + NH₃ ⇌ RCOO⁻NH₄⁺ →(heat) R–CONH₂ + H₂O. Phthalic acid with NH₃ gives phthalamide, and on strong heating, phthalimide.

Reduction: LiAlH₄ or diborane (B₂H₆) reduce –COOH to –CH₂OH (diborane does not easily reduce esters, nitro or halo groups; NaBH₄ does not reduce –COOH). Decarboxylation: sodium carboxylates heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO, 3 : 1) lose CO₂ to give an alkane with one carbon fewer; Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous salts gives an alkane with twice the carbons of the alkyl group.

example.q: What product is obtained when sodium ethanoate is (i) heated with soda lime and (ii) electrolysed in aqueous solution?

learn.reallife: Esters such as ethyl butanoate give pineapple and other fruity flavours to Indian sweets and soft drinks; they are made by acid-catalysed esterification.

games.title: Mechanism of acid-catalysed esterification
items: The carbonyl oxygen of the acid is protonated
The alcohol attacks the carbonyl carbon
A proton transfer turns an –OH into –OH₂⁺
The protonated ester loses H⁺ to give the ester

quiz.q: Which reagent is preferred for converting a carboxylic acid into an acid chloride?
quiz.explain: Its by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, so the acid chloride is obtained pure.
quiz.mistake: Picks a reagent with a liquid by-product

quiz.q: What is formed when sodium propanoate is heated with soda lime?
quiz.explain: Decarboxylation removes CO₂, giving an alkane with one carbon fewer.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the same number of carbons

quiz.q: What is the product of Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous sodium propanoate?
quiz.explain: Two ethyl radicals (from CH₃CH₂COO⁻) combine: C₂H₅–C₂H₅ = butane.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the whole acid instead of the alkyl group

quiz.q: What is formed when ethanoic acid is reduced with LiAlH₄ followed by hydrolysis?
quiz.explain: LiAlH₄ reduces –COOH to –CH₂OH.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the aldehyde

quiz.q: Which reducing agent does NOT reduce a carboxylic acid?
options: LiAlH₄ in ether followed by H₃O⁺
quiz.explain: NaBH₄ is too mild to reduce –COOH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all hydrides reduce acids

quiz.q: What is formed when phthalic acid is treated with NH₃ and then strongly heated?
quiz.explain: Ammonium phthalate → phthalamide → (strong heat) phthalimide.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with anhydride formation

quiz.q: In acid-catalysed esterification, which group is lost from the carboxylic acid?
options: The –OH group (with H from the alcohol, as water)
quiz.explain: The acyl–oxygen bond breaks: R–CO–OH + H–OR′ → R–CO–OR′ + H₂O.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the alcohol loses its OH

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is reversible. Reason (R): The ester formed can be hydrolysed back by water in the presence of acid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Because hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, water is often removed to drive esterification forward.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect reversibility to hydrolysis

teach.ask: Gappu has sodium ethanoate: 'How can I get methane from it, and how can I get ethane?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Soda lime removes CO₂ to give methane (one carbon less); Kolbe electrolysis joins two methyls to give ethane!
teach.nudge: Which method removes a carbon, and which doubles the alkyl group?

topics.title: HVZ reaction, ring substitution, uses and multi-step conversions

learn.hook: Board exams love 'Convert A into B in not more than two steps'. Knowing a handful of key reactions — HVZ, Rosenmund, Grignard, oxidation — unlocks most of them.
points: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction: acids with an α-hydrogen, treated with Cl₂ or Br₂ and a small amount of red phosphorus, then water, give α-halo acids: R–CH₂–COOH → R–CH(X)–COOH.

The –COOH group is deactivating and meta-directing: benzoic acid gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄) and 3-bromobenzoic acid (Br₂/FeBr₃). Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions because –COOH deactivates the ring and the AlCl₃ catalyst binds to the carboxyl group.

Uses: methanoic acid in rubber, textile, dyeing, leather and electroplating industries; ethanoic acid as a solvent and as vinegar; hexanedioic acid for nylon-6,6; esters of benzoic acid in perfumery; sodium benzoate as a food preservative; higher fatty acids for soaps and detergents.

Common conversions: toluene → benzoic acid (KMnO₄); benzoic acid → benzaldehyde (SOCl₂, then Rosenmund); ethanoic acid → 2-chloroethanoic acid (HVZ); ethanol → 3-hydroxybutanal (oxidise to ethanal, then aldol); benzene → m-nitroacetophenone (Friedel–Crafts acylation, then nitration).

example.q: Convert ethanoic acid into 2-hydroxyethanoic acid.
steps: Step 1 (HVZ): CH₃COOH + Cl₂ (red P), then H₂O → ClCH₂COOH
example.answer: HVZ chlorination, then hydrolysis of the C–Cl bond

learn.reallife: Nylon-6,6 made from hexanedioic acid goes into the tyre cords and ropes produced in Indian factories, and sodium benzoate preserves bottled pickles and sauces.

games.title: Uses of carboxylic acids and derivatives
items: Methanoic acid in leather and electroplating
Esters of benzoic acid in perfumery

quiz.q: What is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction?
options: Decarboxylation of acids with soda lime
α-Halogenation of carboxylic acids using X₂ and red phosphorus
quiz.explain: Acids with α-H are converted to α-halo acids.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other named reactions

quiz.q: What is the product of nitration of benzoic acid?
quiz.explain: –COOH is meta directing.
quiz.mistake: Treats –COOH as ortho/para directing

quiz.q: Why does benzoic acid not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions?
options: –COOH deactivates the ring and AlCl₃ binds to the carboxyl group
Benzoic acid has no benzene ring
quiz.explain: The deactivated ring and the loss of the catalyst to the carboxyl group stop the reaction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is too reactive

quiz.q: Which acid is used in making nylon-6,6?
quiz.explain: Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine form nylon-6,6.
quiz.mistake: Picks a monocarboxylic acid

quiz.q: Which sequence converts benzoic acid into benzaldehyde?
quiz.explain: Acid → acid chloride → Rosenmund reduction to the aldehyde.
quiz.mistake: Uses a reagent that reduces all the way to the alcohol

quiz.q: Which compound is the product of HVZ reaction of propanoic acid with Br₂/red P followed by water?
quiz.explain: Halogenation occurs at the α-carbon (C-2).
quiz.mistake: Puts bromine on the terminal carbon

quiz.q: How can benzene be converted into m-nitroacetophenone?
options: Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl/AlCl₃, then nitration
quiz.explain: The acetyl group is meta directing, so nitration then goes meta. Nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts.
quiz.mistake: Nitrates first, which blocks Friedel–Crafts

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative. Reason (R): Benzoic acid undergoes the HVZ reaction readily.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true, but benzoic acid has no α-hydrogen (the –COOH is attached directly to the ring), so it cannot undergo the HVZ reaction; R is false.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that HVZ needs an α-hydrogen

teach.ask: Gappu is stuck on a conversion: 'How do I turn ethanoic acid into chloroethanoic acid?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The HVZ reaction with Cl₂ and red P puts chlorine on the α-carbon: ClCH₂COOH!
teach.nudge: Which named reaction, and which position gets the halogen?

topics.title: Structure, classification and nomenclature of amines

learn.hook: The fishy smell of a fish market, the adrenaline rush before a board exam and the dyes in a Banarasi saree all trace back to amines.
points: Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more H atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
Nitrogen is sp³ hybridised; three orbitals bond to H or C and the fourth holds a lone pair, so amines are pyramidal. The C–N–E angle (E = C or H) is less than 109.5°, e.g. 108° in trimethylamine.
Primary (1°) R–NH₂, secondary (2°) R₂NH and tertiary (3°) R₃N amines, by the number of H atoms replaced. Simple amines have all groups the same; mixed amines have different groups.
Common names: alkylamine (methylamine, dimethylamine). IUPAC: alkanamine — CH₃NH₂ methanamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ propan-1-amine, (CH₃)₂CHNH₂ propan-2-amine, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ hexane-1,6-diamine.

For 2° and 3° amines, the largest group gives the parent name and others are N-prefixes: (CH₃)₂NH is N-methylmethanamine, (CH₃)₃N is N,N-dimethylmethanamine, CH₃NHC₂H₅ is N-methylethanamine. Aniline is benzenamine; C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂ is N,N-dimethylbenzenamine.

example.q: Name and classify CH₃–NH–CH₂CH₃.
steps: Two groups on N: methyl and ethyl, one H left → secondary amine
Largest group (ethyl) gives the parent: ethanamine

learn.reallife: The fishy smell of stale fish is largely due to volatile amines such as trimethylamine; squeezing nimbu (lemon) on fish works because the acid turns them into odourless salts.

quiz.q: What is the shape of an amine molecule around nitrogen?
quiz.explain: N is sp³ with three bonds and a lone pair, giving a pyramidal shape.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the lone pair

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃N?
quiz.explain: Parent is methanamine; the other two methyl groups are on N.
quiz.mistake: Uses a non-IUPAC name

quiz.q: Classify C₆H₅NHCH₃.
quiz.explain: Two groups (phenyl and methyl) are attached to N with one H remaining.
quiz.mistake: Counts carbons rather than groups on N

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of aniline?
quiz.explain: Aniline is named benzenamine in IUPAC.
quiz.mistake: Confuses aniline with benzylamine

quiz.q: Why is the C–N–C angle in trimethylamine (108°) less than 109.5°?
options: Repulsion by the lone pair on nitrogen
quiz.explain: The lone pair occupies more space and compresses the bond angles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bulky groups always widen angles

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃?
quiz.explain: The NH₂ group is on C-2 of a three-carbon chain.
quiz.mistake: Puts the NH₂ on C-1

quiz.q: Which is a mixed (unsymmetrical) tertiary amine?
quiz.explain: The three groups on N are not all the same.
quiz.mistake: Picks a simple amine

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Amines are pyramidal in shape. Reason (R): The nitrogen atom in amines is sp³ hybridised with one lone pair.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Three bonding pairs and one lone pair around sp³ N give a pyramidal geometry.
quiz.mistake: Does not relate hybridisation to shape

teach.ask: Gappu sees (CH₃)₂NH: 'Is this a primary or secondary amine, and what's its IUPAC name?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Two methyls and one H on N makes it secondary: N-methylmethanamine!
teach.nudge: How many groups are on N, and how do you show the extra methyl in the name?

topics.title: Preparation of amines: reduction and ammonolysis

learn.hook: India's dye and drug industries make tonnes of aniline every year by reducing nitrobenzene with scrap iron and a little acid — a reaction you can write in one line.
points: Reduction of nitro compounds: H₂ with finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt, or metal + acid (Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl). C₆H₅NO₂ → C₆H₅NH₂. Fe scrap with HCl is preferred because the FeCl₂ formed is hydrolysed to release HCl, so only a small amount of acid is needed.

Ammonolysis of alkyl halides: R–X + NH₃ → R–NH₃⁺X⁻; the primary amine can react further, giving a mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and the quaternary salt R₄N⁺X⁻. With a large excess of ammonia, the primary amine is the main product. The free amine is liberated with a strong base: R–NH₃⁺X⁻ + NaOH → R–NH₂ + H₂O + NaX.
Order of reactivity of halides with amines: RI > RBr > RCl.
Reduction of nitriles with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni gives primary amines with one more carbon than the starting alkyl halide (ascent of the series): R–C≡N → R–CH₂–NH₂.
Reduction of amides with LiAlH₄ gives amines with the same number of carbons: R–CONH₂ → R–CH₂–NH₂.

example.q: Convert bromoethane into propan-1-amine.
steps: One carbon is added by the cyanide group

learn.reallife: Aniline from Indian chemical plants goes into making paracetamol, rubber chemicals and many dyes.

A mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and quaternary salts forms
quiz.explain: The primary amine is itself a nucleophile and reacts further with the alkyl halide.

options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because the nitrile carbon is retained, the amine has one more carbon than the alkyl halide used to make the nitrile.
quiz.mistake: Does not see where the extra carbon comes from

teach.ask: Gappu has nitrobenzene: 'How do factories turn it into aniline cheaply?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Reduce it with scrap iron and a little HCl — FeCl₂ even regenerates acid. Cheap and cheerful!
teach.nudge: Which metal and acid are used, and why is so little acid needed?

topics.title: Gabriel and Hoffmann methods; physical properties

learn.hook: Gabriel's method is the only clean way to get a pure primary amine from an alkyl halide, and Hoffmann's trick removes a carbon atom on the way.
points: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: phthalimide + ethanolic KOH → potassium phthalimide; heating with R–X gives N-alkylphthalimide; alkaline hydrolysis gives the pure primary amine. It cannot make aromatic primary amines because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

Hoffmann bromamide degradation: R–CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → R–NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O. The amine has one carbon fewer than the amide (the alkyl or aryl group migrates from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen).

Physical state and smell: lower aliphatic amines are gases with a fishy odour; primary amines with three or more carbons are liquids; higher ones are solids. Aniline is colourless when pure but darkens on storage due to atmospheric oxidation.

Lower aliphatic amines are water-soluble (H-bonding with water); solubility falls with larger alkyl groups. Amines are less polar than alcohols, so their H-bonds and water solubility are weaker than those of comparable alcohols.
Boiling points of isomeric amines: 1° > 2° > 3°. Tertiary amines have no H on nitrogen, so they cannot H-bond among themselves.

example.q: How many carbon atoms does the amine have when propanamide undergoes Hoffmann bromamide degradation?
steps: Hoffmann degradation removes the carbonyl carbon as carbonate

learn.reallife: Aqueous solutions of amines such as ethanolamine are used in Indian fertiliser plants and refineries to scrub CO₂ from gas streams; their water solubility comes from the same H-bonding studied here.

Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Without N–H, tertiary amines lack H-bonding between molecules.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect N–H to H-bonding

teach.ask: Gappu needs pure ethylamine: 'Why use Gabriel synthesis instead of reacting ethyl bromide with ammonia?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Ammonia gives a messy mixture, but Gabriel's phthalimide route gives only the pure primary amine!
teach.nudge: What problem does ammonolysis have, and what does Gabriel's method guarantee?

topics.title: Basic character of amines

learn.hook: Is dimethylamine a stronger base than trimethylamine? In the gas phase, no; in water, yes. Three competing effects decide the winner.
points: Amines are Lewis and Brønsted bases because of the lone pair on N: R–NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ R–NH₃⁺ + OH⁻; they react with acids to form salts, R–NH₂ + HX → R–NH₃⁺X⁻. Kb = [RNH₃⁺][OH⁻]/[RNH₂] and pKb = −log Kb: a smaller pKb means a stronger base.
Alkanamines are stronger bases than ammonia (pKb 4.75) because alkyl groups release electrons (+I). In the gas phase the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃.

In water, the order also depends on solvation of the ammonium ion (more N–H bonds → better H-bonding with water → more stable) and steric hindrance. Methyl amines: (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃. Ethyl amines: (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃.
pKb values: CH₃NH₂ 3.38, (CH₃)₂NH 3.27, (CH₃)₃N 4.22, C₂H₅NH₂ 3.29, (C₂H₅)₂NH 3.00, (C₂H₅)₃N 3.25, C₆H₅NH₂ 9.38, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ 4.70.

Aryl amines are much weaker bases than ammonia: the lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring (aniline has five resonance structures, the anilinium ion only two). Electron-donating groups (–CH₃, –OCH₃) increase and electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂, –SO₃H, –COOH, –X) decrease the basicity of aniline.

example.q: Arrange C₆H₅NH₂, C₂H₅NH₂, (C₂H₅)₂NH and NH₃ in decreasing order of basic strength in water.

learn.reallife: Many medicines (like the antihistamines in cold tablets) are amines sold as hydrochloride salts, because the salts dissolve better in water — a direct use of amine basicity.

The phenyl group is electron releasing

quiz.mistake: Thinks the phenyl group pushes electrons onto N

quiz.mistake: Confuses pKb with Kb

quiz.explain: With only one N–H in (C₂H₅)₃NH⁺, H-bonding with water is weaker, and steric hindrance adds to this.

quiz.q: Why is benzylamine (pKb 4.70) a much stronger base than aniline (pKb 9.38)?
options: Aniline has an electron-releasing CH₂ group
In benzylamine the NH₂ is on an sp³ CH₂, so its lone pair is not delocalised into the ring
Benzylamine is aromatic and aniline is not
quiz.explain: The CH₂ group isolates the lone pair from the ring's π system.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both have the same structure

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia. Reason (R): The electron-releasing methyl group increases electron density on nitrogen.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The +I effect of CH₃ makes the lone pair more available for protonation and stabilises the ammonium ion.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect +I effect to basicity

teach.ask: Gappu sniffs two bottles: 'Why is methylamine more basic than ammonia, but aniline less basic?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Methyl pushes electrons onto N (more basic); in aniline the lone pair spreads into the ring (less basic)!
teach.nudge: What does the methyl group do to the lone pair, and what happens to it in aniline?

topics.title: Alkylation, acylation, carbylamine, nitrous acid and Hinsberg tests

learn.hook: Is your unknown amine 1°, 2° or 3°? One sulphonyl chloride reagent and a little alkali can answer — Hinsberg's elegant test.
points: Alkylation: amines react with alkyl halides to form higher amines and finally quaternary ammonium salts. Acylation: 1° and 2° amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides or esters to form amides, usually in the presence of a base such as pyridine (stronger than the amine) to remove HCl: C₂H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → C₂H₅NHCOCH₃ + HCl. Benzoylation uses benzoyl chloride: CH₃NH₂ + C₆H₅COCl → C₆H₅CONHCH₃ (N-methylbenzamide) + HCl.

Carbylamine (isocyanide) test: 1° amines (aliphatic or aromatic) heated with chloroform and ethanolic KOH give foul-smelling isocyanides: R–NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → R–NC + 3KCl + 3H₂O. 2° and 3° amines do not respond.

Nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl): 1° aliphatic amines give unstable diazonium salts that decompose to alcohols with quantitative evolution of N₂ (used to estimate amino acids and proteins). 1° aromatic amines at 273–278 K give stable diazonium salts.

Hinsberg's reagent (benzenesulphonyl chloride, C₆H₅SO₂Cl): 1° amines give N-alkylbenzenesulphonamides, which have an acidic H on N and dissolve in alkali; 2° amines give N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamides with no H on N, insoluble in alkali; 3° amines do not react. (p-Toluenesulphonyl chloride is now often used instead.)
Lab safety: chloroform and isocyanides are toxic and foul-smelling; do the carbylamine test only in small amounts in a fume hood.

example.q: How would you distinguish ethanamine, N-ethylethanamine and N,N-diethylethanamine using Hinsberg's reagent?
steps: Ethanamine (1°) → sulphonamide with acidic N–H → dissolves in KOH
N-Ethylethanamine (2°) → sulphonamide with no N–H → insoluble in KOH
example.answer: 1° dissolves in alkali, 2° gives an alkali-insoluble product, 3° does not react

learn.reallife: Hinsberg and carbylamine tests are part of CBSE organic qualitative analysis; Indian forensic and quality-control labs use similar functional-group tests.

topics.title: Electrophilic substitution in aniline

learn.hook: Add bromine water to aniline and you instantly get a white precipitate with three bromines on the ring. Want just one? You must first tame the –NH₂ group.
points: –NH₂ is a strongly activating, ortho/para-directing group. Aniline with bromine water at room temperature gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

To get a monosubstituted product, protect –NH₂ by acetylation with acetic anhydride to form acetanilide; the lone pair on N is partly delocalised onto the acetyl oxygen, reducing activation. Bromination then gives mainly 4-bromoacetanilide, and hydrolysis gives 4-bromoaniline.

Direct nitration of aniline gives tarry oxidation products along with nitro derivatives. In strongly acidic medium aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing, so a large amount of m-nitroaniline forms (about 51% para, 47% meta, 2% ortho). Acetylation first gives mainly p-nitroaniline after hydrolysis.
Sulphonation: aniline + conc. H₂SO₄ forms anilinium hydrogensulphate, which on heating at 453–473 K gives p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid (sulphanilic acid), existing as a zwitterion.
Aniline does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions: it forms a salt with the Lewis acid AlCl₃, and the positively charged nitrogen strongly deactivates the ring.

example.q: How would you prepare 4-bromoaniline from aniline?
example.answer: Protect by acetylation, brominate, then hydrolyse

learn.reallife: Sulpha drugs, among the first antibacterial medicines and still made in India, are built on sulphanilic acid chemistry from aniline.

It forms a salt with AlCl₃, and the positive nitrogen deactivates the ring
quiz.explain: Aniline acts as a Lewis base towards AlCl₃.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is too reactive

quiz.q: What is the main product when acetanilide is brominated, followed by hydrolysis?
quiz.explain: Acetylation controls the reaction so mainly one Br enters at para.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of acetylation

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of p-nitroaniline is formed in the direct nitration of aniline (in acidic medium)?
quiz.explain: The products are about 51% para, 47% meta and 2% ortho.
quiz.mistake: Thinks para is the only product

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Acetanilide is less reactive than aniline towards electrophilic substitution. Reason (R): The lone pair on nitrogen in acetanilide is partly delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen of the acetyl group.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Less of the lone pair is available to the ring, so activation is reduced.
quiz.mistake: Does not explain why acetylation tames –NH₂

teach.ask: Gappu wants only one bromine on aniline: 'Bromine water gives three! How do I stop at one?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Acetylate to tame –NH₂, brominate to get mainly para, then hydrolyse back. One bromine, as ordered!
teach.nudge: What do you do to the –NH₂ group first, and how do you get it back at the end?

topics.title: Diazonium salts: preparation, properties and replacement reactions

learn.hook: Benzenediazonium chloride is a chemist's Swiss army knife: one intermediate that can become a halide, a nitrile, a phenol or plain benzene.
points: Diazotisation: C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl →(273–278 K) C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H₂O. Arenediazonium salts are stable for a short time in the cold because the positive charge is dispersed over the ring by resonance; aliphatic diazonium salts are highly unstable. They are used immediately.

Benzenediazonium chloride is a colourless crystalline solid, readily soluble in water, stable in the cold but reacting with water on warming; it decomposes easily when dry. Benzenediazonium fluoroborate is water-insoluble and stable at room temperature.
Sandmeyer reaction: CuCl/HCl, CuBr/HBr or CuCN/KCN replace –N₂⁺ by Cl, Br or CN. Gattermann reaction: copper powder with HCl or HBr does the same for Cl/Br (yields are usually better in Sandmeyer).

Other replacements: KI → iodobenzene; HBF₄ → fluoroborate, which on heating gives fluorobenzene + BF₃ + N₂ (Balz–Schiemann); H₃PO₂ or ethanol → benzene (reduction); warming with water (when the temperature rises to about 283 K) → phenol; fluoroborate + NaNO₂ with Cu, heat → nitrobenzene.

example.q: How would you convert aniline into benzonitrile?
steps: Diazotise: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻
example.answer: Diazotisation followed by Sandmeyer reaction with CuCN

learn.reallife: Indian manufacturers of dyes and agrochemicals use diazonium chemistry daily, always keeping the reaction vessels ice-cold for safety.

items.text: Aniline is diazotised at ___ K.
Replacement of –N₂⁺ by Cl using CuCl/HCl is the ___ reaction.
Using copper powder and HCl instead is the ___ reaction.
Arenediazonium salts are stabilised by ___.

quiz.q: At what temperature is diazotisation of aniline carried out?
quiz.explain: Diazonium salts decompose on warming, so the reaction is done in ice-cold conditions (0–5 °C).
quiz.mistake: Assumes room temperature

quiz.q: Why are arenediazonium salts more stable than alkyldiazonium salts?
options: They form hydrogen bonds with water
The positive charge is dispersed over the benzene ring by resonance
quiz.explain: Delocalisation of the charge stabilises arenediazonium ions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks alkyl groups stabilise the ion

quiz.q: Which reagent converts benzenediazonium chloride into benzene?
quiz.explain: H₃PO₂ (or ethanol) reduces the diazonium group, replacing it by H.
quiz.mistake: Picks a halide-introducing reagent

quiz.q: How is fluorobenzene prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
options: By forming the fluoroborate with HBF₄ and then heating
By treatment with KF in water
quiz.explain: Ar–N₂⁺BF₄⁻ decomposes on heating to Ar–F + BF₃ + N₂.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a Sandmeyer-type fluoride reagent

quiz.q: What is the Gattermann reaction?
options: Replacement of –N₂⁺ by CN using CuCN
Coupling of diazonium salt with phenol
Replacement of –N₂⁺ by Cl or Br using copper powder and the halogen acid
quiz.explain: It uses Cu powder with HCl/HBr; Sandmeyer uses cuprous salts.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Gattermann with Sandmeyer

quiz.q: Which statement about benzenediazonium chloride is correct?
options: It is a colourless, water-soluble solid that is stable only in the cold
It is stable when dry and hot
It is a stable red dye
quiz.explain: It decomposes on warming with water and explodes easily when dry.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is stable like an ordinary salt

quiz.q: What is formed when benzenediazonium chloride solution is warmed?
quiz.explain: Water replaces the diazonium group: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl.
quiz.mistake: Thinks warming gives back aniline

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Benzenediazonium fluoroborate can be stored at room temperature. Reason (R): Unlike the chloride, it is insoluble in water and fairly stable.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The fluoroborate's insolubility and stability are why it can be isolated and stored.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all diazonium salts are unstable

teach.ask: Gappu wants iodobenzene and benzonitrile from aniline: 'What's the common first step?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Diazotise aniline with NaNO₂ and HCl in the cold, then swap –N₂⁺ for I (KI) or CN (CuCN)!
teach.nudge: What is the first step, and at what temperature must it be done?

topics.title: Coupling reactions and diazonium salts in synthesis

learn.hook: The orange of a traditional bandhani dupatta may well come from an azo dye — made when a diazonium salt couples with a phenol.
points: In coupling reactions the diazo group is retained (–N=N–). Benzenediazonium chloride (a weak electrophile) attacks the para position of activated rings.

With phenol in alkaline medium: p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye. With aniline in mildly acidic medium: p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye. These are electrophilic substitution reactions, and the products are azo compounds with extended conjugation, hence coloured.

Diazonium salts let us introduce groups that cannot be put on a benzene ring directly: F, I, CN, OH (and H to remove a group), e.g. iodo and fluoro compounds cannot be made easily by direct halogenation, and CN cannot be introduced by nucleophilic substitution of chlorobenzene.

Classic conversions: aniline → 1,3,5-tribromobenzene (Br₂ water, then diazotise, then H₃PO₂); nitrobenzene → benzoic acid (reduce, diazotise, CuCN, hydrolyse); ethanoic acid → methanamine (via ethanamide and Hoffmann degradation).

Distinguishing tests: aniline vs benzylamine — with HNO₂ in the cold, aniline gives a diazonium salt that couples with β-naphthol to an orange dye, while benzylamine releases N₂; methylamine vs dimethylamine — only methylamine gives the carbylamine test.

example.q: Convert aniline into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.
steps: Treat with H₃PO₂ to replace –N₂⁺ by H → 1,3,5-tribromobenzene
example.answer: Brominate, diazotise, then reduce with H₃PO₂

learn.reallife: Azo dyes make up a large share of the dyes used by India's textile industry, from Surat to Tiruppur; regulators restrict certain azo dyes that can break down into harmful amines.

Diazotise aniline with NaNO₂/HCl at 273–278 K
Treat with CuCN/KCN to get benzonitrile
Hydrolyse with H₃O⁺ to get benzoic acid

quiz.q: What is formed when benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol in alkaline medium?
quiz.explain: Coupling at the para position of phenol gives an orange azo compound.
quiz.mistake: Thinks nitrogen is lost

quiz.q: What is the product of coupling benzenediazonium chloride with aniline in mildly acidic medium?
quiz.explain: The diazonium ion attacks the para position of aniline.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the amine nitrogen is attacked to form a different product

quiz.q: What kind of reaction is diazo coupling?
quiz.explain: The diazonium ion is an electrophile that attacks the activated ring.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the diazonium ion is a nucleophile

quiz.q: How can benzylamine be distinguished from aniline?
options: Only benzylamine gives the carbylamine test
With HNO₂ in the cold, only aniline gives a diazonium salt that couples with β-naphthol to give an orange dye
quiz.explain: Benzylamine is aliphatic-type and gives N₂; aniline gives a stable diazonium salt.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both are aromatic amines in behaviour

quiz.q: Which reagent sequence converts aniline into benzoic acid?
quiz.explain: The diazonium salt is converted into benzonitrile, which is hydrolysed to benzoic acid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks aniline can be oxidised directly to benzoic acid

quiz.q: Which group can be introduced on a benzene ring via a diazonium salt but not by direct electrophilic substitution?
quiz.explain: Direct fluorination is too violent; fluorobenzene is made via the fluoroborate.
quiz.mistake: Picks a group easily introduced directly

quiz.q: How can methylamine be distinguished from dimethylamine?
options: Litmus test: only methylamine is basic
Carbylamine test: only methylamine gives a foul-smelling isocyanide
quiz.explain: The carbylamine test is specific to primary amines.
quiz.mistake: Uses a test both pass

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Azo compounds are coloured. Reason (R): The –N=N– group connects two aromatic rings, creating an extended conjugated system.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Extended conjugation lets them absorb visible light, so they are coloured dyes.
quiz.mistake: Does not link conjugation with colour

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do diazonium salts make dyes, and why are those dyes coloured?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The diazonium ion couples at the para position of phenol or aniline, making –N=N– azo dyes with extended conjugation — colourful!
teach.nudge: What does the diazonium salt react with, and what structural feature makes the product coloured?

topics.title: Carbohydrates: definition and classification

learn.hook: Roti, rice, gur, the cotton of your kurta and the paper of your notebook: all carbohydrates. Chemically they are far more interesting than 'just sugar'.
points: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give such units on hydrolysis. Many fit Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ, but not all (rhamnose, C₆H₁₂O₅, is a carbohydrate; acetic acid, C₂H₄O₂, fits the formula but is not).
Sugars are sweet, crystalline and water-soluble (monosaccharides, oligosaccharides); polysaccharides like starch and cellulose are non-sugars — not sweet.

Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further (glucose, fructose, ribose). Oligosaccharides give 2–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose) give two. Polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen, gums) give a large number.
Reducing sugars reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent: all monosaccharides, and disaccharides with a free aldehyde or ketone group (maltose, lactose). Sucrose is non-reducing.
Monosaccharides are aldoses (with –CHO) or ketoses (with C=O), named by carbon count: triose, tetrose, pentose, hexose. Glucose is an aldohexose; fructose is a ketohexose.

example.q: Classify glucose, sucrose and starch, and say which are reducing sugars.
steps: Starch: polysaccharide (many glucose units) — non-reducing, not a sugar

learn.reallife: India is one of the world's biggest producers of sugarcane; the sucrose from it goes into sugar, gur and khandsari, while its fibre is cellulose.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-reducing sugar?
quiz.explain: In sucrose, the reducing groups of glucose (C1) and fructose (C2) are tied up in the glycosidic bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every disaccharide is non-reducing

quiz.q: Glucose is classified as:
quiz.explain: Glucose has six carbons and an aldehyde group.
quiz.mistake: Confuses glucose with fructose

quiz.q: How many monosaccharide units does an oligosaccharide give on hydrolysis?
quiz.explain: Oligosaccharides give two to ten units; disaccharides give two.
quiz.mistake: Confuses oligo- with polysaccharides

quiz.q: Which statement about the formula Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ is correct?
options: Not all carbohydrates fit it, and not all compounds fitting it are carbohydrates
Every compound fitting it is a carbohydrate
quiz.explain: Rhamnose (C₆H₁₂O₅) is a carbohydrate but does not fit; acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂) fits but is not a carbohydrate.
quiz.mistake: Takes the 'hydrates of carbon' idea literally

quiz.q: Which is a ketohexose?
quiz.explain: Fructose has six carbons with a ketone group at C-2.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up aldoses and ketoses

quiz.q: Why is starch called a non-sugar?
options: It is not sweet in taste
quiz.explain: Polysaccharides such as starch are not sweet, so they are called non-sugars, although they are made of glucose units.
quiz.mistake: Thinks starch is made of something other than glucose

quiz.q: Which disaccharide is a reducing sugar?
quiz.explain: Maltose has a free aldehyde group at C-1 of its second glucose unit.
quiz.mistake: Picks sucrose or a polysaccharide

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Glucose reduces Tollens' reagent. Reason (R): Glucose is a monosaccharide with a free aldehyde group.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: All monosaccharides are reducing sugars; the aldehyde group of glucose is oxidised.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the free carbonyl group with reducing power

teach.ask: Gappu nibbles gur: 'How do chemists classify carbohydrates, and what makes a sugar reducing?'
teach.praise: Chirp! By how many units they give on hydrolysis, and a free aldehyde or ketone group makes a sugar reducing!
teach.nudge: What decides the class, and what group must be free for a sugar to be reducing?

topics.title: Glucose: preparation and open-chain structure

learn.hook: Glucose drips at every hospital, glucose biscuits in school tiffins — but how did chemists work out its structure without modern instruments? With a few clever reactions.
points: Preparation: boiling sucrose with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ in alcoholic solution gives glucose and fructose. Commercially, starch is hydrolysed by boiling with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under 2–3 atm pressure: (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ + nH₂O → nC₆H₁₂O₆.
Molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Prolonged heating with HI gives n-hexane, so the six carbons are in a straight chain.

Glucose forms an oxime with hydroxylamine and a cyanohydrin with HCN, so it has a carbonyl group. Bromine water (a mild oxidant) converts it into gluconic acid, a six-carbon acid, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde group.
Acetylation with acetic anhydride gives glucose pentaacetate: five –OH groups, on different carbons since the compound is stable.
Nitric acid oxidises glucose (and gluconic acid) to saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid, showing a primary alcohol (–CH₂OH) group. Open-chain structure: CHO–(CHOH)₄–CH₂OH.

example.q: Which reaction of glucose shows that it contains an aldehyde group rather than a ketone group?
steps: Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent
It oxidises glucose to gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid with six carbons
Only an aldehyde can be oxidised to an acid without losing carbon
example.answer: Oxidation by bromine water to gluconic acid

learn.reallife: Glucose for India's ORS sachets and hospital drips is made mostly by hydrolysing maize or tapioca starch.

games.title: Reaction of glucose ↔ what it shows
pairs: Six carbons in a straight chain

games.title: Commercial glucose from starch

quiz.q: What does the formation of n-hexane on heating glucose with HI show?
options: All six carbon atoms are linked in a straight chain
quiz.explain: HI reduces glucose completely, and the straight-chain hydrocarbon reveals the unbranched carbon skeleton.
quiz.mistake: Links the HI reaction to functional groups

quiz.q: What is formed when glucose reacts with bromine water?
quiz.explain: Bromine water oxidises only the –CHO group to –COOH.
quiz.mistake: Confuses mild and strong oxidation

quiz.q: What does the formation of saccharic acid with nitric acid show?
options: Glucose contains a primary alcohol group
quiz.explain: Both ends (–CHO and –CH₂OH) are oxidised to –COOH, giving a dicarboxylic acid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it shows the aldehyde group only

quiz.q: How many –OH groups does glucose pentaacetate show glucose to have?
quiz.explain: Five acetyl groups attach, one to each –OH.
quiz.mistake: Counts all oxygen atoms

quiz.q: Which reagent forms an oxime with glucose, showing a carbonyl group?
quiz.explain: C=O + NH₂OH → C=N–OH (oxime).

quiz.q: How is glucose obtained commercially?
options: By hydrolysis of starch with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under pressure
quiz.explain: Starch from maize or potatoes is boiled with dilute acid under pressure.
quiz.mistake: Confuses preparation with other reactions

quiz.q: What products are obtained when sucrose is boiled with dilute HCl in alcoholic solution?
quiz.explain: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sucrose with maltose or lactose

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Glucose pentaacetate is a stable compound. Reason (R): The five –OH groups of glucose are attached to different carbon atoms.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: If two –OH groups were on the same carbon, the compound would lose water; stability shows they are on different carbons.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why stability matters

teach.ask: Gappu is a detective: 'How did chemists prove glucose has an aldehyde group and a straight chain?'
teach.praise: Chirp! HI gives n-hexane (straight chain) and bromine water gives gluconic acid (aldehyde). Case closed!
teach.nudge: Which reaction shows the straight chain, and which one shows the aldehyde?

topics.title: Configuration and cyclic structure of glucose

learn.hook: Glucose crystallises in two different forms with different melting points. The open-chain formula cannot explain this — a ring can.
points: D and L describe configuration relative to glyceraldehyde: if the –OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon (C-5 in glucose) is on the right in the Fischer projection, the sugar is D (like (+)-glyceraldehyde). D/L has no link to the sign of rotation, (+) or (−). Natural glucose is D-(+)-glucose.

Facts the open-chain structure cannot explain: glucose does not give Schiff's test or form a hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO₃; glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine (no free –CHO); and glucose exists in two crystalline forms, α and β.
α-D-glucose (m.p. 419 K) crystallises from a concentrated solution at 303 K; β-D-glucose (m.p. 423 K) from a hot saturated solution at 371 K.

The –OH at C-5 adds to the –CHO group, forming a cyclic hemiacetal with a six-membered ring (pyranose form, like pyran). C-1 becomes a new asymmetric centre: the anomeric carbon. The α and β forms, differing only at C-1, are called anomers.
Haworth projections draw the pyranose ring as a flat hexagon; in α-D-glucopyranose the C-1 –OH points down (opposite side to the –CH₂OH), and in β it points up.

example.q: Why does glucose not react with NaHSO₃ although it is an aldehyde?
steps: In solution, glucose exists almost entirely as a cyclic hemiacetal
The aldehyde group is tied up in the ring (C-1 bonded to the C-5 oxygen)
So typical aldehyde reactions like NaHSO₃ addition and Schiff's test do not occur
example.answer: Because its –CHO group is locked in the cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose) form

learn.reallife: Diabetes test strips used across India detect glucose through enzyme reactions that work on its cyclic β form in blood.

quiz.q: Which observation cannot be explained by the open-chain structure of glucose?

quiz.q: What are α- and β-D-glucose called?
quiz.explain: They differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon (C-1).

quiz.q: Which carbon of glucose is called the anomeric carbon?

quiz.q: What is the melting point of α-D-glucose?

quiz.q: Why is the six-membered ring form of glucose called a pyranose?

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine. Reason (R): In glucose pentaacetate there is no free aldehyde group.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu sees two kinds of glucose crystals: 'How can one sugar exist in two forms?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Glucose forms a ring, making C-1 a new stereocentre, so α and β anomers exist!
teach.nudge: What happens when glucose forms a ring, and which carbon becomes special?

topics.title: Fructose and disaccharides

learn.hook: Table sugar turns 'left-handed' when you boil it with a little acid. That's why honey-like syrup made from sugar is called invert sugar.
points: Fructose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a ketohexose with the ketone at C-2; it belongs to the D-series and is laevorotatory: D-(−)-fructose. It forms a five-membered ring (furanose, like furan) by addition of the C-5 –OH to the C-2 carbonyl, giving α and β anomers.
In disaccharides, two monosaccharides are joined by a glycosidic linkage (an oxide bridge formed with loss of water).

Sucrose: α-D-glucose (C-1) linked to β-D-fructose (C-2); both reducing groups are used, so it is non-reducing. Sucrose is dextrorotatory, but hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose (+52.5°) and D-(−)-fructose (−92.4°), and the mixture is laevorotatory. This change of sign is inversion; the product is invert sugar.
Maltose: two α-D-glucose units joined C-1 to C-4; the second unit has a free aldehyde at C-1 (in solution), so maltose is reducing.
Lactose (milk sugar): β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose joined C-1 (galactose) to C-4 (glucose); it is a reducing sugar.

example.q: Why is sucrose called a non-reducing sugar, while maltose is reducing?
steps: Sucrose: C-1 of glucose bonds to C-2 of fructose — both reducing groups are used up
Maltose: C-1 of one glucose bonds to C-4 of the other — C-1 of the second glucose stays free
A free C-1 (hemiacetal) can open to –CHO and reduce Fehling's solution
example.answer: Sucrose has no free reducing group; maltose has one

learn.reallife: Indian sweet-makers use 'invert syrup' made by heating sugar with a little citric acid (nimbu) to stop sweets from crystallising.

quiz.q: Why is the hydrolysis product of sucrose called invert sugar?
options: It is formed by reversing photosynthesis
The sign of rotation changes from dextro (+) to laevo (−)
quiz.explain: Fructose (−92.4°) outweighs glucose (+52.5°), so the mixture becomes laevorotatory.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'invert' refers to molecular structure

quiz.q: Which monosaccharides are obtained by hydrolysis of lactose?
quiz.explain: Lactose, milk sugar, is made of galactose and glucose.
quiz.mistake: Confuses lactose with sucrose

quiz.q: Which linkage joins the two glucose units in maltose?
options: C-1 of one α-D-glucose to C-4 of the other
quiz.explain: Maltose has an α(1→4) glycosidic linkage.
quiz.mistake: Uses the sucrose linkage

quiz.q: What size of ring does fructose form?
quiz.explain: The C-5 –OH bonds to C-2, giving a ring of four carbons and one oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Assumes fructose rings like glucose

quiz.q: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar?
options: It has no carbonyl groups at all in its units
The reducing groups of both glucose (C-1) and fructose (C-2) are involved in the glycosidic bond
quiz.explain: No free hemiacetal or hemiketal group remains to open up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sucrose has no glucose

quiz.q: What is a glycosidic linkage?
options: A peptide bond between amino acids
An oxide (ether-type) linkage joining two monosaccharide units, formed with loss of water
quiz.explain: The C–O–C bridge links monosaccharides in di- and polysaccharides.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with bonds in proteins or nucleic acids

quiz.q: What is the sign of specific rotation of D-fructose?
quiz.explain: D-fructose is D-(−)-fructose; the D refers to configuration, not rotation.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all D sugars are dextrorotatory

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Maltose is a reducing sugar. Reason (R): Maltose is composed of two α-D-glucose units.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the reason maltose is reducing is that one glucose unit has a free C-1 (hemiacetal) group, not merely that it contains glucose (sucrose also contains glucose).
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sugar containing glucose is reducing

teach.ask: Gappu stirs sugar in acid: 'Why does sucrose become invert sugar, and why isn't sucrose reducing?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Hydrolysis gives glucose and fructose, flipping the rotation to laevo; and sucrose's C1–C2 link leaves no free reducing group!
teach.nudge: What does sucrose split into, and why does the rotation change sign?

topics.title: Polysaccharides and importance of carbohydrates

learn.hook: Cows thrive on grass but we cannot digest it, though both grass (cellulose) and rice (starch) are made of glucose. The difference is a tiny twist at one carbon.
points: Starch, the main storage polysaccharide of plants, is a polymer of α-glucose with two components: amylose (15–20%), water-soluble, an unbranched chain of 200–1000 α-D-(+)-glucose units joined C-1 to C-4; and amylopectin (80–85%), water-insoluble and branched, with C-1 to C-4 chains and C-1 to C-6 branch points.

Cellulose, the main component of plant cell walls and the most abundant organic substance in the plant kingdom, is a straight-chain polymer of β-D-glucose joined C-1 to C-4. Humans cannot digest it; ruminants can, with the help of microbes in their gut.

Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals (animal starch), found in liver, muscles and brain. Its structure resembles amylopectin but is more highly branched; it is broken down to glucose when the body needs energy.

Importance: carbohydrates are essential food and energy sources; they store energy as starch (plants) and glycogen (animals); cellulose builds plant cell walls. Wood and cotton (cellulose) are used for furniture, clothes, paper, lacquers and in breweries. Honey has long been used in Ayurveda. D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose are parts of nucleic acids.

example.q: Why can cattle digest cellulose while humans cannot, though both starch and cellulose are made of glucose?
steps: Starch has α-glycosidic links; cellulose has β-glycosidic links
Human digestive enzymes break α-links but not β-links
Microbes in the gut of ruminants produce enzymes that break β-links
example.answer: Because of the β-glycosidic linkage, which only microbial enzymes in ruminants can break

learn.reallife: Cricketers 'carbo-load' with rice and roti before long matches so that their muscles store extra glycogen for energy late in the innings.

teach.praise: Chirp! Starch uses α-glucose (some branched), cellulose β-glucose in straight chains — and only cows can digest the β-links!

topics.title: Amino acids

learn.hook: Dal, paneer, eggs and soya chunks are prized for protein — but your body really wants the amino acids inside, especially the ones it cannot make itself.
points: α-Amino acids have –NH₂ and –COOH on the same carbon: R–CH(NH₂)–COOH. The side chain R decides the amino acid (glycine R = H, alanine R = CH₃).

Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from food (e.g. valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, arginine, histidine); non-essential ones (e.g. glycine, alanine) can be made by the body.
Neutral amino acids have equal numbers of amino and carboxyl groups; acidic ones have more carboxyl groups (aspartic acid, glutamic acid); basic ones have more amino groups (lysine, arginine).
In water, the –COOH loses a proton and –NH₂ gains it, forming a zwitterion H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻. Amino acids are therefore amphoteric, crystalline, water-soluble, high-melting solids that behave like salts.
All α-amino acids except glycine are optically active, because the α-carbon is asymmetric; most naturally occurring ones have the L-configuration.

example.q: Why is glycine optically inactive while alanine is optically active?
steps: Glycine: H₂N–CH₂–COOH — the α-carbon carries two H atoms
Alanine: H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COOH — the α-carbon has four different groups
Only alanine has an asymmetric carbon
example.answer: Glycine has no asymmetric carbon; alanine does

learn.reallife: India's Poshan Abhiyaan and the PM POSHAN mid-day meal scheme add pulses and eggs to diets so children get enough essential amino acids such as lysine.

topics.title: Peptides and levels of protein structure

learn.hook: Hair, silk and muscle are fibrous proteins; insulin and egg albumin are globular. The difference begins with how chains fold.
points: A peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms when the –COOH of one amino acid reacts with the –NH₂ of another, with loss of water. Two amino acids make a dipeptide (e.g. glycylalanine, Gly-Ala). More than ten make a polypeptide; a polypeptide with more than a hundred residues and molar mass above 10,000 u is called a protein.

Fibrous proteins have long parallel chains held by hydrogen and disulphide bonds; they are usually water-insoluble (keratin in hair, wool and silk; myosin in muscles). Globular proteins have chains coiled into spheres; they are usually water-soluble (insulin, albumins).
Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids. Any change in it creates a different protein.

Secondary structure is the shape of the chain: α-helix (a right-handed coil in which each –NH group is H-bonded to a C=O of an adjacent turn) or β-pleated sheet (chains stretched almost fully and laid side by side, held by intermolecular H-bonds).

Tertiary structure is the overall folding of the chain, held by hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals forces and electrostatic attractions. Quaternary structure is the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits).

example.q: Draw the dipeptide glycylalanine and mark the peptide bond.
steps: The –COOH of glycine reacts with the –NH₂ of alanine, losing H₂O
Product: H₂N–CH₂–CO–NH–CH(CH₃)–COOH; the –CO–NH– link is the peptide bond

learn.reallife: Silk from Mysuru and Kanchipuram owes its strength to β-pleated sheets of the protein fibroin, while keratin's α-helices give wool its stretch.

topics.title: Denaturation of proteins and enzymes

learn.hook: Boil an egg and the clear white turns opaque forever; add nimbu to hot milk and it curdles into paneer. Both are proteins losing their shape.
points: Denaturation: a change in temperature or pH disturbs the hydrogen bonds of a native protein, so the globules unfold and helices uncoil; the protein loses its biological activity. Secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed, but the primary structure stays intact.
Examples: coagulation of egg white on boiling; curdling of milk, caused by lactic acid formed by bacteria (or by added acids like lemon juice).

Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins. They are very specific to their substrate and reaction and are usually named after the substrate or reaction with the suffix -ase: maltase converts maltose into glucose; invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose; enzymes catalysing oxidation–reduction are oxidoreductases.

Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy of the reaction. For example, the hydrolysis of sucrose has a much lower activation energy with invertase than with acid alone, so it happens fast at body temperature.
Being proteins, enzymes are denatured by high temperatures and extreme pH; this is why fever or strong acids disrupt their action.

example.q: Why does a boiled egg not become raw again on cooling?
steps: Heating breaks the H-bonds holding the albumin's folded secondary and tertiary structures
The chains unfold and tangle irreversibly (coagulation)
The primary sequence remains, but the native shape is lost for good
example.answer: Because heat denatures the protein irreversibly, destroying its secondary and tertiary structures

learn.reallife: Paneer is made in Indian homes by curdling hot milk with lemon juice or vinegar — a delicious denaturation of milk proteins.

topics.title: Vitamins: classification, sources and deficiency diseases

learn.hook: Sailors once died of scurvy on long voyages; a few amlas or lemons would have saved them. Vitamins are needed in tiny amounts, but missing them causes real disease.
points: Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health; their deficiency causes specific diseases. Most cannot be made by our bodies (plants can make almost all).

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) dissolve in fats and oils and are stored in the liver and adipose (fat-storing) tissue. Water-soluble vitamins (B group and C) must be supplied regularly, because they are excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin B₁₂).

A: fish liver oil, carrots, butter, milk → xerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea) and night blindness. D: sunlight, fish, egg yolk → rickets (children) and osteomalacia (soft bones and joint pain in adults). E: vegetable oils like wheat germ and sunflower oil → fragile red blood cells and muscular weakness. K: green leafy vegetables → increased blood clotting time.

B₁ (thiamine): yeast, milk, green vegetables, cereals → beri-beri (loss of appetite, retarded growth). B₂ (riboflavin): milk, egg white, liver, kidney → cheilosis (cracks at the corners of the mouth and lips), digestive disorders, burning skin. B₆ (pyridoxine): yeast, milk, egg yolk, cereals, grams → convulsions.
B₁₂: meat, fish, egg, curd → pernicious anaemia (red blood cells deficient in haemoglobin). C (ascorbic acid): citrus fruits, amla, green leafy vegetables → scurvy (bleeding gums).

example.q: Why must vitamin C be included in the diet every day, while vitamin A need not be?
steps: Excess is excreted in urine and is not stored
Vitamin A is fat-soluble and is stored in the liver and fat tissue
example.answer: Because water-soluble vitamin C cannot be stored, but fat-soluble vitamin A can

learn.reallife: Amla, rich in vitamin C, has been prized in Indian diets for centuries; the national vitamin A supplementation programme for children helps prevent night blindness.

quiz.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes scurvy?
quiz.explain: Lack of ascorbic acid causes scurvy, with bleeding gums.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up vitamin deficiency diseases

quiz.q: Which vitamin's deficiency causes rickets in children?
quiz.explain: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets (bone deformities) in children and osteomalacia in adults.
quiz.mistake: Confuses vitamin D with others

quiz.q: Which water-soluble vitamin can be stored in the body?
quiz.explain: Unlike other water-soluble vitamins, B₁₂ can be stored.
quiz.mistake: Thinks no water-soluble vitamin is stored

quiz.q: Which group of vitamins is fat-soluble?
quiz.explain: These dissolve in fats and are stored in the liver and adipose tissue.
quiz.mistake: Includes B or C

quiz.q: Deficiency of vitamin B₁ causes:
quiz.explain: Thiamine deficiency causes beri-beri (loss of appetite, retarded growth).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up B-group vitamins

quiz.q: Which vitamin deficiency increases blood clotting time?
quiz.explain: Vitamin K is needed for normal blood clotting.
quiz.mistake: Confuses K with E

quiz.q: Which disease is caused by deficiency of vitamin B₆?
quiz.explain: Pyridoxine (B₆) deficiency causes convulsions.
quiz.mistake: Gives the B₂ deficiency disease

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

quiz.mistake: Does not link excretion with the need for regular intake

teach.praise: Chirp! Vitamins prevent deficiency diseases; A, D, E, K are fat-soluble and stored, while B and C are water-soluble and must be eaten daily!
teach.nudge: What happens without vitamins, and which ones can the body store?

topics.title: Nucleic acids: composition and structure

learn.hook: Every one of your cells holds about two metres of DNA, coiled into a space smaller than a full stop. Its secret is a simple double helix.
points: Nucleic acids are long polymers of nucleotides (polynucleotides). Complete hydrolysis gives a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogenous bases.
DNA contains β-D-2-deoxyribose; RNA contains β-D-ribose. DNA bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). RNA has A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine.

A nucleoside is a base attached to C-1′ of the sugar. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with a phosphate group attached at C-5′ of the sugar. Nucleotides join by phosphodiester linkages between C-5′ and C-3′ of neighbouring sugars.
DNA (Watson–Crick model) is a double helix of two antiparallel strands held by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.
RNA is usually single-stranded (it can fold back on itself). Three main types are messenger RNA (m-RNA), ribosomal RNA (r-RNA) and transfer RNA (t-RNA).

example.q: If one strand of DNA has the sequence A-T-G-C-C-A, what is the complementary strand?
steps: A pairs with T and T with A
G pairs with C and C with G

learn.reallife: India's Genome India project has sequenced the DNA of thousands of Indians to map genetic diversity — all built on reading A, T, G and C.

topics.title: Biological functions of nucleic acids and DNA fingerprinting

learn.hook: Indian investigators have used DNA evidence to identify victims of disasters and to solve crimes. The idea rests on one fact: your base sequence is uniquely yours.
points: DNA is the chemical basis of heredity: it stores genetic information and is responsible for keeping the identity of a species over millions of years.
DNA can copy itself (replication) during cell division, so identical DNA passes to daughter cells.
Proteins are synthesised by the various RNA molecules in the cell, but the message for making a particular protein is present in DNA.
DNA fingerprinting: the sequence of bases in DNA is unique for each person (except identical twins), is the same in every cell and cannot be altered by any known treatment.

Uses: identifying criminals in forensic labs, settling questions of paternity, identifying bodies after accidents by comparing DNA with that of parents or children, and studying evolutionary relationships.

example.q: How does DNA fingerprinting help identify a victim after a disaster?
steps: Collect DNA from the possible parents or children
Compare the base-sequence patterns; close relatives share many of them
example.answer: By matching DNA patterns with those of close relatives

learn.reallife: The Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD) in Hyderabad, set up after pioneering work by Dr Lalji Singh, provides DNA testing for courts and investigations in India.

The breakdown of DNA to bases

quiz.mistake: Confuses replication with protein synthesis

quiz.q: Which is NOT a use of DNA fingerprinting?
options: Measuring a person's blood sugar level
quiz.explain: Blood sugar is measured chemically, not by DNA analysis.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DNA tests measure everything

quiz.q: Where is the message for synthesising a particular protein stored?
quiz.explain: DNA holds the code; RNA molecules use it to build proteins.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the message is in t-RNA

quiz.q: Why can DNA fingerprinting identify a person from a hair root or a drop of blood?
options: DNA changes from tissue to tissue
Every cell of a person carries the same DNA sequence
Hair and blood have special DNA
quiz.explain: The sequence is identical in all body cells, so any sample works.
quiz.mistake: Thinks different tissues have different DNA

quiz.q: Assertion (A): DNA fingerprinting is used to settle paternity disputes. Reason (R): A child inherits DNA from both parents.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because half of the child's DNA comes from each parent, patterns can be matched.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why inheritance allows matching

teach.ask: Gappu watches a crime show: 'How does DNA fingerprinting catch the culprit?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Each person's DNA base sequence is unique and the same in every cell, so a sample can be matched to them!
teach.nudge: What is special about each person's DNA that allows identification?

topics.title: Hormones

learn.hook: The 'adrenaline rush' before a big match and the insulin that millions of Indians with diabetes rely on are both hormones — chemical messengers in the blood.
points: Hormones are intercellular messengers produced by endocrine glands and released directly into the bloodstream, which carries them to their target sites. Chemically they are steroids (oestrogens, androgens), polypeptides (insulin, endorphins) or amino acid derivatives (epinephrine, norepinephrine).
Insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose within narrow limits: insulin is released when blood glucose rises rapidly and lowers it; glucagon raises blood glucose.
Epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine mediate responses to external stimuli. Growth hormones and sex hormones control growth and development.

Thyroxine, made by the thyroid gland, is an iodinated derivative of the amino acid tyrosine. Too little causes hypothyroidism (lethargy, obesity); too much causes hyperthyroidism. Low dietary iodine leads to hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, prevented by adding iodide to table salt.

Adrenal cortex steroids: glucocorticoids control carbohydrate metabolism, moderate inflammation and are involved in stress responses; mineralocorticoids control the kidney's excretion of water and salt. Failure of the adrenal cortex causes Addison's disease. Sex hormones: testosterone (male), estradiol (female) and progesterone (prepares the uterus for implantation of the fertilised egg).

example.q: Why is iodised salt used throughout India?
steps: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine
Low dietary iodine causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre)
Adding iodide to common salt ensures everyone gets enough iodine
example.answer: To prevent iodine deficiency, hypothyroidism and goitre

learn.reallife: India's National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme made iodised salt widespread, sharply cutting goitre cases in hilly and other iodine-poor regions.

quiz.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
quiz.explain: Insulin is released when blood glucose rises and brings it back down.
quiz.mistake: Confuses insulin with glucagon

quiz.q: Thyroxine is an iodinated derivative of which amino acid?
quiz.explain: Thyroxine is made from tyrosine with iodine atoms attached.
quiz.mistake: Picks a common but wrong amino acid

quiz.q: What is the chemical nature of insulin?
quiz.explain: Insulin is a polypeptide hormone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all hormones are steroids

quiz.q: Which disease results from failure of the adrenal cortex?
quiz.explain: Insufficient adrenal cortex hormones cause Addison's disease.
quiz.mistake: Confuses hormone disorders with vitamin deficiencies

quiz.q: What is the role of glucocorticoids?
options: They lower blood glucose like insulin
They control salt and water excretion only
They control carbohydrate metabolism, moderate inflammation and respond to stress
quiz.explain: Glucocorticoids are adrenal cortex steroids with these roles.
quiz.mistake: Confuses them with mineralocorticoids

quiz.q: Which hormones belong to the steroid class?
quiz.explain: Sex hormones are steroids.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up hormone classes

quiz.q: What is the effect of deficiency of thyroxine?
quiz.explain: Low thyroxine slows metabolism.
quiz.mistake: Gives the effect of excess thyroxine

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Hormones act at sites far from the glands that make them. Reason (R): Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The blood carries hormones to distant target organs.
quiz.mistake: Does not link secretion into blood with distant action

teach.ask: Gappu feels nervous before an exam: 'What are hormones, and which one is racing through me right now?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Hormones are chemical messengers from endocrine glands carried by blood — and adrenaline is my exam-day rush!
teach.nudge: What are hormones, how do they travel, and which one handles sudden stress?
